question_text: Which of the following is not a concussion?
explanation:
Rugger jersey spine is not a concussion. It is an X-ray finding, which is characteristic of hyperparathyroidism seen in renal osteodystrophy. However, railway spine, commotio cordis, and Berin edema are concussions.

A concussion is a violent jerk or shock, or the condition which results from such an injury. The following are concussions of different organs:

  1. Railway spine: It can occur without any evidence of external injury to the spinal column. It results from a forcible blow on the back, a fall from height, or a bullet injury. It is commonly seen in railway accidents and motor car collisions, also known as the concussion of the spine.
  2. Berlin’s edema: It is the edema around the macular region of the retina, caused by a severe blow to the eyeball. It is also known as the concussion of the retina.
  3. Commotio Cordis: It is the damage to the heart that is frequently fatal. It is due to a sharp non-penetrating blow to the adjacent body surface. Involves young (8-18 Y; average age is 15 Y). Predominantly male, athletes. Sudden blunt trauma to the anterior chest results in death from ventricular fibrillation

References: Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology: Principles & Practice 5th Edition, Page No. 287

question_text: During a postmortem examination of a 24-year-old man, ladder rung tears were seen in the aorta. What is the likely mechanism of the sustained injury?
explanation:
Ladder rung tears are the multiple parallel intimal tears of the aorta, that are seen in deceleration trauma.

When the thorax is suddenly decelerated, the heart – being relatively mobile in the chest – attempts to continue in the original direction. This causes severe traction on the root of the heart, and a common sequel is complete or partial rupture of the aorta in the descending part of its arch.

The mechanism is a sudden rise in intra-aortic pressure. Sometimes, there may be multiple parallel intimal tears near the main transection, the so-called ‘ladder-rung tears. In deceleration trauma, these incomplete tears, which affect only the intima and inner media, may be found without major transection; where death is delayed, false aneurysms and dissections may be diagnosed on aortograms

Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, Page No. 222

question_text: A deceased male was brought to the morgue for a post-mortem examination. His relatives reported that he had a tattoo over his skin, which was not found on examination. Which of the following structures would you examine?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The lymph nodes should be examined in this case.
  • Some amount of material or dye used for creating tattoo marks is transported through lymph to the regional lymph nodes. Hence cases where a tattoo mark has disappeared naturally or has been removed, the lymph nodes must be examined.

Migration of tattoo pigment particles from the dermis to lymph nodes can mimic other disease processes at surgery and on imaging. The gross black appearance of a sentinel lymph node is highly suggestive of metastatic disease when lymph node dissection is performed for melanoma treatment.

question_text: A lineman working on an electric pole suffered an electrical injury. Which of the following statements is false about this condition?
option_a: The most common cause of death is ventricular fibrillation ending in cardiac arrest
option_b: The most dangerous contact path is entry through the right hand and exit through the feet
option_c: With repeated exposure, tolerance develops to electric shock
option_d: Direct current is more damaging than alternating current
explanation:
Alternating current is more damaging than direct current.

The most common is the passage of a current across the heart, usually when a hand is brought into contact with a live conductor, and the body is earthed either through the feet or the opposite hand.

It has been claimed that the most dangerous current path is contact with the right hand and exit through the feet, as this causes the maximum (up to 8.5 per cent) of the total body current to flow through the heart when compared with head to feet (up to 5.9 per cent), left hand to feet (up to 5.1 per cent), hand to hand (up to 4.4 per cent) or foot to foot (up to 0.4 per cent).

The fatal process is a cardiac dysrhythmia, usually a ventricular fibrillation ending in asystole.

Rarely, the current passes through the head and neck, usually in circumstances when the head of a worker on overhead power lines comes into contact with the conductor. In such instances, there may be a direct effect on the brainstem so that cardiac or respiratory centres are paralysed.

Most deaths from electricity are from cardiac arrhythmias, usually, ventricular fibrillation ending in cardiac arrest.

It is commonly said that tolerance can be gained to electric shock and that professional electricians often work on live 240 V conductors with impunity.

There is no doubt that direct current (d.c.) is less dangerous than alternating current (a.c.); Alternating current is four to six times as likely to cause death, partly because of the 'let-go' or 'hold-on' effect, which is the result of tetanoid muscle spasm and prevents the victim from releasing the live conductor. Alternating current is also much more likely than direct current to cause cardiac arrhythmias.

Note: As per Dr. Krishan Vij's TB of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology: Principles and Practice, 5th edition (Page No. 177), the most dangerous path of electric current to affect the heart is from the left arm to the opposite leg.

Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th edition, Page No. 326

question_text: Identify the given image
explanation:
Marbling refers to a characteristic post-mortem change observed in decomposing bodies. It results from the breakdown of hemoglobin in the blood and the subsequent infiltration of decomposed blood into the subcutaneous veins. The veins become prominent, forming a web-like pattern of greenish-black or purplish discoloration, resembling a marbled appearance.

Mechanism: Decomposition bacteria produce gases, increasing intravascular pressure, which forces hemolyzed blood into the superficial veins.

Appearance: The pattern of marbling typically follows the venous structures, especially in areas with thin skin like the thighs, abdomen, and arms.

In the given scenario, the image likely depicts this characteristic marbling pattern, identifying it as a post-mortem change due to decomposition.

Rule Out

Post-mortem lividity (a):

Post-mortem lividity (or hypostasis) refers to the settling of blood in the dependent parts of the body due to gravity after death. It appears as a uniform purplish-red discoloration and does not follow venous patterns like marbling.

Filigree burns (c):

Filigree burns occur due to high-voltage electrical injuries where the current creates an arborescent (tree-branch-like) pattern on the skin. Unlike marbling, filigree burns are linear, raised, and do not involve discoloration due to decomposition.

None (d):

The described image clearly matches the features of marbling and thus cannot be categorized as "none."

Key Takeaways

Marbling is a prominent decomposition change seen in the early stages of putrefaction and follows the superficial venous patterns.

It should not be confused with other post-mortem changes like lividity or external injuries like burns.

Proper identification of marbling aids in determining the post-mortem interval (PMI) and understanding the progression of decomposition in forensic cases.

question_text: You notice the given findings on the body on which you have to perform an autopsy. Which test can be used to differentiate this from antemortem bruising?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given image shows postmortem hypostasis. To differentiate this finding (postmortem hypostasis) from an antemortem bruise, the classic test used is the incision test.

  • Incision Test Procedure:
    • The suspected area is incised.
    • In case of hypostasis, blood is seen within the blood vessels, which is easily washed away
    • In case of bruise, there is extravasation of blood in surrounding tissue & cannot be washed away
  • Hypostasis vs. Bruise: In hypostasis, the subcutaneous tissues beneath the blood collection are typically pale, whereas in bruises, they appear deep reddish-black due to extravasated blood.

Explanation of Other Options:

Getter's chloride test (Option A): This test is used to differentiate between freshwater and saltwater drowning and is not widely used now. It is not relevant for differentiating hypostasis from bruising.

Precipitin test (Option C): It is a species-specific test. In the precipitin test, a specific antiserum reacts with seminal fluid, blood, or saliva to confirm human origin. This test is used for species identification of body fluids or tissue, not for differentiating types of injury or post-mortem changes.

Breslau's second life test (Option D): This test is performed to determine whether a child was born alive or not by the presence of air in the stomach and intestine. It is not applicable for differentiating post-mortem changes from ante-mortem injuries in an adult body.

Key Takeaway:

The incision test is the standard method used in forensic pathology to distinguish postmortem hypostasis from antemortem bruising by observing whether the blood is intravascular and washable (hypostasis) or extravasated and clotted in the tissues (bruise).

question_text: Post-mortem examination of a dead body reveals contraction of the hands with absent primary relaxation. What is this suggestive of?
explanation:
Explanation:

Cadaveric spasm (also called instantaneous rigor) is a rare postmortem event where the muscles contract immediately at the time of death, without passing through the usual stage of primary flaccidity.

  • Onset: Instantaneous (at the moment of death).
  • Muscle groups: Typically affects small muscles (hands, fingers).
  • Context: Frequently linked with sudden, violent, or highly emotional deaths (e.g., drowning, suicides, combat).
  • Classic sign: Clenched fist, often preserving the last act of the deceased (e.g., weapon in hand, grass in a drowning victim).

Explanation of Other Options:

Rigor mortis (Option A):

  • True rigor mortis begins after a short relaxation phase, usually within 2-6 hours post-death, and spreads in a predictable sequence (head → trunk → limbs).
  • The absence of primary relaxation rules this out.

Livor mortis (Option B):

  • Refers to postmortem hypostasis/lividity, where blood settles in dependent areas due to gravity, producing a purplish discoloration.
  • It does not cause muscle contraction.

Algor mortis (Option D):

  • Represents postmortem cooling of the body.
  • Temperature change, not muscle stiffening, is its main feature.

Reference: Cadaveric spasm

question_text: A patient who was involved in a road traffic accident 20 minutes ago has been brought in for autopsy. Rigidity was observed in the neck, upper, and lower limbs without any initial relaxation phase. What does this finding indicate?
explanation:
Explanation:

Cadaveric spasm is an instantaneous stiffening of specific voluntary muscles that occurs immediately at the time of death without preceding primary relaxation. It is caused by sudden depletion of ATP due to intense emotional or physical activity just before death.

  • It is typically observed in accidental deaths, where the individual makes a sudden, forceful movement in distress just before dying.
  • It involves voluntary muscle groups such as those of the legs, neck, and eyes, as well as small muscle groups like those in the hands.
  • It represents an instantaneous form of rigor mortis, occurring immediately after death.
    The spasm affects the same voluntary muscles that were active at the moment of death.
  • It is of purely antemortem origin and cannot be artificially induced.
  • A key feature of cadaveric spasm is the absence of primary muscle relaxation following death.

Explanation of other options:

Rigor mortis (Option A): Generalized postmortem stiffening due to chemical changes in muscles, appears after 1–2 hours.

Heat stiffness (Option B): Coagulation of muscle proteins due to exposure to temperatures above 65°C.

Cold stiffness (Option D): Temporary hardening due to freezing at subzero temperatures (<–5°C).

Key takeaways:

  • Cadaveric spasm = instantaneous rigor (antemortem in origin).
  • No primary relaxation phase.
  • Seen in violent deaths (accidents, drowning, suicides).

References: Cadaveric spasm

question_text: A 2-month-old previously healthy baby was brought to the casualty when the parents found that the baby was not breathing while asleep. You suspected sudden infant death syndrome in this child. Which of the following is not a risk factor of this condition?
option_a: Sharing a bed with a family member
option_c: Sleeping in prone position or on the side
explanation:
Sleeping on hard/firm surfaces is not associated with sudden infant death syndrome(SIDS).

Crowded sleeping areas with many pillows, blankets and stuffed toys or old, soft mattresses are associated with an increased risk of SIDS.

SIDS is also known as a 'cot' or 'crib' death. Usually, the parent finds the infant expired in the crib after putting them to sleep. It is an unexpected death in a healthy infant, whose autopsy may not reveal a cause of death.

Most cases of SIDS occur between 1-7 months of age but can occur up to 2 years. The risk increases with male infants, multiple births, colder climates and lower socioeconomic status families.

Ways to reduce the risk of SIDS include:

  • Avoiding sharing a bed with the infant
  • Abstinence from smoking
  • Using hard/firm bedding and keeping the sleeping area clear
  • Ensuring the infant sleeps supine
  • Keeping the room temperature comfortable
  • Breastfeeding

Option A: Sharing a bed with a family member is associated with SIDS. The risk is augmented if the parent has consumed alcohol or sedative medications.

Option C: Sleeping prone or on the side is strongly associated with SIDS. The risk of regurgitation and choking is high in infants who sleep prone. These positions are associated with instability.

Option D: Overheating while sleeping can occur if the baby has a fever or has been placed in excessive clothing or in a warm room.

Overheating has been associated with SIDS.

Reference: Simpson's Forensic Medicine, Page: 144, 145.

question_text: An ICU patient dies. After some time, you notice that the deceased's body has become cold. What is this phenomenon known as?
explanation:
Explanation:

The cooling of the body after death is termed Algor mortis or postmortem cooling or Chill of death.

  • It results from the cessation of metabolic heat production.
  • Body temperature falls gradually and approaches the ambient temperature via conduction, convection, and radiation.
  • It is one of the early postmortem signs, useful for estimating time since death, especially within the first 18 hours.
  • Rectal temperature is typically used for measurement (unless contraindicated, e.g., in cases of sodomy).

Related Important Points and Concepts:

  • The rate of cooling is influenced by ambient temperature, clothing, body size, and environment.
  • Algor mortis follows the rule of thumb: body cools ~1.0-1.5°C per hour in temperate climates.
  • Other early signs include Rigor mortis, postmortem lividity, and ocular changes.

Explanation of Other Options:

Vibices (Option A): In areas of intense hypostasis, cutaneous petechial haemorrhages are seen due to rupture of capillary called vibices

Livor mortis (Option B): Means postmortem lividity or hypostasis or suggillation or postmortem staining. It is due to the discoloration of the skin and internal organs in the dependent areas of the body due to gravity shifting of the blood into the capillaries.

Postmortem caloricity (Option D): In this condition, the temperature of the body remains raised for the first two hours or so after death. This occurs:

(1) When the regulation of heat production has been severely disturbed before death, as in sunstroke and in some nervous disorders,

(2) When there has been a great increase in heat production in the muscles due to convulsions, as in tetanus and strychnine poisoning, or increased muscular activity as in cases of violent asphyxial deaths (Struggle prior to death) etc., and

(3) When there has been excessive bacterial activity, as in septicemic conditions, cholera, lobar pneumonia and any other infections associated with fever.

(4) When the environmental temperature itself is more than normal body temperature

Key Takeaway:

Algor mortis is a key early postmortem sign, helpful in forensic estimation of time since death, especially within the first few hours.

question_text: All the following can lead to an increase in temperature of the body in the first two hours following death except:
explanation:
Explanation:

Cyanide poisoning, although rapidly fatal, does not increase postmortem body temperature; it halts cellular respiration by blocking cytochrome c oxidase.

  • Cholera, septicaemia, and sunstroke lead to an increase in body temperature in the first two hours following death. It is due to post-mortem caloricity (Option A, C, and D ruled out)
  • Postmortem caloricity is the condition in which the temperature of the body remains raised for the first two hours or so after death. This occurs:
    • When the regulation of heat production has been severely disturbed before death, as in sunstroke, pontine haemorrhage and some nervous disorders
    • When there has been a great increase in heat production in the muscles due to convulsions, as in tetanus and strychnine poisoning, or increased muscular activity as in cases of violent asphyxial deaths (Struggle before death as in case of strangulation), etc.
    • When there has been excessive bacterial activity, as in septicemic conditions, cholera, lobar pneumonia and any other infections associated with fever.
    • When the environmental temperature itself is more than normal body temperature

Key Takeaway:

Postmortem caloricity is an exception to the rule of cooling after death and helps in estimating the cause and time of death. Cyanide poisoning does not cause it.

question_text: A poison which is luminescent and waxy and have a garlic smell is:
explanation:
Yellow phosphorus is a luminescent and waxy and have a garlic smell.

Yellow phosphorus is a waxy, white or yellow crystalline solid with a garlicky odour.

On exposure to air, it is highly combustible and ignites into flame.

It is luminescent and glows in the dark (Phosphorescence)

Yellow phosphorus is highly toxic and can cause death if ingested or inhaled. It is also a carcinogen and can cause cancer if it comes into contact with the skin.

Ammonium bromide is a white, odourless white crystals or granules that is soluble in water. It is used in photography in films, plates, and papers; in fireproofing of wood; in lithography and process engraving; in corrosion inhibitors; and in pharmaceutical preparations. It causes skin and serious eye damage, corrosion or irritation.

Opium is a bitter, black substance that is obtained from the poppy plant. It is highly addictive and can cause respiratory depression and death.

AlPhos is the trade name of aluminium phosphide. It is available as dark grey to dark yellow or greyish green tablets.

Reference: Textbook of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, VV Pillay, 20th edition, Page No. 425

question_text: Following is/are recommended primary management of a patient with snakebite, except.
option_b: Keep the site of bite below heart
explanation:
Primary management (First aid) in a case of snake bite:

  • Best is immobilization → By application of splint
  • Assurance/Reassurance
  • Do not wash the area of the bite.
  • No tourniquet application.
  • Sutherland wrapping: Pressure application by crepe bandage if the victim is expected to reach the hospital in more than 30 minutes but less than 3 hours. The bandage is wrapped over the bitten area as well as the entire limb with the limb placed in a splint.  It should be capable of admitting a finger beneath it.
  • Keep the affected area below heart level to reduce the flow of venom.
  • No incision & suction.
  • No ice application.
  • No electrotherapy.

Hospital treatment  

  • Wait and watch for signs & symptoms.
  • If indicated → Begin PASV (Polyvalent anti snake venom) with 10 vials.
  • PASV is effective against 1. Common cobra, 2. Common krait, 3. Russel’s viper, and 4. Saw scaled viper
  • PASV produced by Hoffkine biopharmaceutical company neutralises venom of pit viper due to para-specific activity.

Fixation of toxins

  • Common cobra → neurotoxins get fixed at post synaptic region. Hence, neostigmine has a role.
  • Common krait → neurotoxins get fixed at pre-synaptic region. Hence, neostigmine has no role.

Reference: https://nhm.gov.in/images/pdf/guidelines/nrhm-guidelines/stg/Snakebite_QRG.pdf http://repository-tnmgrmu.ac.in/18612/1/14110400021mohanraj.pdf

question_text: Mens rea means
explanation:
• Mens rea: Guilty mind
  • Actus rea: Guilty act
  • Mutatis Mutandis: The necessary changes having been made
  • Pari Passu: Equal in all respects
  • Ultra Vires: Beyond the power/authority/scope

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 489 & 490

question_text: The modernized versions of the Hippocratic Oath comprise the
explanation:
• Declaration of Sydney is related to the definition of death (Brain death).
  • Declaration of Geneva comprises the modernized versions of the Hippocratic Oath.
  • Declaration of Venice is related to terminal illness.
  • Declaration of Istanbul is related to Organ Trafficking and Transplant Tourism.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 20

question_text: Which of the following is an early sign of death?
explanation:
• Rigor mortis is an early sign of death.
  • Immediate signs of death (somatic death):
    • Insensibility and loss of voluntary power
    • Cessation of respiration
    • Cessation of circulation
  • Early signs of death (cellular death):
    • Pallor and loss of elasticity of the skin
    • Eye changes
    • Primary flaccidity of muscles
    • Cooling of the body
    • Postmortem lividity/suggillation
    • Rigor mortis
  • Late signs of death:
    • Putrefaction
    • Adipocere
    • Mummification

Rigor mortis or postmortem rigidity or cadaveric rigidity refers to the stiffness of the muscles and joints of the body after the death of an individual. After the first stage of primary relaxation of muscles, the second stage in muscles is the stage of rigor mortis which is followed by the third stage of secondary relaxation due to putrefaction. Rigor mortis occurs because of the chemical changes (Depletion of ATP) in the muscles leading to stiffening of the muscles.

Reference:The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 117, 118

question_text: A critically ill patient who is a registered organ donor collapses even after resuscitative measures. All of the following tests can be used to check the cessation of circulation, except:
explanation:
• Winslow's test is used to check the cessation of respiration.

Tests for respiration (Obsolete)

  1. Winslow’s test:
    • No movement of reflection of light shown on mirror or surface of water in bowl kept on the chest
  1. Mirror test:
    • No haziness is seen on the reflecting surface of the mirror held in front of mouth & nostrils
  1. Feather test:
    • No movement is seen, if a feather or fine cotton fibers are held before the nostrils

Tests for circulation (Obsolete)

  1. Diaphanus test (Transillumination test):
    • Hands with closed fingers are held against the strong source of light
    • During life, it appears red and translucent; After death, it is yellow and opaque
  1. Icard's dye test:
    • Fluorescein dye on being injected at a given site in a dead body fail to produce yellowish-green discoloration as seen in a living person
  1. Magnus test:
    • Ligature applied to finger. It swells and becomes blue if the person is alive
  1. Fingernail test:
    • Pressure is applied to the nail bed, During life nail bed is red and on pressure it turns pale. After death, remains pale throughout

Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, Principles and Practice, Krishan Vij, 5th Edition, Page No. 78

question_text: A forensic expert is assisting the police in investigating the death of a woman. On examination, the Kevorkian sign is noticed. What is the estimated time since the death?
explanation:
• The Kevorkian sign is a postmortem change that occurs in the retinal vessels. It lasts for about 1 hour.
  • It is characterized by fragmentation of the blood column in the retinal vessels. It appears within minutes after death
  • It can be visualized by using an ophthalmoscope as shown below.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 112

question_text: What is Zasko's phenomenon related to?
explanation:
• Zasko's phenomenon/ tendon reaction is related to muscular changes following death.
  • It is elicited in the quadriceps femoris muscle. Striking the lower third of the muscle about 10 cm. above the patella with a reflex hammer causes upward movement of the patella due to contraction of the muscle. It can be seen 1 to 2 hours after death.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35thEdition, Page No. 100

question_text: An ICU patient dies. After some time, you notice that the deceased body has become cold. What is this phenomenon known as?
explanation:
• The phenomenon of cooling of the body following death is called algor mortis/postmortem cooling/chill of death.
  • After death, the body loses heat by conduction, convection, and radiation. It is one of the early changes occurring after death.
  • The rectum is the ideal place to record the temperature except in case of sodomy.

Algor mortis is translated from Latin as "cold death" and describes the postmortem temperature change after someone has died. After death, individuals no longer produce body heat or cooling mechanisms, and the decedent temperature slowly approaches ambient temperature.

Incorrect options:

Option (A): Vibices: In areas of intense hypostasis, cutaneous petechial hemorrhages are seen due to rupture of capillary called vibices.

Option (B): Livor mortis: Means postmortem lividity or hypostasis or suggillation or postmortem staining. It is due to the discoloration of the skin and internal organs in the dependent areas of the body due to gravity shifting of the blood into the capillaries.

Option (D): Postmortem caloricity: In this condition, the temperature of the body remains raised for the first two hours or so after death. This occurs:

  1. When the regulation of heat production has been severely disturbed before death, as in sunstroke and in some nervous disorders,
  2. When there has been a great increase in heat production in the muscles due to convulsions, as in tetanus and strychnine poisoning, or increased muscular activity as in cases of violent asphyxial deaths (Struggle prior to death) etc., and
  3. When there has been excessive bacterial activity, as in septicemic conditions, cholera and other fevers.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology by KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page Number 112-113.

question_text: Identify the following post-mortem change.
explanation:
The image shows suggillation.

Postmortem lividity (Postmortem Staining/Cadaveric lividity/Hypostasis/Suggillations/Vibices/Darkening of death)

  • Postmortem hypostasis is a bluish purple or purplish red discoloration which appears under the skin (rete mucosum) of the dependent parts of the body after death due to capillo-venous distention.
  • P. M. Lividity is not seen at the areas of contact flattening of dependent parts, e.g., shoulder-blades, buttocks, calves, and heel (as seen in the image) due to compression of the capillary-venous vessels.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology by KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page Number-114.

question_text: The sequential onset of rigor mortis is described by which of the following?
explanation:
• Nysten's rule describes the sequential onset of rigor mortis in the various muscle groups.
  • Rigor mortis (cadaveric rigidity or death stiffening) refers to the stiffening and shortening of muscles following death. The basic sequence of the rigor mortis begins from the head and continues downwards the body. It disappears in the same order of appearance.
  • Heart (left chamber of the heart is affected first) is the first organ to undergo rigor mortis first.

Externally, the muscles are affected in following order:

  1. Eyelids
  2. Neck & lower jaw
  3. Face
  4. Chest
  5. Upper limbs
  6. Abdomen
  7. Lower limbs
  8. Fingers & toes

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 118

question_text:
Which of the following statements are true about cadaveric rigidity in contrast to cadaveric spasm?
1. It is due to the depletion of ATP
2. Muscles respond to electrical stimuli
3. It happens instantaneously after death
4. It is an antemortem phenomenon
5. It indicates time since death
explanation:
• Cadaveric rigidity is also known as rigor mortis. It is due to the depletion of ATP and indicates time since death. Muscle stiffening is not marked and can be overcome by moderate force. The rigor starts occurring1-2 hours after death(postmortem nature) and muscles do not respond to electrical stimuli.

Cadaveric spasm/instantaneous rigor/cataleptic rigidity/death clutch

  • It is a phenomenon where a group of muscles which have been actively working and contracted at the moment of death become stiff and rigid immediately after death without passing into the stage of primary relaxation.
  • Three important factors required for Cadaveric spasm are:
    • Sudden death
    • The person must be under great emotional tension and
    • The particular muscles should be acting at the time of death
  • Cadaveric spasm is usually limited to a single group of muscles and frequently involves hands
  • Very rarely seen in the entire body
  • It mainly occurs in voluntary muscles
  • It cannot be produced by any method after death
  • Exact mechanism is not known; may be explained on the basis of diminished or exhausted ATP in the affected muscle
  • Only a moderate force is required to overcome the muscle stiffness in rigor mortis (breaking of rigor mortis); whereas a great force is required to overcome cadaveric spasm
  • It disappears along with the onset of putrefaction

Examples:

  • In case of drowning, weeds and grass caught in hand during struggle remain firmly grasped even after death. This indicates that the person was alive when entering the water.
  • In case of suicides, weapons remain firmly grasped in the hand.

ATP is required to reuptake calcium into the sarcomere's sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR). When a muscle is relaxed, the myosin heads are returned to their "high energy" position, ready and waiting for a binding site on the actin filament to become available. Because there is no ATP available, previously released calcium ions cannot return to the SR. These leftover calcium ions move around inside the sarcomere and may eventually find their way to a binding site on the thin filament's regulatory protein. Since the myosin head is already ready to bind, no additional ATP expenditure is required and the sarcomere contracts.

When this process occurs on a larger scale, the stiffening associated with rigor mortis can occur. It mainly occurs during high ATP use. Sometimes, cadaveric spasms can be associated with erotic asphyxiation resulting in death

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 120

question_text: Which of the following is responsible for postmortem autolysis to occur?
explanation:
• Decomposition involves two processes: 1. Autolysis and 2. Putrefaction
  • Autolysis is due to enzymes and putrefaction is due to bacteria
  • Autolysis is the self-digestion of tissues by lysosomes and their digestive enzymes (mainly hydrolases).
  • The earliest autolytic changes occur in parenchymatous(brain) and glandular tissues. The earliest external sign is the whitish, cloudy appearance of the cornea. It is a sterile process, i.e., bacteria are not involved.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 121, 122

question_text: A dead body was recovered from a forest during winter. On close examination, maggots were seen crawling on it. What is the estimated time since the death?
explanation:
• Maggots are seen on dead bodies during summer in about 8-12 hours and during winter or rainy season in 1-2 days.
  • Pupae are seen on dead bodies during summer in 5 - 6 days and during winter or rainy season in 16-17 days.
  • The life cycle during summer is about 10-11 days and during winter or rainy season is about 22 days.

Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, Anil Aggrawal, Page No. 196

question_text: All of the following are postmortem changes except
explanation:
• Bichat's criteria- Before the era of heart transplantation, the criteria of death were the so-called tripod of life, also known as Bichat's tripod of life.
  • Bichat believed that life could be compared to a tripod with the three legs representing brain, heart, and lungs. If any leg perished, very soon (i.e., within minutes) all legs would perish, and the tripod of life would fall (death).
  • Atria mortis(Latin, Gateways of death, death's portals of entry) - Since death could "enter" only by stoppage of these organs, each was called as “atrium mortis”.
  • Atria mortis means Clinical death

Algor mortis means cooling of the body. Rigor mortis means stiffening of the body and Livor mortis means hypostasis. All are postmortem changes

Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, Anil Aggrawal, Page No. 164

question_text: While doing the Raygat's test, an unrespired lung may float due to:
explanation:
In Raygat's test, an unrespired lung(stillbirth) may float due to gases of decomposition, as seen in putrefaction.

It is also known as the floatation test/Breslau's first life test/ hydrostatic test.

It is done to determine whether the newborn has respired (breathed) or not.

Principle:

  • The specific gravity of the lungs before respiration is about 1.050, i.e., heavier than water.
  • The specific gravity of the lungs after respiration is about 0.950 (D/t presence of air), i.e., lighter than water.
  • Therefore, non-respired lungs sink in water and the respired lungs float.

Method:

  • Remove the lungs along with bronchi, trachea and larynx after ligating.
  • Place in a container containing water.
  • See whether they float or sink.
  • Separate each lung and test similarly.
  • Cut each lung into about 15-20 pieces and test for floatation.
  • Firmly press each piece between thumb and fingers (to expel the tidal air and putrefactive gases) and test again.

Inference:

  • If all the pieces float, it indicates that the respiration has taken place.
  • If all the pieces sink, it means the child has not breathed.
  • If some pieces sink and some pieces float, it indicates partial or feeble respiration.

Fallacies of hydrostatic test:

1. The expanded lungs may sink (False - ve) in cases of

  • Acute edema
  • Pneumonia
  • Congenital syphilis
  • Atelectasis

2. The unexpanded lungs may float (False + ve) in cases of

  • Putrefaction
  • Artificial respiration

Other tests to determine if respiration has taken place or not are:

  • Fodere's test (Static test): Weight of lungs before respiration → 30-40g, and after respiration → 60-66g
  • Ploucquet's test: Weight of lungs before respiration → 1/70 of body weight, and after respiration → 1/35 of body weight
  • Wredin's test: Assesses the changes in the middle ear. The gelatinous substance in the middle ear is replaced by air if respiration has taken place.

Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 2nd edition, PC Dixit, Page No. 175-177

question_text: You are performing an autopsy on a fetus born dead at 6 months. Which of the following is least likely to be seen in this case?
explanation:
Adipocere formation is not seen in a dead born fetus of 6 months.

Dead-born child:

A dead-born child is a child, which has died in utero and may or may not show the signs of

  1. Rigor mortis
  2. Maceration
  3. Mummification or
  4. Putrefaction

Adipocere

  • Adipocere is a modification of putrefaction.
  • It is due to postmortem hydrolysis or hydrogenation of the fats.
  • In this, the fatty tissues of the body change into a substance known as adipocere which is soft greyish-white, waxy, greasy material with an offensive, sweet rancid smell.
  • It is seen most commonly in bodies immersed in water or in damp, warm environment.
  • Foetuses under 7 months do not show this change.

Mummification: It is a process of drying and desiccation of the fetus died in utero and has remained in the uterus for a few days with deficient blood supply, scanty liquor amnii with exclusion of air. Takes about 2 weeks.

Putrefaction: Seen in a fetus died in utero, with ruptured membrane, where air gains entry.

Resorption: If the pregnancy with the dead foetus continues, it may be gradually resorbed.

The most important post-mortem change in an intrauterine death is maceration, which is an autolytic process by which there is self-disintegration of the body by cellular enzymes.

References: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 339.

question_text: In case of infant deaths, Ploucquet's test is carried out to determine live birth by:
option_a: Increase in weight of lungs in relation to body weight following respiration
option_b: Presence of air in middle ear
option_c: Presence of air in stomach following respiration
option_d: Change in shape of chest after respiration
explanation:
Ploucquet's test: This test helps to demonstrate establishment of respiration. Weight of lungs before respiration → 1/70 of body weight and after respiration → 1/35 of body weight.

  • Fodere's test(Static test): Weight of lungs before respiration → 30-40g and after respiration → 60-66g.
  • Wredin's test: Assesses the changes in the middle ear. The gelatinous substance in the middle ear is replaced by air if respiration has taken place.

Shape of the Chest: Before respiration, the chest is flat, and its circumference is one to two cm. less than the abdomen at the level of the umbilicus. After respiration, the chest expands and becomes arched or drum shaped.

Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 2nd edition, PC Dixit, Page No. 175-177.

question_text: In both water and food are completely withheld to a person, death usually occurs in
explanation:
• Total deprivation of water and food results death in about 10 to 12 days.
  • Newborns may survive for 7 to 10 days without food and water.
  • If food alone is withdrawn, death may occur in 6 to 8 weeks or even more.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 259

question_text: A person in police custody was placed in prone position with his wrist & ankles bound behind his back and secured by a cord. This method is called
explanation:
Hog-tying (total appendage restraint procedure): It is a type of physical restraint in which the person is placed in prone position with his wrists and ankles bound behind his back and secured by a cord. The person may have difficulty in breathing or may become unresponsive.

Choke (bar arm) hold: Forearm is placed straight across the front of the neck. The free hand grips the wrist and pulls it back, which causes obstruction of the airway and carotid arteries and immediate unconsciousness. The hypopharynx is also occluded by displacement of the tongue. Fracture of the hyoid bone or larynx may occur if great force is used. Rarely death may occur due to hypoxia and release of catecholamines due to struggle, resulting in fatal cardiac arrhythmia. Pressure on the carotid bodies can cause death by sudden cardiac arrest.

Carotid sleeper hold (lateral vascular neck restraint): Standing behind a person the arm is placed about the neck with the antecubital fossa centred at the midline of the neck. The free hand grips the wrist, and the arm is pulled backwards, which compresses the carotid arteries and jugular veins but not vertebral arteries and the trachea. Consciousness is lost in 10 to 15 seconds. If pressure is released the victim regains consciousness in 10 to 20 seconds. The neck structures are not damaged. Rarely death may occur due to hypoxia and release of catecholamines.

Falanga (bastinado, falaka): In this canes or rod are used to beat on the soles of the feet, or rarely to the palms of the hands or hips, which is very painful and debilitating. Contusions are found deep in the tissues. Faint red lines may be seen, and often hyperpigmentation along the lines of injury.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 229

question_text: Study of death in all aspects is known as:
explanation:
Explanation:

Thanatology is the comprehensive study of death in all its aspects-biological, medical, psychological, cultural, legal, and social.

Key Domains of Thanatology:

  • Death and Dying: Examines biological, physiological, and medical processes of death, including somatic, systemic, clinical, and molecular death.
  • Bereavement and Grief: Explores emotional, psychological, and social responses to loss, coping mechanisms, and theories of grief.
  • End-of-Life Care: Covers palliative care, hospice management, pain control, advance directives, and ethical/legal issues in end-of-life decisions.
  • Cultural & Religious Perspectives: Studies rituals, beliefs, mourning practices, funeral rites, and concepts of the afterlife across different traditions.
  • Social & Legal Aspects: Involves discussions on euthanasia, assisted suicide, organ donation, funeral industry practices, and legal frameworks related to death.

Explanation of Other Options:

Forensic Anthropology (Option B):

  • Focuses on the identification of human remains using skeletal analysis, descriptive data, body marks, and photographs.
  • While relevant in forensic contexts, it does not encompass all aspects of death (medical, psychological, social, legal).

Toxicology (Option C):

  • Concerned with the detection and study of toxins in biological samples.
  • It deals only with poisoning-related deaths, which is one specific aspect, not the entire spectrum of death.

Molecular Death (Option D):

  • Refers to the death of individual cells and tissues after cessation of vital functions.
  • Usually occurs 1-2 hours post mortem, but it is just a stage in the dying process, not the overall study of death.

Reference: Thanatology

question_text: Identify the postmortem finding shown in the image of a body recovered from water.
explanation:
The image given shows the washerwoman's foot (Skin maceration). It occurs faster in warm water than in cold water.

Washer woman's hands and feet

  • D/t absorption of water into outer layers of skin.
  • Starts at fingertips.
  • Occurs early in warm water.
  • Seen in about 24 hours.
  • It is only a sign of immersion.
    • 2-4 hours: Wrinkling & soddening of fingertips
    • 4-8 hours: Bleaching of epidermis
    • 24 hours: Entire hand shows bleached, wrinkled, and soddened appearance (Washer woman's Hands/Feet)
    • 48 hours: Peeling of cuticle from palm and sole
    • 3-4 days: Skin can be peeled off like a glove

Incorrect options:

Cutis anserina (Goose skin/flesh/bump) (Option B):

  • Granular & puckered appearance of skin.
  • D/t spasm of arrector pili muscles due to cold.
  • Especially seen over thighs.
  • Also seen in case of rigor mortis of arrector pili muscles.

Postmortem lividity (Option C):

  • In running water (river) → Will be absent
  • In stagnant water: Body usually floats face down, buttocks up with limbs hanging down. So, seen in the face, upper part of the chest, hands & forearm, and feet & legs.

Cadaveric spasm (Option D): This is a rare form of muscular stiffening that occurs at the moment of death, instantly "locking" the body or a group of muscles in its final position (e.g., a drowning victim clutching weeds).

Reference:

Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology by Anil Aggrawal, Page Number: 396.

question_text: A 45-year-old male was found dead in a desert region after being missing for several weeks. On autopsy, the body appeared dry, leathery, and shrunken, with preserved facial features and absence of internal decomposition. The forensic pathologist confirmed mummification as the likely process. Based on these findings, what odour is most expected from the body?
explanation:
Explanation:

Mummification is a dry form of preservation that occurs in hot, dry, and well-ventilated environments like deserts.

  • It involves dehydration of tissues, inhibition of bacterial growth, and prevention of putrefaction.
  • As a result, no foul-smelling gases or fluids are produced.
  • The body remains leathery, shrunken, and typically odourless.

Related Important Points and Concepts:

  • The three important environmental factors for mummification are
    • High temperature (Hot weather)
    • No moisture (dry weather)
    • Free flow of air
  • Timeframe: Varies from 3 months to a year.
  • Forensic importance: In case of mummification, the general facial features are preserved, aiding in identification even after prolonged intervals.

Pungent (Option B): Associated with early adipocere formation, not mummification.

Putrid (Option C): Seen in bacterial decomposition during putrefaction-not seen in dry, preserved bodies.

Offensive (Option D): Typical of wet decay processes; mummification does not produce offensive odours.

Key Takeaway:

Mummified bodies are odourless because dehydration prevents bacterial growth and putrefaction.

question_text: While performing an autopsy, you notice honeycombing of the liver. What does it signify?
explanation:
Explanation:

Honeycombing of the liver (foamy liver) is a sign of putrefaction.

  • In putrefaction, Clostridium welchii (Cl. Perfringens) produces small clumps in tissue space and produces gas. This tends to increase the size of the liver, and it becomes soft and studded with blisters. When bubbles develop in the liver, the organ develops a honeycombed, vesicular and foamy appearance on cut section.

Mummification (Option A): Refers to dehydration and shriveling of the body in dry environments - no gas formation or honeycombing is seen.

Livor mortis (Option C): Also called postmortem lividity; it's due to gravitational pooling of blood and staining of the skin at the dependent areas of the body, not related to liver vesicles.

Fatty liver (Option D): Characterised by hepatocyte fat accumulation, not by gas-filled vesicles or honeycombing.

Key Takeaway:

Honeycombing of the liver during autopsy is a classical sign of putrefaction, caused by gas-forming bacteria such as Clostridium welchii (Cl. Perfringens).

question_text: Identify the characteristic odor produced during the change shown in the given image.
explanation:
Explanation:

The image depicts a mummified body, which is classically odorless.

Mummification is a late postmortem change where the body undergoes dehydration and shriveling due to the evaporation of body fluids. Despite the drying, the body retains its overall shape and recognizable facial features.

Key features include:

  • Begins in exposed areas such as the face, hands, and feet, then spreads to the rest of the body.
  • Weight loss of 60-70% may occur as internal organs dry and shrink into a single mass.
  • Dry, hot climates or sandy soil favor rapid evaporation and aid mummification.
  • Chronic arsenic or antimony poisoning can promote this process.
  • Differs from putrefaction because there is no foul odor.

Explanation for other options:

Pungent (option B): Represents a sharp or acrid smell, not associated with mummification.

Putrid (option C): Typical rotten smell of putrefaction, absent in mummification.

Offensive (option D): Refers to unpleasant decomposition odors, which are not present in mummified remains.

question_text: Foamy liver is seen in: TN 08; UP 08; NIMS 11; NEET 13
explanation: Ans. Putrefaction

question_text: If a family dies in a closed room filled with smoke from a wood fire, which of the following findings would most likely be observed on their bodies?
explanation:
Explanation:

In this case, the family's death in a smoke-filled closed room suggests carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. A classic postmortem finding in CO poisoning is cherry-red staining of the body.

Postmortem Staining in Poisoning:

Livor mortis, or postmortem staining, is the discoloration of the skin after death caused by blood pooling in dependent areas. The specific color of this staining can help indicate certain types of poisoning.

Explanation of other options:

Cyanosis (Option B): is not appreciated in CO poisoning.

question_text: A 28-year-old male presents with bradycardia (50 bpm), hypotension (80/60 mmHg), respiratory depression (7/min), hypothermia (95°F), pinpoint pupils, and disorientation. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Explanation:

The classic opioid overdose triad is coma, pinpoint pupils (miosis), and respiratory depression. The additional findings of bradycardia, hypotension, and hypothermia further solidify this diagnosis. Opioids act on CNS mu-receptors, causing profound CNS and respiratory depression.

The lethal quantities for common opiates are as follows:

  • opium is fatal at approximately 2 grams
  • morphine at 0.2 grams
  • codeine at 80 milligrams.

Death typically occurs within 6 to 12 hours following a lethal overdose.

Stages of opium poisoning:

The diagnosis of opium poisoning can be confirmed using specific chemical tests, notably the Marquis test (M), Deninges test (D), and Husemann test (H).

For the management of acute opioid poisoning, intravenous naloxone is the standard treatment. To prevent relapse, naltrexone, administered orally, is the drug of choice. For opioid substitution therapy, buprenorphine is preferred over methadone.

Explanation of other options:

Benzodiazepine overdose (Option A): Causes sedation and respiratory depression but typically does not cause miosis, bradycardia, or significant hypotension to this degree.

Cocaine intoxication (Option B): A sympathomimetic toxidrome causing tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, mydriasis (dilated pupils), and agitation the exact opposite of this presentation.

Opioid withdrawal (Option C): Presents with lacrimation, rhinorrhea, yawning, piloerection, diarrhea, anxiety, and tachycardia a hyperadrenergic state, not CNS depression.

Key Takeaways:

  • Opioid overdose: Miosis, respiratory depression, coma.
  • Opioid withdrawal: Dilated pupils, autonomic hyperactivity.
  • "Pinpoint pupils" are a cardinal sign of opioid intoxication.

question_text: Identify the condition shown in the image
explanation:
Filigree burns, also known as arborescent or lightning burns, are caused by high-voltage electrical injury, often from lightning strikes. These burns present a distinct branching or fern-like pattern on the skin, resembling the shape of tree branches or delicate filigree designs. This pattern is due to the electrical discharge traveling through the skin, causing superficial dermal damage along lines of least resistance, such as sweat ducts or small blood vessels.

Key features of filigree burns:

Fern-like patterns on the skin.

Typically superficial and do not involve deep tissue destruction.

Caused by the passage of electricity or lightning over the body.

Transient in nature and may disappear within hours or days, making them more diagnostic than harmful.

This condition is unique to high-voltage electrical injuries and is often a hallmark sign of a lightning strike injury.

Rule Out:

(a) Hypostasis:

Hypostasis, also known as postmortem lividity, is the pooling of blood in the dependent parts of the body after death due to gravity.

It appears as purple or reddish discoloration on the lower parts of the body but lacks any branching or fern-like patterns.

(b) Marbling:

Marbling is a postmortem phenomenon in which veins become visible under the skin due to decomposition.

It appears as a network of greenish or black lines tracing the veins, especially in the abdomen and extremities. This is entirely different from the fern-like patterns of filigree burns.

(d) Poisoning

Poisoning does not produce any characteristic skin patterns like filigree burns. Poisoning symptoms typically include changes in color (e.g., cyanosis, pallor) or specific marks around the mouth (in corrosive poisoning), but it does not resemble the lightning-burn pattern.

Key Takeaways:

Filigree burns are a diagnostic marker of high-voltage electrical injury, particularly from lightning strikes.

The burns are superficial and present as fern-like, branching patterns, which are unique and transient.

Filigree burns must not be confused with postmortem phenomena like hypostasis or marbling, as their appearance and cause are entirely different.

Recognition of filigree burns is crucial in forensic and clinical settings to identify high-voltage electrical injuries or lightning strikes.

question_text: Among the following, which organs are the first and the last to putrefy respectively?
explanation:
Among the given options, the first organ to putrefy is the larynx and the last to putrefy is a non-gravid uterus.

The decreasing order of organ putrefaction (from first to last):

  1. Larynx and trachea
  2. Stomach, intestine
  3. Spleen
  4. Liver
  5. Brain
  6. Gravid uterus
  7. Heart
  8. Lungs
  9. Kidney and the bladder
  10. Esophagus
  11. Blood vessels
  12. Skin, muscle, tendons
  13. Prostate and Non-gravid uterus
  14. Bones
  15. Teeth

Reference:Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, Anil Aggrawal, Page No. 186, 187

question_text: What weather is favourable for mummification?
explanation:
• The absence of moisture in the air and continuous action of dry or warmed air is necessary for the process of mummification.
  • Mummification is a process of dehydration or drying and shrivelling of the cadaver that occurs from the evaporation of water. The natural appearances of the body and general facial features are preserved.

During the process of mummification, the body becomes progressively dehydrated and the normal putrefactive decomposition is inhibited. It occurs most readily in a current of dry warm air. Although dryness is clearly necessary, exactly how warm the atmosphere needs to be is less certain.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 127, 128

question_text: What is the odour of the mummified body?
explanation:
The mummified body is odourless.

  • The absence of moisture in the air and continuous action of dry or warmed air is necessary for the process of mummification.
  • Mummification is a process of dehydration or drying and shrivelling of the cadaver that occurs from the evaporation of water. The natural appearances of the body and general facial features are preserved.

During the process of mummification, the body becomes progressively dehydrated and the normal putrefactive decomposition is inhibited. It occurs most readily in a current of dry warm air. Although dryness is clearly necessary, exactly how warm the atmosphere needs to be is less certain.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 127, 128

question_text: Which of the following organs is tested in Breslau's second life test?
explanation:
In Breslau's second life test, also known as the stomach bowel test, the stomach and the duodenum are tested.

This test is done to determine whether the baby was born alive or not.

It works on the principle that some air is swallowed during respiration in a live-born child. Detecting the presence of this air in these viscera constitutes the basis for this test.

Procedure:

The stomach and duodenum are removed after tying double ligatures at each end and placed in water. If they float, make a small cut while under water to see air bubbles coming up. A floating viscera giving out air bubbles when opened under water is a positive test.

Interpretation:

  • A positive test proves live birth even in the absence of a positive hydrostatic lung test. This may happen if there had been some obstruction in the respiratory passages.
  • A negative test does not mean still birth since air does not necessarily enter the stomach in adequate amounts during the breathing act.
  • Putrefaction invalidates the result.

Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 2nd edition, PC Dixit, Page No. 177

question_text: Putrefaction is likely to be delayed in which of the following poisoning cases?
option_a: A case of suicide of a 19-year-old woman by taking multiple tablets of aspirin
option_b: Death of a 5-year-old child due to accidental consumption of aconite roots
option_c: A 45-year-old man committing suicide by drinking carbolic acid
option_d: A 30-year-old man who died due to consumption of malathion
explanation:
• Putrefaction is delayed in carbolic acid poisoning.
  • Putrefaction is the fifth stage, following pallor mortis, algor mortis, rigor mortis, and livor mortis in the decomposition of dead bodies.
  • It is the decomposition of proteins, the eventual breakdown of the cohesiveness between tissues, and the liquefaction of most organs.
  • In the matter of death by poisoning, the putrefaction of the body is chemically delayed by poisons.
  • Death by septic diseases, puerperal sepsis, kidney diseases with generalized edema can hasten putrefaction.

Option A: It is a case of salicylic acid poisoning.

Option B: It is a case of aconite poisoning.

Option D: It is a case of organophosphate poisoning.

  • Putrefaction sets in rapidly in cases of
    • Septicemia, Peritonitis, Inflammatory, septic conditions etc. (More bacteria)
    • Anasarca and Asphyxia (More moisture)
  • Conditions which retard/delays putrefaction are:
    • Wasting disease: Anaemia (decreased blood) & Debility (atrophy of tissue)
    • Poisons: Arsenic, antimony and other heavy metals, carbolic acid, zinc chloride, strychnine

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 125

question_text:
A body was brought to the forensic department after being discovered in a rocky cave system in Rajasthan, where it had been lying undisturbed for several weeks. On examination, the cadaver showed a leathery texture, dry and shrunken skin, preserved facial features, and complete absence of decomposition or odour. The forensic pathologist confirmed that the body had undergone mummification.
Which of the following environmental conditions is most favourable for such a postmortem change to occur?
explanation:
Explanation:

The absence of moisture in the air and the continuous action of dry or warm air is necessary for the process of mummification.

  • Mummification is a process of dehydration or drying and shriveling of the cadaver that occurs from the evaporation of water. The natural appearances of the body and general facial features are preserved.
  • The three important environmental factors for mummification are
    1. No moisture
    2. High temperature
    3. Free flow of air

During the process of mummification, the body becomes progressively dehydrated, and the normal putrefactive decomposition is inhibited. It occurs most readily in the current of dry hot air. Although dryness is necessary, exactly how warm the atmosphere needs to be is less certain.

Warm and humid weather (Option A): Promotes putrefaction or sometimes adipocere formation, not mummification.

Cold and dry weather (Option B) and Cold and humid weather (Option D): Does not favour the process of formation of mummification.

Key Takeaway:

Hot and dry climates favour mummification by accelerating tissue dehydration and inhibiting bacterial growth.

question_text: What is first external sign of decomposition of dead body -
option_b: Greenish discolouration over right iliac fossa
explanation: Ans. is 'b' i.e., Greenish discolouration over right iliac fossa [Ref Reddy 30th/e p. 150-152] First external sign of putrefaction - Green discoloration in right iliac fossa. First internal sign of putrefaction Green discoloration under liver. These are due to involvement of caecum which contains more gas and is full of bacteria.

question_text: Which of the following is false regarding adipocere formation?
option_a: Facial features are not preserved making identification difficult
option_b: It inhibits growth of putrefactive bacteria
option_c: It is commonly seen in bodies immersed in water
option_d: It has distinct offensive or sweetish smell
explanation:
• In case of Adipocere, when the process involves the face, the features are well preserved, which helps to establish the identity.
  • Adipocere is a modification of putrefaction. In this, the fatty tissues of the body change into a substance known as adipocere. The change is due to the gradual hydrolysis and hydrogenation of body fats into higher fatty acids, such as palmitic acid, oleic acid, stearic acid and hydroxy stearic acid forming insoluble soaps. These soaps are acidic, which prevents the growth of putrefactive bacteria.
  • Adipocere has a distinct offensive or sweetish smell, but during the early stages of its production, a penetrating ammoniacal odour is also noticed. A warm, moist, anaerobic environment favours adipocere formation. e.g., bodies immersed in water.

Adipocere, also known as saponification, corpse wax, grave wax or mortuary wax, is a wax-like organic substance formed by the anaerobic bacterial hydrolysis of fat in tissue, such as body fat in corpses. In its formation, putrefaction is replaced by a permanent firm cast of fatty tissues, internal organs, and the face.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 127

question_text: A woman, married for four years, committed suicide leaving a note alleging dowry harassment. Who is authorized to conduct the investigation into her death?
explanation:
Explanation:

The death of a married woman within seven years of marriage is generally presumed to be a case of dowry death.

Magistrate’s inquest is conducted in cases such as:

  • Infanticide or suspicious death
  • Deaths in mental asylums
  • Deaths due to police beating or in borstals (juvenile correctional institutions)
  • Police custodial deaths
  • Dowry deaths – when a married woman dies within 7 years of marriage and there is an allegation of dowry-related abuse
  • Exhumation – when a body is dug out for examination
  • Deaths due to police firing

Police inquest:
Conducted in cases of unnatural deaths that are not caused by disease.

Examples include:

  • Accidents
  • Suicides
  • Homicides

Key takeaways:

  • Magistrate’s inquest: Required for dowry death, custodial death, and exhumation.
  • Ensures judicial impartiality in sensitive deaths.
  • Dowry death defined under Section 304B IPC.

References: Inquest

question_text: The enquiry into the circumstances of death is called
explanation:
• Inquest means enquiry into the causes of death which is apparently not due to natural causes.
  • Corpus delecti means "Body of offence" or "essence of crime"; means, the facts (elements) of any criminal offence e.g. murder.
  • Verdict is a decision on an issue of fact in a civil or criminal case or an inquest.
  • Open verdict means an announcement of the commission of crime without information regarding the accused.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 5

question_text: Artificial bruise can be differentiated from true bruise by which of the following
explanation:
All others are features of true bruise except presence of vesicles which is a feature of false bruise.

Incorrect Options:

  • (b) Color change noted with time: True bruises undergo color changes (from red to purple, green, yellow) over time as blood breaks down.
  • (c) Diffuse irregular margins: True bruises often have irregular margins, but this can also appear in artificial bruises.
  • (d) No itching: True bruises can cause itching as part of the healing process, while false bruises may not.

Key Takeaway:

The key differentiator between an artificial bruise (false bruise) and a true bruise is the presence of vesicles in the artificial bruise. Vesicles, which are small blisters or fluid-filled sacs, are not typically seen in true bruises, where the damage is more about blood accumulation beneath the skin.

Following are the differences between true and false bruise:

question_text: Identify the image.
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows the injury 'tramline' or "railway-line" bruising. This specific type of bruise is caused when the skin surface is struck by a rod or similar objects such as a cane or lathi.

A blow with a rod, a stick or a whip produces two parallel, linear haemorrhages (railway line or tram line type). The intervening skin appears unchanged, because the rod forcibly dents the tissues inwards and momentarily stretches each side of the dent. This causes rupture of vessels in the marginal zones with a line of bruising, whereas the base of the dent becomes compressed and the vessels are not injured. Blood from the base of the dent gets displaced to the sides due to the pressure by the object. When the rod is removed and the skin comes back to its normal position, the two sides of the depression remain as contused lines (As seen in the image).

Causes: Impact from objects like lathi, pipe, broom handles, narrow planks, wood or metal rods etc.

Explanation of Other Options:

Ehler Danlos bruise (Option A): This refers to bruising that occurs easily in individuals with Ehler-Danlos Syndrome due to fragile blood vessels and connective tissues. It describes a predisposition to bruising, not a specific pattern caused by a particular type of impact.

Mottling (Option C): Mottling refers to patchy, irregular discoloration of the skin, often seen in shock, cold exposure, or circulatory compromise. It's a general skin appearance, not a specific injury pattern caused by blunt force trauma.

Postmortem lividity (Option D): Postmortem lividity (livor mortis) is the purplish-red discoloration that appears on dependent parts of the body after death due to the gravitational settling of blood in capillaries and small veins. It is a post-mortem change, not an injury caused by external force.

Key Takeaway:

The description of a bruise with two parallel lines and an undamaged center, caused by a rod-like object, is characteristic of 'tramline' or "railway-line" bruising.

question_text: Which feature is NOT characteristic of a true bruise?
explanation:
Explanation:

Itching (pruritus) is a feature associated with artificial bruises caused by irritant chemicals like marking nut juice or calotropis.

A true bruise, resulting from blunt trauma, is typically tender or painful but not itchy. True bruises do show color evolution, often have irregular margins, and yield negative results on tests for artificial irritants (Options A, B & C ruled out).

Artificial bruises, created to falsely allege assault, are typically produced by rubbing substances like marking nut juice, plumbago, madar (calotropis), or semicarpium onto easily accessible areas of the body. These lesions appear as dark brown, irregularly shaped patches with well-defined margins and are often surrounded by redness and inflammation.

Characteristic features include the presence of small vesicles and intense itching, which help distinguish them from true traumatic bruises.

Key Takeaways:

  • True bruise: Painful, color changes, negative chemical tests.
  • Artificial bruise: Itchy, may have vesicles, positive chemical tests.

question_text: Which of the following is a true statement about pugilistic attitude?
option_c: Generalised extension of the body is present
option_d: Occurs due to coagulation of muscle protein
explanation:
• Pugilistic attitude/ heat stiffening is due to coagulation of muscle proteins.
  • It is a condition simulating rigor mortis. It occurs when the body is exposed to temperatures above 65°C like in deaths from burning, high voltage electric shock, or from falling into hot liquid.
  • The mechanism is the coagulation of muscle protein. The flexors, being bulkier than the extensors, contract more and force the limbs into a position of general flexion, the so-called boxer's or pugilistic attitude. It could be due to antemortem or postmortem burns,especially when the body is extensively burnt and charred. Other conditions simulating rigor mortis are - cold stiffening, gas stiffening, cadaveric spasm/cataleptic rigidity.

The ''Pugilistic Attitude'' This condition results from the muscles being contracted, after death, by the heat of a fire. is produced in nearly every fire, and chemical examination of the blood for its presence is essential in the investigation of any death where fire may have been a factor.

References: Estimation of the Time Since Death, 3rdEdition, Page No. 92 Knight's Forensic Pathology 4thEdition, Page No. 317

question_text: A man was found dead in a secluded area with his hands tied. Postmortem revealed cyanosis, petechial hemorrhages, abrasions, and bruises around the mouth and lips, along with facial congestion and edema. Which of the following is the least likely cause of death?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of tied hands, facial injuries, and features of asphyxia (cyanosis, petechiae, and congestion) point toward smothering, typically of homicidal nature. Suicide is least likely because self-restraint and facial trauma are uncommon in self-inflicted asphyxial deaths.

Key findings:

  • Tied hands: Indicate restraint, strongly pointing toward homicide.
  • Cyanosis and petechial hemorrhages: Typical features of asphyxia.
  • Abrasions and bruising around the mouth and lips: Suggest smothering, caused by external obstruction of the airway.
  • Facial congestion and edema: Result from venous obstruction associated with asphyxia.

Differentiation of causes:

  • Asphyxia: Evident from the presence of petechiae, cyanosis, and facial congestion.
  • Smothering (type of asphyxia): Supported by the presence of tied hands and mouth injuries, indicating blockage of external air passages.
  • Homicide: Most consistent explanation, given the evidence of physical restraint and facial trauma.

Explanation of other options:

Asphyxia (Option A): Evident from petechiae, congestion, and cyanosis.

Smothering (Option C): External airway obstruction — consistent with mouth and lip bruises.

Homicide (Option D): The most probable manner due to tied hands and external injuries.

References: Deaths

question_text: Jack knife position causes death due to:
explanation:
Jack-knife position may cause death usually by positional asphyxia and occasionally by traumatic asphyxia.

Jack-knife position is a position where the victim's thighs and knees are driven against the chest causing indirect compression of the chest and restriction of breathing movements.

Persons who have been trapped upside down or even only in a ‘jack-knife’ position, with the upper half of their body bent acutely downwards from the waist, may have such impairment of their respiratory movements that they become hypoxic and suffer marked disturbance of their circulatory system, especially the venous return to the heart.

Occasionally traumatic asphyxia results from indirect compression, when the body is subjected to force in such a manner that his thighs and the knees are driven against his chest, the so-called "jack-knife" position.

References: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th edition Page No. 366; The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 283, 284

question_text: A 13-year-old girl is brought to the OPD by her mother with a complaint of abdominal pain. The patient's urine pregnancy test (UPT) is positive. What should be the first step by you as a medical officer?
option_c: Take consent from the patient's mother
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In cases involving minors with a positive pregnancy test, suspicion of sexual assault or abuse must be considered.
  • The first step is to inform the police, as mandated by the Protection of Children from Sexual Offenses (POCSO) Act.
  • Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act: Enacted in 2012, it was designed to protect children under the age of 18 from sexual abuse, sexual harassment, and pornography.
  • Key Features:
    • Gender-neutral law
    • It covers penetrative and non-penetrative assault, sexual harassment, and use of children for pornography
    • Burden of proof is on the accused, unlike many other criminal laws where the burden is on the prosecution
    • Mandatory reporting by adults and failure to do so can be punishable
    • Special courts for the trial of offenses to ensure a child-friendly environment
    • Identity of the victim is to be protected, and the proceedings are to be conducted in camera to prevent exposure
  • Recent Changes and Developments in the POCSO Act:
    • 2019 Amendment
      • Stricter Punishments: Death penalty for aggravated sexual assault against children
      • The minimum punishment for penetrative sexual assault increased to 10 years, and for aggravated penetrative sexual assault increased to 20 years, with the possibility of life imprisonment or death in extreme cases.
    • Fast-track Courts to ensure swift disposal of POCSO cases, given the backlog of pending cases.
    • Clarifications on 'Touch' and Sexual Intent:
      • The intent behind physical contact is crucial in determining whether it qualifies as an offense under POCSO.
    • Digital Crimes Against Children:
      • Provisions related to the use of children for pornographic and online exploitation purposes have been emphasized with stricter penalties.

Reference:

https://bnblegal.com/bareact/the-protection-of-children-from-sexual-offences-amendment-act-2019/

question_text: The test based on specific gravity of the lungs which is useful in the diagnosis of live birth is:
explanation:
Hydrostatic test is based on specific gravity of the lungs which is useful in the diagnosis of live birth.

It is also known as the floatation test/Breslau's first life test.

It is done to determine whether the newborn has respired(breathed) or not.

Principle:

  • The specific gravity of the lungs before respiration is about 1.050, i.e., heavier than water.
  • The specific gravity of the lungs after respiration is about 0.950(D/t presence of air), i.e., lighter than water.
  • Therefore, non-respired lungs sink in water and the respired lungs float.

Method:

  • Remove the lungs along with bronchi, trachea and larynx after ligating.
  • Place in a container containing water.
  • See whether they float or sink.
  • Separate each lung and test similarly.
  • Cut each lung into about 15-20 pieces and test for floatation.
  • Firmly press each piece between thumb and fingers(to expel the tidal air and putrefactive gases) and test again.

Inference:

  • If all the pieces float, it indicates that the respiration has taken place.
  • If all the pieces sink, it means the child has not breathed.
  • If some pieces sink and some pieces float, it indicates partial or feeble respiration.

Fallacies of hydrostatic test:

  1. The expanded lungs may sink(False - ve) in cases of
    • Acute edema
    • Pneumonia
    • Congenital syphilis
    • Atelectasis
  2. The unexpanded lungs may float(False + ve) in cases of
    • Putrefaction
    • Artificial respiration
  • Fodere's test(Static test): Weight of lungs before respiration → 30-40g and after respiration → 60-66g
  • Wredin's test: Assesses the changes in the middle ear. The gelatinous substance in the middle ear is replaced by air if respiration has taken place.
  • Breslau's second life test: Also known as the stomach bowel test, the stomach and the duodenum are tested. This test is done to determine whether the baby was born alive or not. It works on the principle that some air is swallowed during respiration in a live-born child. Detecting the presence of this air in these viscera constitutes the basis for this test.

Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 2nd edition, PC Dixit, Page No. 175-177.

question_text: All the following increase the rate of postmortem cooling except:
option_a: Higher humidity and rapid air velocity
explanation:
• Obesity decreases the rate of postmortem cooling.

Factors increasing the rate of postmortem cooling:

  • The greater difference in the temperature between the body and the atmosphere
  • Large body surface area
  • Children and old aged people
  • Higher humidity and rapid air velocity
  • A body immersed in running water

Rate of cooling is decreased in:

  • Excess fat, as the fat is bad conductor of heat
  • Clothing
  • Body covered with clothing
  • Bodies in small, ill-ventilated room

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 113
