question_text: An autopsy may be performed at the site of recovery of the body in all of the following cases except?
explanation:
In deaths due to RTA, autopsy is usually performed in an equipped mortuary.

An autopsy may be performed at the site of recovery of the body, in the following scenarios:

  • Advanced stage of putrefaction as materials of evidentiary value may be lost during transportation.
  • Exhumation
  • If the District Magistrate desires, it to be conducted at the site due to some law-and-order problems.

Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology: Principles & Practice, Krishan Vij, 5th edition, Page No. 18.

question_text: 'En masse' removal of organs in autopsy is which technique?
explanation:
Evisceration Methods (Techniques of autopsy) :

I. Letulle’s technique:

  • Described by Letulle.
  • Also known as, 'En masse' or 'En bloc' dissection
    En masse = In a group; all together
    En bloc = All together or all at the same time
  • In this technique, oral, cervical, thoracic, abdominal, and pelvic organs are removed as one large organ block.
  • Leaves all attachments intact.
  • Commonly done in medical colleges to teach students

II. Virchow's Method:

  • Organ by organ removal
  • Individual organ removal one by one.
  • Subsequent dissection of isolated organs.
  • Useful for assessing individual organ pathology.
  • Quick and effective for single organ focus.
  • Most common method in India

III. Gohn’s technique:

  • Developed by Ghon.
  • Also known as, 'Block by block' dissection
  • Cervical & thoracic organs, abdominal organs and the urogenital system are removed as separate organ blocks.

IV. In Situ Dissection:

  • Developed by Rokitansky.
  • Also known as In-situ dissection
  • Organs dissected in situ with minimal evisceration.
  • Rarely performed.
  • Done in infected & suspected infection cases.

Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th Edition, Page N0. 22; The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 80

question_text:
A second autopsy is performed in which of the following scenarios?
1. The relatives are not satisfied with the first autopsy report
2. The first autopsy was not performed in the light of the circumstances which are now available
3. The investigating authority demands a second autopsy
4. The first autopsy was done in the absence of the investigating officer
5. The first autopsy was done in the absence of relatives
explanation:
A second autopsy may be performed when:

  1. Relatives are not satisfied.
  2. New circumstances emerge, or
  3. The investigating officer demands it.

After an autopsy, when a repeat medicolegal postmortem is performed with the authorization by law it is called a second autopsy.

The Magistrate/commissioner of the police vested with such power, orders the second autopsy.

It is done usually by a board of 3 doctors.

The presence of first autopsy surgeon is must.

A second autopsy may be performed in the following cases:

  1. The relatives of the deceased are not satisfied with the first autopsy report and they have pointed out certain lapses in the first autopsy.
  2. The first autopsy was not performed in the light of the circumstances which are now available.
  3. The investigating authority demands a second autopsy for setting the investigation on the right track.

A second autopsy, as the name suggests, refers to a postmortem examination that occurs after another party has conducted the first autopsy. People interested in obtaining a second autopsy need a medical record review, according to the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 2nd edition, P C Dixit, Page No. 183

question_text: Mental ability to make a valid will is
option_a: Curren's rule is basis for this
explanation:
• Testamentary capacity (Testament = will): It is the mental ability of a person to make a valid will.
  • To make a valid Will, it should have following components:
    • He should be major.
    • The person should be of sound mind.
    • The person making Will should understand the nature of Will.
    • The person should have knowledge of his property that has to be disposed of.
    • The person should recognize the individuals who have moral claims to heir his property.
  • Curren’s rule states that “an accused person will not be criminally responsible, if at the time of committing the act, he did not have the capacity to regulate his conduct to the requirements of law, as a result of mental disease or defect”.
  • Vicarious liability is a legal doctrine that assigns liability for an injury to a person who did not cause the injury but who has a particular legal relationship to the person who did act negligently. It is also referred to as imputed negligence.
  • McNaughten's rule: An accused person is not criminally responsible, if it is proved that, at the time of committing the crime that he was suffering from such a defect of reason from disease of mind that he did not know the nature and quality of act he was doing or if he did know this that he did not know that what he was doing was wrong.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 376

question_text: Autopsy of a patient shows an entire absence of fat in the omentum, mesentery, and internal organs. Which of the following most likely leads to this?
explanation:
In starvation, the loss of adipose tissue will also be evident internally in the internal fat depots like omentum, mesentery and perirenal fat. This is never seen in wasting diseases and cancer.

Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology: Principles & Practice 5th edition, Krishan Vij, Page No. 174

question_text: Blood during autopsy is preserved in?
explanation:
Explanation:

For toxicological analysis, such as in cases of alcohol abuse, the preferred blood preservative is sodium fluoride.

Methods for preserving viscera include:

  • Saturated salt solution
  • Formalin fixation
  • Freezing
  • Alcohol preservation
  • Formaldehyde solution
  • Formalin-alcohol solution
  • Frozen section
  • Liquid nitrogen preservation

Specimens for Analysis

Explanation for other options:

Formalin (Option C): is widely used for general tissue preservation and fixation in anatomical pathology; however, it is not the preferred choice for toxicology autopsies, as it can interfere with toxicological test results.

question_text: A victim who allegedly died in a fire at his house was brought in for an autopsy. On examination, he has wounds that appear like lacerations on his forehead and extensor surfaces. There is no sign of bleeding within the deeper tissues in the wound. Which of the following can be an indicator of homicidal death?
option_c: Elevated COHb in blood of the heat hematoma
explanation:
In the above scenario, there is no evidence that indicates the victim might have died from a homicidal injury and that the fire may have been used to cover up the crime.

The lacerated-looking wounds found in this victim are spurious findings commonly found in burn victims.

Spurious wounds in burns:

  • Skin splits - Heated skin contracts markedly and splits often appear. These splits may be anywhere but are especially seen over extensor surfaces and joints, as well on the head. The false split will show no bleeding in the deeper tissues and its position is usually suggestive.
  • Heat hematoma - the mass of blood resembling a true extradural hematoma may form between the skull and the dura. This may arise either from venous sinuses or out of the diploic space in the skull through emissary venous channels.

(The heat hematoma will have an elevated level of carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) similar to blood in the rest of the body. However, in case of antemortem traumatic extradural hematoma, that occurred before the fire began, it will be free from carbon monoxide).

Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th Edition, Page No. 317

question_text: An autopsy revealed a gunshot entry wound with inverted edges and surrounding tattooing, but no evidence of blackening or singeing of hair. What is the most likely range of firing?
explanation:
Explanation:

A near shot (also known as a close-contact shot) is characterized by the following features:

  • Inverted wound margins: Indicate an entry wound.
  • Tattooing (stippling): Produced by partially burnt or unburnt gunpowder particles that become embedded in the skin.
  • Lack of blackening or singeing: Implies that the muzzle was close to the body but not in direct contact, preventing flame effects from reaching the skin.

Gunshot classification:

Explanation of other options:

Contact shot (Option A): Muzzle pressed against skin; burning and blackening occur inside the track.

Close shot (Option C): Tattooing, blackening, and singeing are all present.

Distant shot (Option D): No tattooing, blackening, or singeing - only abrasion collar seen.

References: Gunshot wounds

question_text: On autopsy examination of a victim of firearm injury, singeing of hair is seen around the entry wound, What is the likely distance between the gun and the victim?
explanation:
Singeing of hair and burning of skin is because of flame. The flame will travel up to 8cm in case of rifled firearm and up to 15cm in case of shotguns. So, the answer for the above question is <15cm.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 164, 168.

question_text: During a forensic autopsy, a gunshot victim is examined, and the doctor observes that the firearm injury has a stellate shape. What will be the range of a gunshot?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • A contact shot occurs when the muzzle of the firearm is placed directly against the skin at the time of firing.
  • In such cases, the hot gases and smoke are forced under the skin, causing it to split and produce a stellate (star-shaped) wound.
  • Findings may include soot deposition, burning, or blackening around the entry wound. This stellate appearance is considered a classic sign of a contact firearm injury.

Explanation of Other Options:

Close shot (Option A): Seen when the muzzle is close but not touching the skin. Characterized by powder tattooing (stippling) and the presence of soot around the wound. Stellate splitting is not typically seen.

Near shot (Option C): Occurs when the firearm is fired from a slightly greater distance. There may be powder tattooing without soot deposition, but no stellate wound.

Distant shot (Option D): At long range, only a clean circular entry wound is produced, with no powder tattooing or soot deposition. Stellate pattern is absent.

Reference: Gunshot wounds

question_text: While doing an autopsy on a victim of strangulation, you are examining his brain. Which of the following areas of the brain is the most likely to show evidence of hypoxic damage in this victim?
explanation:
From the given options, the hippocampus is most likely to show evidence of damage in the case of a hypoxic brain injury like strangulation. However, third and fourth cortical layers are best for displaying the histological changes of hypoxia.

The parts of the brain most suitable for seeking evidence of hypoxic damage are:

  • Hippocampus (especially CA1 sector = Sommer's area and subiculum)
  • Cerebellar folia
  • Globus pallidus in the basal ganglia
  • Boundary zones of the cerebral cortex where the grey matter is most vulnerable because it lies at the terminal reaches of the arterial supply (for example, parasagittally at the middle frontal gyrus where the watershed between middle and anterior cerebral arteries lies). The third and fourth cortical layers are best for displaying the histological changes of hypoxia.

Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th Edition, Page No. 207

question_text: A dead body with an alleged history of suicide by hanging has come to mortuary for autopsy. On external examination, there was a ligature mark covering about one-third of the circumference of neck, salivary stain, dilated pupils and opened right eye and closed left eye. The reason for opened right eye is
explanation:
The phenomenon of the right eye remaining open in a hanging case is due to the compression of the cervical sympathetic chain on the right side of the neck. The cervical sympathetic chain controls autonomic functions in the head and neck, including the eyelid (via the levator palpebrae superioris muscle) and pupil (via the dilator pupillae muscle).

Mechanism:

Compression of the cervical sympathetic chain by the ligature disrupts sympathetic nerve activity on the affected side (in this case, the right side).

This leads to a loss of sympathetic input, resulting in:

Ptosis (drooping of the eyelid) or incomplete eyelid closure on the affected side.

The right eye remains open because the sympathetic control of eyelid closure is impaired.

Additionally, compression can also affect pupillary response, leading to pupil dilation (mydriasis) on the opposite side or sometimes on the same side, depending on the pressure distribution.

This autonomic dysfunction contributes to the asymmetry of eyelid appearance, such as one eye being open while the other remains closed, a common finding in cases of hanging.

Rule Out:

(a) Compression of carotid artery:

Compression of the carotid artery would result in compromised blood flow to the brain, leading to hypoxia and loss of consciousness. While this is critical in the mechanism of death by hanging, it does not explain why the right eye remains open.

(b) Compression of internal jugular vein:

Compression of the jugular vein impedes venous return from the brain, causing congestion and cyanosis of the face. However, this does not directly affect the sympathetic nerve supply to the eyelids and, therefore, is unrelated to the phenomenon of one eye remaining open.

(d) Compression of vagus nerve:

The vagus nerve is primarily involved in parasympathetic functions, including heart rate regulation and control of visceral functions. While vagus nerve compression can lead to cardiac arrest in cases of hanging, it does not influence the eyelid's ability to open or close.

Key Takeaways:

Compression of the cervical sympathetic chain in hanging cases causes autonomic dysfunction, including:

Ptosis or incomplete eyelid closure.

Pupil dilation on the same or opposite side, depending on the knot's position.

The asymmetrical appearance of the eyes (e.g., one open and one closed) is a forensic clue to the direction and impact of the ligature knot.

Structures compressed in hanging (arteries, veins, nerves) result in distinct clinical and forensic findings. However, eyelid asymmetry is specifically linked to cervical sympathetic chain compression.

Forensic examination of such findings is crucial for confirming the mechanism of hanging and differentiating it from other causes of death.

question_text: During autopsy, a doctor ties the bronchus and submerges the lungs in water to observe if they float or sink. What is this procedure called?
explanation:
Explanation:

The described procedure in which the bronchus is tied and the lungs are submerged in water to observe whether they float or sink is called the Hydrostatic test.

Also known as Raygat's test, Breslau's first life test, or the lung floatation test, this method helps determine whether an infant has taken a breath after birth.

If respiration has occurred, the alveoli expand and fill with air, decreasing the lung';s specific gravity to less than 1, causing the lungs to float in water. Conversely, unrespired lungs, being denser, will sink.

The test evaluates lung buoyancy as an indication of air entry and is also used as supportive evidence in drowning, since inhalation of water during drowning increases the lungs' buoyancy.

Explanation of other options:

Gettler's test (Option A): Compares chloride levels in blood from the right and left heart chambers; in drowning, the left side shows reduced chloride concentration.

Ploucquet's test (Option B): Determines the ratio of lung weight to body weight to assess whether respiration occurred.

Diatom's test (Option D): Detects diatoms (microscopic algae) in tissues and organs to confirm ante-mortem drowning, as their presence indicates inhalation of water before death.

Key takeaways:

  • Floating lungs → live birth or respiration occurred.
  • Non-floating lungs → stillbirth or no respiration.
  • Hydrostatic test is supportive, not definitive, for live birth determination.

References: Hydrostatic test

question_text:
You are working as a medical officer at a PHC. A 17-year-old girl presents after an alleged sexual assault and refuses to undergo physical examination. Which of the following steps should you take next as per the POCSO Act provisions?
1. Prophylaxis for sexually transmitted diseases, including HIV, should be offered.
2. It is mandatory to register a medico-legal case in all cases of child sexual abuse.
3. Medical examination must be performed regardless of consent in minors under 18 years.
4. Arrange a monthly follow-up for at least six months to check for the development of psychiatric disorders.
explanation:
Explanation:

Consent is still required for examination of minors, but the doctor must register an MLC, offer STD prophylaxis, and ensure long-term psychiatric follow-up after a sexual assault under the POCSO Act 2012.

POCSO Act, 2012 - Medical Examination & Care Provisions:

  • Medical examination of the child must be done in the least distressing manner.
  • Doctors should not demand completion of legal records/procedures or documentation before starting treatment or examination.
  • Legal procedures can be completed after initiating medical care.
  • Doctors must register a medico-legal case in all cases of child sexual abuse. (Statement 2)
  • Failure to report such cases can lead to six months' imprisonment and/or a fine under Section 21 of the POCSO Act, 2012.
  • Duties of the Registered Medical Practitioner:
    • Collect evidence after a thorough medical examination.
    • Treat physical and genital injuries.
    • Conduct an age assessment of the victim (if required).
    • Offer prophylaxis for sexually transmitted diseases, including HIV. (Statement 1)
    • Discuss emergency contraceptives with the pubertal child and her parent.
    • Perform baseline evaluation for mental health issues.
    • Arrange a monthly follow-up for at least six months to check for the development of psychiatric disorders. (Statement 4)
    • Provide family counselling.
    • Assist the court in interviewing the child and testifying in court.

Reference:

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4557243/

question_text: During the autopsy of a man who died from prolonged starvation, which of the following findings is most likely?
explanation:
Explanation:

In starvation, little or no food enters the stomach and intestine, so bile secretion into the duodenum is greatly reduced. As a result, bile accumulates and the gallbladder becomes markedly distended.

Key autopsy features of starvation

  • Intense hunger lasts roughly 30-48 hours.
  • Survival: about 10-12 days without food and water, or 6-8 weeks with water but no food.
  • Fatal loss: ~40% of body weight, 70-90% of fat, and ~20% of protein.
  • General: emaciation, dry lustreless hair, brittle nails, pale skin (often with ankle oedema).
  • Fat loss from subcutaneous tissue and omentum (breast and orbital fat are lost later).
  • Organ changes:
    • Heart: atrophied with empty chambers
    • Lungs: pale and collapsed
    • Liver: shrunken with areas of necrosis
    • Intestinal mucosa: thin and delicate, "tissue-paper" appearance
    • Brain: relatively spared in size

Explanation for Other Options:

Enlarged liver (option B): Starvation causes hepatic atrophy and necrosis, not enlargement. Fatty infiltration or hepatomegaly is typical of alcoholic liver disease or certain metabolic disorders, not simple starvation.

Expanded lungs (option C): Lungs in starvation are usually pale and collapsed because of general wasting and reduced perfusion, the opposite of expansion.

Hypertrophied heart (option D): The heart becomes small and atrophied with thin walls and empty chambers. Hypertrophy is more typical of chronic hypertension or valvular disease, not caloric deprivation.

Key takeaway:

question_text: A 34-year-old industrial worker develops nausea, vomiting, garlic odor on breath, and yellowish discoloration of the sclera. He dies after 3 days of illness. On autopsy, the liver is found to be enlarged, yellow, soft, and fatty. Which of the following poisons is most likely responsible?
explanation:
Explanation:

Phosphorus poisoning is associated with severe hepatotoxicity, characterized by:

  • Fatty change (steatosis) in the liver: Yellow, enlarged, soft, and greasy appearance.
  • Progression to acute yellow atrophy in severe cases.
  • Garlic odor in breath and gastric contents.
  • Luminescence of vomitus or stomach contents (due to elemental phosphorus).
  • Jaundice, coagulopathy, and multiorgan hemorrhages on postmortem.
  • Seen in rodenticides, fireworks, and industrial exposure.

Postmortem findings in phosphorus poisoning:

External

  1. Emaciation, purpuric haemorrhages in the skin, jaundice and the smell of garlic may be present.
  2. Mucous membrane of the mouth is corroded.
  3. Hypostasis is dark brown in color.

Internal

  1. Multiple haemorrhages are seen in the muscles, serosal and mucosal membranes of the GIT and respiratory tract, liver, kidneys, endocardium, pericardium, epicardium, peritoneum, lungs and brain.
  2. Stomach and intestines: Mucous membranes are yellowish or greyish white in colour, softened, thickened, inflamed and corroded in patches; luminous material may be found in the stomach. Contents may smell of garlic.
  3. Liver: Swollen, yellow, soft, fatty and easily ruptured.
  4. Kidneys: Enlarged, greasy, yellow.
  5. Heart: Flabby, pale and shows fatty degeneration.
  6. Lungs: Fat emboli may be found in the pulmonary arterioles and capillaries.

Histopathology: Toxic hepatitis with extensive necrosis, ballooning degeneration, and steatosis.

Key Takeaway:

Yellow fatty liver on autopsy is a classical finding in phosphorus poisoning.

question_text: Juice of Semecarpus anacardium can be used for:
explanation:
Explanation:

Medicolegal aspects of semecarpus anacardium:

  • Accidental poisoning may result from the administration of juice by quacks for treatment of rheumatic pain and worm infestation.
  • Cases of contact dermatitis (due to urushiol) related to its use as hair dye, voodoo treatment, remedy for eczema or tattoo removal have been reported.
  • Anaphylaxis due to unintentional oral ingestion related to marking nut has also been reported.
  • Juice may be introduced into the vagina, as a punishment for infidelity.
  • For criminal abortion, juice is applied to the cervical os by means of abortion stick.
  • It may be used by malingerers to produce conjunctivitis or to support a false charge of assault; lesions produced simulate bruises.
  • The juice may be thrown on the face to cause injury (vitriolage).

Key Takeaway:

The irritant juice of Semecarpus anacardium may be used for the purpose of vitriolage, and also to produce artificial bruises and artificial conjunctivitis.

question_text: In cases of alcohol abuse, which substance is blood usually preserved in during an autopsy?
explanation:
Explanation:

For toxicological analysis, especially in cases of alcohol abuse, sodium fluoride is the preferred preservative for blood samples.

Methods of preserving viscera include:

  • Saturated salt solution
  • Formalin fixation
  • Freezing
  • Alcohol preservation
  • Formaldehyde solution
  • Formalin-alcohol solution
  • Frozen section
  • Liquid nitrogen

Explanation of other options:

Formalin (Option B): is widely used for general tissue preservation and fixation in anatomical pathology; however, it is not the preferred choice for toxicological analysis during autopsy, as it can interfere with toxicology test results.

question_text: Cafe coronary commonly occurs when a person is:
explanation:
'CAFÉ CORONARY' SYNDROME':

  • A popular term ‘cafe coronary’ was coined by Dr. Roger Haugen, Medical Examiner of Broward County, Florida for such impaction of food in the respiratory passage.
  • The victim may be observed slumping over the dining table or collapsing suddenly while walking across the room after having meals, with no signs of respiratory distress or any of the ‘classic signs of asphyxia’.
  • The original series of deaths involved well-nourished businessmen dying suddenly and unexpectedly in restaurants and cafes, while sitting or shortly after sitting in their chairs, as if they died of heart attack. Hence, the name ‘cafe coronary’.
  • However, autopsy usually reveals a bolus of food in the pharynx or larynx. Many cases have been reported where the victim was merely seen dead while sitting or just after sitting in a chair, the mode of death probably being cardiac arrest due to overactivity of parasympathetic nervous system through the stimulation of branches of vagus nerve supplying the laryngeal and/or pharyngeal mucosa.
  • Fairly high level of alcohol has been found in most cases of cafe coronary deaths. The suppression of gag reflex due to alcohol or drugs makes the individual susceptible to this calamity.
  • Senile persons in retirement homes and mentally retarded children in institutions are also vulnerable.

References: Knight's Forensic Pathology 4th edition Page no 362; Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology: Principles and Practice, Krishan Vij, 5th edition, Page No. 117

question_text: A 22-year-old male is found dead in his room. On autopsy, the stomach contents emit a strong garlic-like odour, and red-velvet discolouration of the gastric mucosa is noted, along with greyish granular material resembling pesticide powder. Which of the following is the most likely poison involved?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of a strong garlic-like odour, black gastric mucosal discolouration, and grey granular pesticide material is characteristic of acute arsenic poisoning.

  • Arsenic becomes toxic through its compounds, which disrupt cellular respiration by binding to mitochondrial enzymes.
  • The vascular endothelium is particularly affected, leading to oedema, haemorrhage, and tissue damage.
  • Poisoning usually arises from ingestion of arsenic oxide or arsenites, either accidentally, occupationally, or intentionally in suicides and homicides.
  • It can manifest as acute or chronic forms.
  • In chronic cases, the diagnosis is more difficult, often mistaken for gastrointestinal illness.
  • The clinical features of arsenic poisoning are summarised below
  • The skin may show widespread changes, appearing dry, scaly, and thickened. A "raindrop" type of spotty pigmentation can occur, particularly in skin folds and on the forehead and neck. This is shown in the image below.
  • Hair loss, facial swelling, and puffiness resembling myxoedema may also be seen.
  • Inside the body, the stomach can appear normal or reveal chronic gastritis with thickened mucosa and submucosa, sometimes with mucus buildup and patchy redness of the folds.
  • Hemorrhagic gastritis may also occur. The small intestine is often swollen, reddened, and congested, with thickened mucosa resembling general enteritis.
  • The intestinal contents may be watery and abundant, described as "rice-water."

Explanation of other options:

Organophosphorus compound (Option A): Toxic effects appear when cholinesterase activity falls to about 30% of normal. Death may occur within an hour of ingestion, but more often takes several hours in fatal cases. At autopsy, parathion is recognisable because it is mixed with kerosene, giving it a distinct smell, and may also contain green dyes used in commercial preparations. The stomach contents can show an oily, greenish layer.

Aluminium phosphide (Option C): Aluminium phosphide is a commonly used fumigant pesticide in India, available as greyish-green tablets under various trade names. When exposed to air or moisture, it releases phosphine gas, which causes widespread organ damage.

Symptoms include a metallic or garlicky taste, nausea, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhoea, and cough.

Carbamates (Option D): Carbamate insecticides act by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase through carbamylation, producing toxic effects similar to organophosphorus insecticides. Unlike organophosphorus agents, their impact is shorter in duration.
