question_text: A victim of a house fire is brought to you for autopsy. On examination, you find an intracranial collection of blood. It is brown and friable, and the adjacent brain tissue shows discoloration. The carboxyhaemoglobin level in the extradural blood is found to be the same as in the peripheral blood. What is the likely diagnosis?
option_d: A or C, depending on further pathological examination
explanation:
The diagnosis in the given scenario is that of a heat hematoma.

Heat hematoma is an artefact that mimics EDH(Extradural haemorrhage). This occurs when the head has been exposed to severe external heat sufficient to burn the scalp and skull. The blood may be extruded from the diploë and venous sinuses into the extradural space to produce a heat hematoma. This false hematoma is brown and friable, and the adjacent brain tissue shows hardening and discoloration from the heat.

There is often a significant level of carboxyhaemoglobin in the body if the death occurred when the fire was in progress. This should be of the same concentration in the heat hematoma as in the peripheral blood. If the victim suffered a head injury before the fire started (indicating an extradural haemorrhage), then there should be little or no carboxyhaemoglobin in the hematoma.

Extradural hematoma vs subdural hematoma

  • Extradural haematoma (EDH) is a blood clot that forms on the outside of the natural covering of the brain ('dura mater'), while acute subdural haematoma (ASDH) refers to a blood clot on the inner surface of the dura that appears within the first few days of head injury.
  • The difference arises from the pathogenesis. An epidural haematoma caused by blunt trauma results from dural arteriovenous injury due to an external blow, whereas a heat haematoma is caused by blood exuding from the venous sinus following heat contraction of the dura mater.

Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th Edition, Page No.184, 185

question_text: A 48-year-old man was brought unconscious into the ER after he met with a head-on collision accident. His GCS was 4/15 and CT brain did not reveal any significant haemorrhage. MRI brain revealed multiple small elliptical lesions. Which is the most reliable indicator of this condition?
explanation:
• The given scenario is most likely suggestive of diffuse axonal injury. The most reliable indicator is beta-amyloid precursor protein, seen earliest at 2-3 hours.
  • The disruption of axons leads to bulbous and clubbed 'retraction balls or globes' in the axons in the cerebral hemispheres, cerebellum and brainstem.
  • Disturbance of axoplasmic transport causes accumulation of substances in damaged axons that can be demonstrated immunohistochemically.
  • At present, β-amyloid precursor protein (βAPP) is considered to be the most reliable indicator of axonal damage, revealing axonal injury within 2–3 hours of the insult, whereas it takes about 12–18 hours for axonal bulbs to become visible on routine or silver stains.
  • However, one should keep in mind that βAPP is not specific to head injury but is an indicator of derangement of fast axonal transport, which has also been demonstrated in other pathological conditions

Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th Edition, Page No. 203

question_text: A patient died after a car accident and the cause was suspected as diffuse axonal injury. Forensic pathology examination revealed the following finding. After how many hours of injury does this finding appear?
explanation:
The given image shows retraction balls/globes which appear at 12-18 hours after injury.

Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) is primarily a non-impact rotational acceleration–deceleration phenomenon, deformation by stretching probably being the most significant factor.

The disruption of axons leads to bulbous and clubbed ‘retraction balls or globes’ in the axons in the cerebral hemispheres, cerebellum and brainstem.

It takes about 12–18 hours for axonal bulbs to become visible on routine or silver stains.

The number of retraction balls begins to decrease 2-3 weeks after injury. This is followed by the appearance of a cluster of microglial cells, astrocytosis, and demyelination.

The forces generated by violent shaking or rotational injury (as in a passenger ejected from a moving vehicle) can produce stretching of axons in cerebral white matter, called diffuse axonal injury. The force may be strong enough to shear off axons, the ends of which retract into globoid shapes that appear with this silver stain of white matter as "retraction balls". CT imaging of the brain may show subtle petechial hemorrhages at the interface of gray and white matter.

Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th Edition Page No. 203

question_text: Lucid interval is seen in
explanation:
Lucid interval in Psychiatry: This is a period occurring in mental illness, during which all the symptoms of mental illness disappear completely. The individual is able to judge his acts soundly, and he becomes legally liable for his acts. The period of lucid interval varies from person to person and from time to time in the same person, and as such one cannot be certain about the time when a person passes again in the state of mental illness. Therefore, if he commits an offence, he cannot be completely held responsible, because it is very difficult to know, whether he was suffering from some mental abnormality at the time of committing the offence. In mania and melancholia lucid intervals are common.

Lucid interval in head injury: Lucid interval is the period of consciousness between two periods of unconsciousness. The classic lucid interval occurs in 30 -40% of patients with EDH. Initially, the concussive force that caused the head injury results in an alteration of consciousness. After consciousness is recovered, the EDH continues to expand until the mass effect of the haemorrhage itself results in increased intracranial pressure, a decreased level of consciousness, and a possible herniation syndrome.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 197, 370

question_text: Which vessel is responsible for bleeding in an extradural hemorrhage?
explanation:
Explanation:

The middle meningeal artery is the primary bleeding vessel in an extradural (epidural) hemorrhage.

Intracranial Hemorrhages

  • The layers from outside to inside are: skull (cranium), dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater, and brain tissue.
  • The middle meningeal artery runs between the skull and the dura mater.
  • It is most vulnerable at the pterion, where the frontal, parietal, sphenoid, and temporal bones converge.

Injury to this artery at the pterion often leads to extradural hemorrhage.

Anterior cerebral artery (Option D) is not involved in extradural hemorrhage

question_text: A 42-year-old patient, victim of a road traffic accident, presents with an epidural hematoma (EDH) due to rupture of the middle meningeal artery. Where is the likely site of impact?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The pterion is the weakest point on the lateral aspect of the skull, formed by the junction of four bones - frontal, parietal, temporal, and sphenoid.
  • The middle meningeal artery lies just deep to this area. Even a relatively minor trauma can rupture the artery here, leading to an epidural hematoma.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Initial concussion: brief loss of consciousness.
    • Lucid interval: patient regains consciousness, appears fine.
    • Expansion phase: progressive accumulation of arterial blood → increased ICP → neurological deterioration (headache, vomiting, hemiparesis, fixed dilated pupil due to uncal herniation).
  • CT finding: biconvex (lentiform) hyperdense collection that does not cross suture lines.

Explanation of Other Options:

Angle of mandible (Option B): Fractures here can injure the inferior alveolar nerve or facial artery, but not the middle meningeal artery.

Lambdoid suture (Option C): Injury in this region affects venous sinuses but is not associated with EDH from the middle meningeal artery.

Nasion (Option D): Trauma at the nasion leads to nasal bone or ethmoid fractures, sometimes CSF rhinorrhea, but not epidural hematoma.

Key Point:

Pterion fracture → middle meningeal artery rupture → epidural hematoma with lucid interval (classic sign).

Reference: Epidural hematoma

question_text: A temporary period of regained consciousness after a head injury, before deterioration occurs, is known as a lucid interval. This is classically associated with which type of intracranial haemorrhage?
explanation:
Explanation:

A lucid interval is most commonly associated with extradural (epidural) haemorrhage, although it can occasionally be seen in subdural haemorrhage. It occurs when an initial head injury causes a brief loss of consciousness due to concussion, followed by a temporary recovery period during which the patient appears alert and oriented. As blood accumulates in the epidural space, intracranial pressure rises, eventually leading to deterioration in consciousness.

Explanation for Other Options:

Subdural haemorrhage (option A): Usually presents with a gradually progressive decline in consciousness rather than a distinct lucid interval.

Parenchymal haemorrhage (option B): Bleeding within the brain tissue itself; consciousness deterioration is usually immediate or rapidly progressive.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage (option D): Typically presents with sudden severe headache, vomiting, and meningeal signs; lucid intervals are uncommon.

Key takeaway:

  • The term "lucid" or "latent interval" refers to this phase of normal consciousness after the initial trauma.
  • During this period, the patient is legally considered capable, as they exhibit normal awareness and responsiveness.
  • Although classically linked with extradural haemorrhage, only about 27% of cases actually present with a lucid interval, so its presence or absence cannot be solely relied upon for diagnosis.

question_text: A 70 year old lady with an alleged history of impact on head following fall on an ice slab presents to the ER after 4 days with symptoms of headache, nausea, excessive sleep and lethargy. CT scan showed a crescent shaped hyper density crossing the sutural lines. She died after 4 days. What is the finding in the depicted image?
explanation:
The clinical scenario described and the findings on the CT scan (crescent-shaped hyperdensity crossing the sutural lines) are indicative of a subdural hematoma (SDH). SDH typically occurs due to a venous bleed, often as a result of trauma (like a fall) that causes tearing of the bridging veins between the dura mater and the brain. This leads to the accumulation of blood in the subdural space, which is located between the dura mater and the arachnoid layer of the meninges.

Key features of SDH:

  • Crescent-shaped hyperdensity on CT scan, which is characteristic of SDH, especially if it crosses sutural lines.
  • Common in older adults due to brain atrophy, which increases the risk of bridging vein rupture.
  • The symptoms can develop days after the injury, as seen in this case (headache, nausea, lethargy).

Rule Out:

  1. EDH (Epidural Hematoma):
    • EDH usually presents as a biconvex (lens-shaped) hyperdensity on a CT scan, which does not cross sutural lines. It is typically due to an arterial bleed, often resulting from trauma to the middle meningeal artery. EDH presents more acutely with loss of consciousness and a lucid interval.
  2. SAH (Subarachnoid Hemorrhage):
    • SAH presents with diffuse blood in the subarachnoid space, seen on CT as hyperdensity around the brain. It typically involves the cerebral sulci and does not present with a crescent-shaped pattern or cross sutural lines like SDH.
  3. ICH (Intracerebral Hemorrhage):
    • ICH involves bleeding within the brain parenchyma itself and is seen as a localized area of hyperdensity on CT. It does not have the characteristic crescent shape or cross sutural lines associated with SDH.

Key Takeaways:

  • Subdural hematoma (SDH) presents as a crescent-shaped hyperdensity on CT, often crossing sutural lines. It is associated with venous bleeding, typically from bridging veins.
  • Epidural hematoma (EDH) appears as biconvex hyperdensity and is usually arterial in origin.
  • Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) and intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) have different CT appearances and do not present with the crescent-shaped pattern characteristic of SDH.

question_text: A comatose patient was brought to ER with an alleged history of head injury. He was immediately intubated and sent for NCCT which showed normal findings. The most likely diagnosis is
explanation:
Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) is a type of traumatic brain injury (TBI) that involves widespread damage to the brain's white matter. It typically occurs due to rapid acceleration or deceleration, such as in high-impact accidents. DAI often results in coma or severe cognitive dysfunction. One of the key characteristics of DAI is that it may not be immediately visible on non-contrast CT scans (NCCT), especially in the early stages, since it primarily affects the axons and the white matter rather than causing large, identifiable masses or hemorrhages.

Rule Out:

  1. EDH (Epidural Hematoma):
    • An epidural hematoma typically shows up as a lens-shaped hyperdensity on CT scans, typically located between the skull and the dura mater. It often results from trauma to the skull, leading to bleeding from an arterial source (e.g., the middle meningeal artery). Given that the NCCT in this case showed normal findings, EDH is less likely.
  2. SDH (Subdural Hematoma):
    • A subdural hematoma often appears as a crescent-shaped hyperdensity on NCCT, usually located between the dura mater and the brain surface. Similar to EDH, it results from the rupture of venous structures (usually the bridging veins). The absence of abnormal findings on the NCCT rules out SDH.
  3. SAH (Subarachnoid Hemorrhage):
    • Subarachnoid hemorrhage typically presents with blood in the subarachnoid space and is often seen on CT scans as high-density areas around the brain. If there is no blood visible on the NCCT, SAH is unlikely.

Key Takeaways:

  • Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) may not always show up on non-contrast CT scans, especially in the early stages.
  • Epidural hematoma (EDH), subdural hematoma (SDH), and subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) are all more likely to show characteristic findings on CT scans, which is not the case here.

question_text: The body of a hiker is found naked on a snow trail. It is hypothesised that he actively undressed just minutes prior to his death. Which of the following statements regarding this phenomenon is true?
option_a: Indicator of mild to moderate hypothermia
option_b: Associated with increased carbon monoxide in circulation
option_d: The mechanism is that of peripheral vasodilation
explanation:
The given phenomenon of paradoxical undressing is likely due to peripheral vasodilation.

Reciprocal or paradoxical undressing:

  • This is a strange condition seen in accidental hypothermia, particularly in old persons.
  • In this person take off some or all of their clothing.
  • The cause of the condition is not known.
  • It may be due to long exposure to severe cold producing paralysis of the thermal regulatory mechanism (once the body temperature has fallen below about 30°C).
  • This results in failure of vasoconstriction of arterioles of the skin which results in a flow of blood from the core of the body (Reflex vasodilation), thus giving an exaggerated sensation of warmth.
  • Terminal hallucinations occur.
  • Because of the great discomfort (as he feels hot), the person may undress himself.
  • In such case, there may be suspicion of sexual offence.

Other associated features include:

  • Bruises and scratches of the knees, shanks, and upper limbs caused by late-phase attempts at crawling.
  • The hide-and-die phenomenon in some cases.

Paradoxical undressing is a phenomenon characterizing some fatal hypothermia cases. The victims, despite low environmental temperatures, paradoxically remove their clothes due to a sudden feeling of warmth.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 243

question_text: An autopsy was done on a burn victim. Which of the following is a reliable indicator that the victim was alive while the fire was in progress?
option_b: Redness of the exposed skin surface
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Elevated levels of carbon monoxide in the circulating blood (measured as carboxyhemoglobin levels) and the presence of carbon particles in the air passages and lungs are considered reliable indicators that the victim was alive while the fire was in progress.
  • This is because carbon monoxide is inhaled and absorbed into the bloodstream only if the circulatory system is functioning (i.e., the person is alive). Similarly, soot particles would only be inhaled into the lungs if respiration occurred.

Option A: Pugilistic attitude or heat stiffening is due to coagulation of muscle proteins whe the body is subjected to heat. It can be seen in both antemortem and post-mortem burns.

Option B: While a "red flare" indicates a response by living tissue, the classical distinction of a "red flare" is unsafe as an index of infliction before death in burns, as redness can occur in both ante-mortem and post-mortem burns.

Blistering of the skin (Option D): While blistering often occurs in ante-mortem burns, blisters can also form post-mortem; as in cases of post-mortem burns and putrefaction. However, post-mortem blisters contain air, whereas antemortem burn blister contain albumin with RBCs, WBCs and Chloride.

Key Takeaway:

The most reliable indicator that a burn victim was alive during a fire is the presence of elevated carboxyhemoglobin levels in the blood and/or carbon particles in the air passages and lungs, as these signify active inhalation and circulation.

question_text: Paradoxical undressing is seen in case of:
explanation:
Paradoxical undressing is a phenomenon observed in the advanced stages of hypothermia, where individuals experiencing severe cold exposure begin to remove their clothing despite the dangerously low body temperatures.

This behavior occurs due to the failure of the body's thermoregulatory mechanisms. In severe hypothermia, vasoconstriction (the narrowing of blood vessels to conserve heat) starts to fail, causing sudden vasodilation. This leads to a sensation of intense heat in the skin, prompting individuals to undress.

It is a hallmark sign of the terminal stage of hypothermia, often preceding unconsciousness or death.

Rule Out:

b) Datura poisoning: Datura poisoning typically causes symptoms such as delirium, hallucinations, dry mouth, and hyperthermia (increased body temperature). There is no link between datura poisoning and paradoxical undressing.

c) Immersion syndrome: This condition occurs when someone is suddenly immersed in cold water, causing a rapid drop in core temperature and possible cardiac arrest (cold shock). While hypothermia can follow, immersion syndrome itself does not directly lead to paradoxical undressing.

d) Barbiturate poisoning: Barbiturate poisoning primarily causes central nervous system depression, leading to symptoms like drowsiness, respiratory depression, and unconsciousness. It does not cause paradoxical undressing.

Key Takeaways:

Paradoxical Undressing in Hypothermia: This occurs due to the loss of vasoconstriction and sudden vasodilation, giving a false sensation of warmth.

Advanced Hypothermia Sign: It is a critical indicator of late-stage hypothermia and impending fatality if not treated immediately.

Rule Out Based on Mechanism: Conditions like datura poisoning, immersion syndrome, or barbiturate poisoning have distinct symptoms unrelated to paradoxical undressing.

question_text: A patient came to OPD with soddened burn injury along with erythema, blisters and a line of demarcation over his right thigh. The injury is due to
explanation:
A moist burn, also known as a scald, occurs when the skin is exposed to hot liquids or steam. This type of injury typically presents with:

Sodden (waterlogged) appearance of the affected area due to the involvement of liquids.

Erythema (redness) indicating superficial damage to the skin.

Blisters which result from fluid accumulation under the damaged epidermis.

A line of demarcation, separating the injured and uninjured areas, highlighting the extent of exposure to the hot liquid.

In the scenario described, the soddened burn injury, erythema, blisters, and a clear line of demarcation strongly suggest a moist burn caused by hot liquid exposure on the right thigh.

Rule Out

Dry burns (a):

Dry burns are caused by exposure to dry heat sources like flames, heated surfaces, or heated objects. They typically result in charring, blackened skin, or parchment-like dryness without the sodden appearance seen in moist burns. These characteristics are absent in this case.

Chemical burn (c):

Chemical burns occur due to corrosive substances (acids or alkalis) and are marked by irregular and patchy tissue damage. Blisters and erythema can occur, but the soddened appearance and clear line of demarcation are uncommon, as chemicals spread unevenly and continue to cause damage unless neutralized.

Electric burn (d):

Electric burns are caused by electrical currents passing through the body, creating characteristic entry and exit wounds. These burns do not involve soddening or blistering like moist burns. Instead, they are dry and often accompanied by deeper tissue damage along the path of the current.

Key Takeaways

Moist burns (scalds) are caused by hot liquids or steam and exhibit soddened skin, erythema, blisters, and a line of demarcation.

Differentiating between burn types relies on analyzing the injury's appearance, mechanism, and surrounding circumstances.

Proper identification is essential for determining the cause, providing appropriate treatment, and addressing any forensic concerns if necessary.

question_text: Which of the following is not a thermal injury?
explanation:
Gunshot wounds are mechanical injury; not thermal injury.


Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 242

question_text: Which of the following statements about burns is true?
option_a: Minimum temperature for producing burn is 42°C for 5-6 hours
option_b: Minimum temperature for producing burn is 40°C for 3 hours
option_c: Minimum temperature for producing burn is 44°C for 5-6 hours
option_d: Minimum temperature for producing burn is 44°C for 3 hours
explanation:
The degrees of thermal damage were investigated by Moritz and Henriques, who found that the lowest temperature that would cause damage was 44°C, though it required no fewer than 5 hours before a burn appeared.

Only 3 seconds was needed, however, if the object was at 60°C.

Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th Edition, Page Number-311.

question_text: Which of the following statements about heat fractures of the skull is false?
option_b: Seen at the base of the skull
option_c: It requires 20 minutes of heat application
option_d: It does not involve the suture lines
explanation:
Heat fractures are usually seen on either side of the skull above the temples. Sometimes they may be bilateral. They consist of several lines which radiate from a common centre and in some cases may fragment. The skull is often friable with flaking of the outer table.

Fractures to the base of the skull are unheard of in the case of thermal fractures and should be considered to be an antemortem injury.

Heat fractures of the skull take approximately 20 minutes of heat application before the skull starts to crack

The pattern of fracture commonly resembles a spider web. Heat fractures usually do not involve the sutures of the skull even in young persons with un-united sutures. Heat fracture may cross a suture line.

HEAT INDUCED FRACTURES

Reference: Forensic Medicine: Clinical and Pathological Aspects, Page No. 370; The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 249

question_text: Identify the type the burn
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The image displays a characteristic reddish, fern-like pattern on the skin.
  • This appearance is consistent with filigree burn. Filigree burns are also known by several other terms, including arborescent marks, Lichtenberg flower marks, feathering, or ferning, and keraunographic burn.
  • These marks are a superficial, tortuous, thin, and irregular reddish pattern on the skin, often resembling the branches of a tree.
  • They are a finding seen in about 20-33% of lightning strike cases.
  • It's not a true burn. It is due to lysis of RBCs along the path of electric current
  • Do not lie either along the vascular channels or nerve pathways.
  • Disappears in about 1-2 days
  • Common sites for these marks include the shoulder, front of the chest, and flanks.
  • Pink to brownish in color

Crocodile skin (Option A):'In high-voltage burns, such as those sustained from high-tension grid transmission cables, where the voltage is in the multi-kilovolt range, sparking may occur over many centimetres. This can cause multiple spark lesions giving rise to a "crocodile-skin" effect

Joule burn (Option B): It is specific and diagnostic of contact with electricity and is found at the point of entry of the current. It is endogenous thermal burn due to the heat generated in the body from electricity. These marks are round or oval, shallow craters, one to three cm. in diameter, and have a ridge of skin of about one to three mm. high, around part or the whole of their circumference. The crater floor is lined with pale flattened skin. In some marks, the skin may break within or near the margin of the crater, resembling that of a broken blister.

Spark lesion (Option D): When the contact is less firm, an air gap is formed between the skin and the conductor. Thus, the current traverses the gap as a spark. This causes the outer skin keratin to melt over a small area. On cooling, the keratin fuses into a hard brownish nodule, usually raised above the surrounding surface.

Key Takeaway:

The distinct fern-like or tree-branching pattern of reddish marks on the skin, as shown in the image, is characteristic of a filigree burn (also known as Lichtenberg flower marks/Arborescent marks/Feathering/Ferning/Keraunographic burns), which is a sign of a lightning strike and is not considered a true burn.

question_text: True about the picture shown below
explanation:
The picture likely shows Lichtenberg figures (also called ferning or arborescent marks), a characteristic finding in cases of lightning strikes. These marks are transient cutaneous patterns caused by the passage of high-voltage electrical energy through the skin.

  1. Formation:
    • Lichtenberg figures are not burns but rather a dermal reaction due to the rupture of capillaries from the electric discharge.
    • The branching or fern-like appearance follows the path of least resistance, which is determined by the moisture content of the skin and underlying tissues.
  2. Color:
    • The marks are typically pink to brownish in color, consistent with minor vascular damage.
  3. Duration:
    • These marks are transient and disappear within 1-2 days, leaving no permanent scarring.

Rule Out:

  1. Seen in all cases of lightning (a):
    • Why ruled out: Lichtenberg figures are not seen in all cases of lightning strikes. Their occurrence depends on the intensity of the strike and the individual's physiological response.
  2. It's a class of burn (b):
    • Why ruled out: Lichtenberg figures are not burns; they are vascular patterns caused by electrical energy. Burns from lightning strikes are typically deeper and more localized.
  3. Follows vascular channels (c):
    • Why ruled out: While the pattern resembles vascular structures, it does not follow vascular channels. It reflects the discharge path of electricity through the skin.

Key Takeaways:

  1. Lichtenberg figures:
    • Unique to lightning injuries and characterized by their transient, arborescent pattern.
    • They are diagnostic of lightning strikes but not always present.
  2. Not burns:
    • These marks are superficial and result from capillary rupture, not thermal injury.
  3. Color and duration:
    • Typically pink to brownish and disappear within 1-2 days without scarring.
  4. Forensic importance:
    • Presence of Lichtenberg figures is a crucial finding in determining the cause of death or injury in lightning strike cases.
    • Their transient nature emphasizes the importance of timely documentation.

question_text: In which of the following injuries is the pugilistic attitude of the victim seen?
explanation:
Pugilistic attitude (boxing, fencing or defence attitude):

  • The posture of a body which has been exposed to great heat is often characteristic.
  • The legs are flexed at the hips and knees, the arms are flexed at elbows and wrists and held out in front of the body, head slightly extended, all fingers are hooked like claws.
  • Contraction of paraspinal muscles often causes a marked opisthotonus, in an attitude commonly adopted by boxers.
  • This stiffening is due to the coagulation of proteins of the muscles and dehydration which cause contraction. The flexor muscles being bulkier than extensors contract more due to which joints of all limbs are flexed.
  • It occurs whether the person was alive or dead at the time of burning.

PUGILISTIC ATTITUDE

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 247

question_text: In which of the following injuries is the pugilistic attitude of the victim usually seen?
explanation:
Explanation:

The pugilistic attitude (also known as Heat stiffening, Boxing or Defence or Fencing attitude/posture) is caused by coagulation of muscle proteins when a body is exposed to high temperatures (>65°C), specifically in burn injuries.

  • Due to the bulk and strength of flexor muscles, they contract more than extensors during thermal exposure, resulting in flexed posture resembling a boxer's pose.
  • Body attains a posture of generalized flexion, except back; head slightly extended
  • This phenomenon occurs regardless of whether the person was alive or dead at the time of burning.

PUGILISTIC ATTITUDE

Electrical injury (Option A): While electrical injuries involve heat, the typical posture associated with them is often "tetanic spasm" or "grip marks" due to sustained muscle contraction during the electrocution. Pugilistic attitude may be seen in case high voltage electrocution; but very much uncommon.

Lightning injury (Option B): Lightning injuries are a type of electrical injury, but they often produce unique patterns like Lichtenberg figures and can cause immediate cardiac arrest or severe neurological effects.

Blast injury (Option D): Blast injuries result from exposure to explosions and can cause a wide range of trauma, including primary (pressure wave), secondary (projectiles), tertiary (body displacement), and quaternary/quinary (environmental/chemical) injuries. While muscle damage can occur, the characteristic pugilistic attitude is not typically associated with blast injuries.

Key Takeaway:

The pugilistic attitude is a distinctive post-mortem finding in burn injuries, resulting from the heat-induced coagulation and contraction of muscle proteins.

question_text: Which of the following features of electrical injury will develop if the contact with the electrocuting surface is poorly established?
explanation:
When the contact with the electrocuting surface is not firm, the skin lesion that develops is called a spark lesion.

Where the contact is less firm, so that an air gap (albeit narrow) exists between skin and conductor, the current jumps the gap as a spark.

This causes the outer skin keratin to melt over a small area. On cooling, the keratin fuses into a hard brownish nodule, usually raised above the surrounding surface.

SPARK LESION

Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology 4th edition, Page No. 330

question_text: True about heat hematoma:
explanation:
Heat hematoma:

Heat hematoma occurs when the head has been exposed to intense heat, sufficient to cause charring of the skull.

It has the appearance of extradural haemorrhage but is not accompanied by any signs of injury by blunt force.

It consists of a soft, friable clot of light chocolate colour, and may be pink, if the blood contains CO.

The clot has a honeycomb appearance due to bubbles of steam produced by heat.

The thickness of the clot varies from one-and-half to fifteen mm., and the volume up to 120 ml.

The parietotemporal region is the most common site and sometimes frontal or occipital region.

The mechanism of its development is obscure. It may be due to blood being boiled from the diploic layer of bone through emissary veins and venous sinus which rupture or shrinkage of meninges and brain, which may aspirate blood from the venous sinuses.

The carboxyhaemoglobin level in heat haematoma will be the same as in peripheral blood. Heat haematoma will contain carboxyhaemoglobin, but extradural haemorrhage caused by injury before the fire began, will not show carboxyhaemoglobin.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 242

question_text: Hide and die syndrome occurs in:
explanation:
'Hide and die' syndrome:

  • In some hypothermic deaths, bodies are found in some strange places-under a bed or bench, on a shelf or behind a wardrobe, or alternatively may pull down household articles into a heap on top, which may give the impression of their attempt to 'hide' (protective 'burrow-like' or 'cave-like' situation).
  • This may also lead to the assumption of a homicide or robbery. It is due to mental confusion from hypothermia and may be related to hibernation reflex.

An apparent self-protective behaviour, known as "terminal burrowing", or "hide-and-die syndrome", occurs in the final stages of hypothermia. Those affected will enter small, enclosed spaces, such as underneath beds or behind wardrobes. It is often associated with paradoxical undressing.

Reference: Review of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 5th Edition, Gautam Biswas, Page No. 285

question_text: An elderly woman was found dead during winter in her wardrobe. On house inspection, the heater was found to be broken. She was also identified to be a known case of hypothyroidism. Which of the following most likely explains her scenario?
explanation:
The most likely explanation for the given scenario is terminal burrowing behaviour or hide and die syndrome.

An elderly lady with hypothyroidism is more likely to develop hypothermia. About 20% of hypothermia cases are associated with terminal burrowing behaviour.

In some cases the bodies were found in strange situations, i.e. lying under a bed, behind a wardrobe, or on a shelf, etc. indicating that the final positions were a kind of self-protective burrowing-like behaviour.

An apparent self-protective behaviour, known as "terminal burrowing", or "hide-and-die syndrome", occurs in the final stages of hypothermia. Those affected will enter small, enclosed spaces, such as underneath beds or behind wardrobes. It is often associated with paradoxical undressing.

But when people are found after suffering or dying from hypothermia, some will have taken off their clothes; this is called paradoxical undressing. The brain interprets the extreme cold as feeling hot.

Reference: Online Resource https://www.ncbi.nim.nih.gov/pubmed/7632602

question_text: A 35-year-old female is brought to the emergency department after an accidental burn. Upon examination, burns are present on her right upper limb, the entire right lower limb, and the entire front and back of her abdomen. According to the Rule of Nines, what is the estimated percentage of her total body surface area (TBSA) affected by burns?
explanation:
Explanation for answer:

 The Wallace Rule of Nines is used to estimate the total body surface area (TBSA) affected by burns.

Calculation:

  • Right upper limb: 9%
  • Entire right lower limb: 18%
  • Front of the abdomen: 9%
  • Back of the abdomen: 9%

Total burned area = 9% + 18% + 9% + 9% = 45%

Hence options B,C and D are incorrect

Explanation:

  • A common witness (also called an ordinary witness) testifies about facts personally observed, such as the dimensions and appearance of a wound. (Option A)
  • An expert witness, on the other hand, provides professional opinions based on specialised knowledge, for example, the type of weapon used or the nature of injuries. (Option B)

question_text: During hysterectomy surgery, there was a damage to the ureter. This is covered under which doctrine?
explanation:
The doctrine of Res ipsa loquitur is a Latin term meaning "the thing speaks for itself." It applies in situations where the nature of the injury implies negligence because such injuries typically do not occur without a lack of proper care. This doctrine shifts the burden of proof to the defendant (in this case, the doctor or hospital) to show that the injury was not caused by negligence.

In the context of a ureteric injury during a hysterectomy:

The ureters are in close anatomical proximity to the uterus, making them vulnerable during surgical procedures like a hysterectomy. However, damaging the ureter typically indicates that the standard of care expected during such surgeries was not maintained.

Under Res ipsa loquitur, the injury itself is evidence enough to raise the presumption of negligence, as this type of damage does not usually occur when due care is exercised.

Rule Out:

Option A: Medical Maloccurrence

False: Medical maloccurrence refers to an adverse event or complication that arises despite adherence to standard care and without negligence. Ureteric damage during hysterectomy is generally not considered a simple maloccurrence because it usually indicates a lapse in care.

Option B: Novus Actus Interveniens

False: This doctrine refers to an intervening act that breaks the chain of causation between the defendant's act and the plaintiff's injury. In this case, there is no intervening act; the injury is directly attributable to the surgery.

Option C: Therapeutic Misadventure

False: This refers to a rare and unforeseeable adverse outcome of treatment, even when proper care and precautions are taken. Ureteric injury is typically preventable with proper surgical technique, so this doctrine does not apply.

Key Takeaways:

Res ipsa loquitur applies when the nature of the injury itself indicates negligence.

Ureteric damage during a hysterectomy is a preventable complication and generally suggests a breach of standard surgical care.

This doctrine shifts the burden of proof to the defendant to demonstrate that no negligence occurred.

Differentiating between Res ipsa loquitur and other doctrines is crucial in medicolegal cases to determine the liability.

question_text: A doctor was summoned as a public witness to appear and record his evidence in court. What is correct about this witness?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • An expert witness is an individual with specialized training, knowledge, or skill in a specific field, called upon by the court to assist in clarifying technical matters.
  • When a doctor is summoned to provide testimony relating to medical science, injuries, cause of death, or other health-related issues, they are considered an expert witness.
  • Their role is to help the court understand scientific or medical aspects that are beyond the knowledge of a layperson.

Explanation of Other Options:

Oral evidence (Option A): Oral evidence refers to testimony given verbally in court by any witness. While the doctor’s statement is indeed oral, this option does not classify the type of witness correctly.

Common witness (Option B): A common witness is one who testifies to facts they have personally seen, heard, or perceived. In this case, the doctor is not testifying as an ordinary observer but based on specialized expertise.

Hostile witness (Option D): A hostile witness is a person who deliberately gives testimony unfavorable to the party that summoned them or contradicts prior statements. There is no indication in the question that the doctor was hostile.

Reference: Expert witness

question_text: Section 116 of the BNS deals with:
option_d: Definition of voluntarily causing grievous hurt
explanation:
Explanation:

Section 116 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) precisely deals with the definition of 'grievous hurt'. The following kinds of hurt only are designated as "grievous", namely:

(a) Emasculation;

(b) Permanent privation of the sight of either eye;

(c) Permanent privation of the hearing of either ear;

(d) Privation of any member or joint;

(e) Destruction or permanent impairing of the powers of any member or joint;

(f) Permanent disfiguration of the head or face;

(g) Fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth;

(h) Any hurt which endangers life or which causes the sufferer to be during the space of fifteen days in severe bodily pain, or unable to follow his ordinary pursuits.

Section 114 BNS: Hurt - Whoever causes bodily pain, disease or infirmity to any person is said to cause hurt.

Key Takeaway:

Section 116 of the BNS specifically provides the definition of 'Grievous hurt', detailing the severe types of injuries that fall under this classification.

question_text:
Sequentially arrange the clauses of Section 320 IPC
1. Destruction or permanent impairing of the powers of any member or joint
2. Permanent disfiguration of the head or face
3. Emasculation
4. Fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth
explanation:
Section 320 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) defines grievous hurt, enumerating specific injuries that qualify under this category. The clauses are listed in a sequential manner as follows:

Clause 1 - Emasculation:

Refers to the loss or permanent damage to male reproductive capability.

Clause 2 - Destruction or permanent impairment of the powers of any member or joint:

Includes injuries that cause loss of function or permanent impairment of limbs or joints.

Clause 3 - Permanent disfiguration of the head or face:

Refers to injuries causing irreversible physical changes to the appearance of the head or face.

Clause 4 - Fracture or dislocation of a bone or tooth:

Refers to injuries involving the breaking or dislocation of bones or teeth.

The correct sequence as per Section 320 IPC is 3-1-2-4.

Rule Out Explanation:

Option (a): 1-2-3-4:

Incorrect because Clause 1 (Emasculation) precedes the other clauses in the actual section.

Option (b): 3-2-1-4:

Incorrect because Clause 2 (Destruction or impairment of joints) is listed after emasculation in the actual section.

Option (d): 1-4-2-3:

Incorrect because the sequence of Clause 3 (Permanent disfiguration) and Clause 4 (Fracture or dislocation) does not align with the actual order in Section 320 IPC.

Key Takeaways:

Section 320 IPC outlines specific injuries that constitute grievous hurt.

The correct order of clauses is 3-1-2-4, beginning with emasculation and ending with fracture or dislocation.

Understanding the exact sequence is essential for legal and forensic applications.

question_text: A patient comes with bluish discolouration in the post auricular region. The sign is called
explanation:
Battle's sign refers to bruising or bluish discoloration in the post-auricular region (behind the ear) and is typically associated with a basilar skull fracture. It occurs due to blood pooling in the area from a fracture of the temporal bone, which can damage blood vessels and lead to bleeding around the ear. The bruising may appear a few days after the injury and is considered a clinical sign of a significant head injury.

Key points:

Battle's sign is a classic indicator of a basilar skull fracture and suggests a serious head injury.

It often presents with bruising around the mastoid area (behind the ear).

It is associated with potential cranial nerve damage and other life-threatening complications.

Rule Out:

a) Greissinger's sign: Refers to bluish discoloration around the umbilicus, indicative of intra-abdominal hemorrhage or peritoneal irritation, not a skull fracture.

b) Gradenigo's sign: Refers to pain behind the ear, diplopia, and abducens nerve palsy due to an infection of the petrous part of the temporal bone (petrositis), not bruising.

c) Trotter's sign: Refers to the triad of symptoms (nasal obstruction, ear discharge, and facial paralysis) typically seen in chronic sinusitis or nasopharyngeal carcinoma, not bruising.

Key Takeaways:

  1. Battle's sign is indicative of a basilar skull fracture, typically seen with bruising behind the ear.
  2. It is a sign of potential serious trauma and warrants immediate medical attention.
  3. Proper assessment of head injuries is crucial to detect underlying fractures and prevent complications.

question_text: Identify the condition shown in the image
explanation:
Marbling is a postmortem phenomenon that occurs due to the decomposition of blood within the veins. This results in a distinct pattern resembling a web or tree-like structure, typically greenish-black in color. It is caused by the spread of hydrogen sulfide gas produced by bacteria, reacting with hemoglobin in the blood to form sulfhemoglobin.

Onset: Marbling is usually observed within 24-48 hours after death, depending on environmental conditions like temperature and humidity.

Appearance: The pattern follows the venous network, most prominently visible on the skin of the trunk, limbs, and neck.

Rule Out:

Postmortem lividity (a):

Definition: Also called livor mortis, it is the purplish-red discoloration caused by gravitational pooling of blood in dependent areas of the body after death.

Appearance: Unlike marbling, lividity is diffuse and uniform in areas where blood settles and does not form a venous pattern.

Why ruled out: The image shows a distinct web-like venous pattern, not the diffuse discoloration of livor mortis.

Filigree burns (c):

Definition: These are burns caused by electrical injuries, characterized by an arborescent or fern-like pattern on the skin.

Appearance: Filigree burns resemble lightning strikes and are caused by the passage of high-voltage current through the body.

Why ruled out: The image shows venous discoloration typical of marbling, not the superficial burn marks seen in filigree burns.

None (d):

Why ruled out: The described pattern is consistent with marbling, making "none" an incorrect choice.

Key Takeaways:

Marbling is an early decomposition change: It is caused by bacterial decomposition of blood and follows a venous pattern.

Timing: It typically appears 1-2 days postmortem, making it a useful marker for estimating the postmortem interval (PMI).

Differentiation from lividity: Marbling is venous and patterned, whereas lividity is diffuse and dependent.

Forensic significance: Marbling helps determine the stage of decomposition and provides clues about environmental conditions affecting the body.

question_text: Identify the type of injury
explanation:
• The given image shows an abrasion.
  • An abrasion (gravel rash) is a destruction of the skin, which usually involves only the superficial layers of the epidermis.
  • An abrasion is the most superficial of all the injuries.
  • It does not penetrate the full thickness of the epidermis.
  • They are caused by friction against a rough surface or by compression, such as a lateral rubbing action by a glancing blow, a fall on a rough surface, by being dragged in a vehicular accident, fingernails, thorns or teeth bite.
  • Most abrasions are caused by a lateral rubbing action.
  • If sufficient friction is applied, partial or complete removal of the epithelium may occur, and the superficial layer of dermis is damaged.
  • Many abrasions have some deeper areas of subepidermal damage which may result in superficial scarring.
  • Sometimes, full thickness of the skin may be damaged in places, but usually in an interrupted, irregular manner, and intact epidermis remains within the area of the abrasion.
  • A pure abrasion does not bleed, as blood vessels are confined to the dermis. However, the dermal papillae are corrugated in nature.
  • Thus, many abrasions enter the dermis and bleeding commonly occurs.

Reference:The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 136; Knight's Forensic Pathology 4th edition Page no 135

question_text: Which of the following is a false statement regarding contrecoup injuries?
option_a: Fracture of the skull may not occur, even in the presence of severe coup and contrecoup injuries
option_b: A fall on the frontal region will produce an occipital contrecoup
option_c: A fall on the temporal region will produce a contrecoup in the ipsilateral lobe
option_d: The most common site for contrecoup injury is frontal and temporal lobes
explanation:
When an impact is imparted to a mobile head or a stationary head, the site of maximum cortical damage is most likely to be underneath or at least on the same side as the impact. This is so called, 'coup lesion'

When a moving head is suddenly decelerated as in case of a fall, though there might be a coup lesion at the site of the impact, there is usually cortical damage on the opposite side of the brain - 'contrecoup lesion'

There may be no coup damage at all, only contrecoup.

It is virtually unknown for a fall on the frontal region to produce occipital contrecoup, probably due to the relatively smooth internal surface of the posterior cranial fossa of the skull.

Severe coup and/or contrecoup lesions may be present with or without fracture of skull(Option A).

The common sites of cerebral damage are the tips and under-surfaces of the frontal and temporal lobesbecause of rough surface of the bone(Option D).

In a temporal impact, the contrecoup lesion may not appear on the contralateral hemisphere but on the opposite side of ipsilateral hemisphere from the impact against the falx cerebri (Option C).

The extent of contrecoup damage may be disproportionately related to coup damage.

References: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th Edition, Page N0. 201; Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology: Principles & Practice, Krishan Vij, 5th Edition Page No. 281, 282

question_text: Which is the most commonly injured part of the spinal cord?
explanation:
The cervical spine is the most commonly injured part of the spinal cord.

The cervical spine accounts for 60 per cent of the adult spine injuries and the most common part of the spine to be injured is the region of the upper cervical vertebrae (C1–C4), and injury to the C1/C2 complex accounts for 19–25 per cent of the cervical spine injuries.

These are followed by injuries to the thoracolumbar (20 per cent), lumbar (10 per cent), thoracic (8 per cent), and sacral level (2 per cent).

Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th Edition, Page No. 210

question_text: Which of the following is a false statement regarding contrecoup injuries?
option_a: Subdural or Subarachnoid haemorrhage may be caused as contrecoup injuries
option_b: A fall on the frontal region will not produce an occipital contrecoup
option_c: Contrecoup injuries are more common in children less than 3 years of age
option_d: The most common site for contrecoup injury is the frontal and temporal lobes
explanation:
Explanation:

Contrecoup injuries are rare in children under 3 years of age, as

  • Their open sutures and more elastic skulls absorb and dissipate the force of impact better than a rigid, fully fused adult skull.
  • This elasticity and flexibility allow the skull to give and deform on impact, spreading out the force and reducing the likelihood of the brain hitting the opposite side of the skull with significant force.
  • The brain has less room to move within the cranial cavity.

Contrecoup injury:

  • When a moving head is suddenly decelerated, as in the case of a fall, though there might be a coup lesion at the site of the impact,there is usually cortical damage on the opposite side of the brain-contrecoup lesion.
  • Subdural or Subarachnoid haemorrhage may be caused as contrecoup injury(Option A).
  • The most common site for contrecoup injury is the frontal and temporal lobes(Option D).Occipital injuries cause severe and extensive contrecoup lesions.
  • Fall on the frontal region will not produce occipital contrecoup injuries due to relatively smooth internal surface of the posterior cranial fossa (Option B).

Coup Injury:

A coup injury is a type of traumatic brain injury where damage occurs at the site of impact on the brain, located directly under the point of force on the skull. This injury is caused by the direct trauma of the impact, resulting in bruising, bleeding, and contusions. It can be seen when an impact is imparted to a stationary head or a mobile head.

question_text: Identify the type of Fracture
explanation:
A fissured fracture is a type of bone injury characterized by a crack or linear split in the bone that does not result in complete separation of the bone fragments. This fracture typically occurs when the bone is subjected to stress or trauma, and the break is confined to the surface or a single layer of the bone.

Characteristics:

  • It appears as a thin crack running along the length of the bone.
  • It does not involve displacement or fragmentation of the bone.
  • Common in long bones (e.g., tibia, femur) due to impact injuries or repetitive stress.
  • In radiographic imaging, fissured fractures are seen as fine, linear lines that follow the contour of the bone without disrupting its structural alignment.

Rule Out:

(a) Ring fracture:

This is a specific type of fracture often associated with the base of the skull, particularly around the foramen magnum. It typically occurs due to a severe compressive force, such as a fall from height, and is not related to linear or stress-related bone cracks.

(b) Comminuted fracture:

A comminuted fracture involves the bone breaking into three or more fragments. This occurs due to high-impact trauma, such as in motor vehicle accidents, and is distinctly different from the single-line crack seen in fissured fractures.

(d) Sutural fracture:

Sutural fractures occur in the skull along the cranial sutures, which are the joints between the bones of the skull. These fractures are more common in specific traumatic skull injuries and are entirely unrelated to the linear crack pattern observed in a fissured fracture.

Key Takeaways:

A fissured fracture is a linear crack in the bone, often caused by stress or moderate trauma. It does not involve fragmentation or displacement of bone.

It is most commonly seen in long bones and can be identified through radiological imaging as a thin, linear break.

Other fracture types, such as ring fractures (associated with the skull), comminuted fractures (bone fragmentation), and sutural fractures (skull sutures), are fundamentally different in cause, appearance, and associated trauma.

Accurate identification of fracture types is crucial for appropriate treatment planning and recovery.

question_text: The sequence of bullet injuries in the following image can be identified by?
explanation:
The sequence of gunshots in this case is 1 → 2 → 3 according to Puppe's rule.

Puppe's rule: It states that the path of a second fracture line does not cross the path of an existing fracture line that appears or was caused before it. This helps the forensic expert determine the chronology(order) in which the bullets were lodged into the skull.

Puppe's rule is used in forensic examination of skull fractures caused by multiple blunt force impacts as well, as it is not limited to the examination of bullet injuries only.

Hess's rule or Rule of Haase is used to estimate the gestational age of a foetus by crown-heel length.

Kassowitz's law is an empirical observation used in context of congenital syphilis stating that the greater the duration between the infection of the mother and conception, the better the outcome for the infant. Features of a better outcome include less chance of stillbirth and of developing congenital syphilis.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 173.

question_text: Identify the source of the trauma given in the image below.
explanation:
Explanation:

Bullet injuries to the skull produce distinct features such as:

  • Entry wound: Clean, punched-out appearance with beveling on the inner table.
  • Exit wound: Larger and irregular, with beveling on the outer table.
  • Radiating fracture lines extending outward from the entry site.
    These features are diagnostic of firearm-related injuries.

Features of Entry and Exit Wounds


Puppe's Rule: It indicates that when two fracture lines meet, the second one will stop at the first and not cross it. This principle is useful for determining the order of fire in cases involving multiple gunshot wounds to the skull and is also applicable to situations with repeated blunt force trauma to the head.

Kronlein Shot: A rare type of injury caused by a high-velocity bullet leads to explosive skull fracture, tearing of the dura mater, and extrusion of brain tissue. During autopsy, the extent of damage prevents identification of the primary gunshot wound and differentiation between entry and exit sites.

Explanation of other options:

Rod (Option B): Trauma from a rod or similar blunt instrument usually produces linear or depressed skull fractures and contusions, rather than a neat, circular opening.

Axe (Option C): Axe injuries cause deep, sharp cuts with uneven margins and bone splintering, which do not match the described injury pattern.

Scissor (Option D): Scissor wounds are typically puncture or stab injuries with irregular edges and lack the radiating fracture lines and beveled margins typical of bullet wounds.

question_text: The 'hold-on effect' is characteristically seen in
explanation:
The hold-on effect is seen in electrical injuries.

When, as most often happens, the entry point is in the hand, the stronger flexor muscles of the arm go into spasm and cause a hold-on effect.

This means that any object being held in the hand is involuntarily clenched and, as it is likely to be the faulty electrical appliance or a wire, the object cannot be released and the current thus continues to flow.

This adds to the time element and progressively worsens the risk of both cutaneous burns and the risk of cardiac or respiratory arrest.

Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology 4th edition, Page No. 326-328

question_text: A 23-year male patient was brought to the hospital with a history of stove burst. Burns involving face & head with singeing of hair, neck, both arms and front of chest bilaterally noted. The percentage of burns is:
explanation:
Explanation:

To calculate the percentage of burns, the "Rule of Nine" (or Wallace's Rule) is typically used for adults.

Based on the provided explanation, the breakdown of body surface area for this male patient is as follows:

  • Head (including face) = 7%
  • Neck = 2%
  • Both arms = 4% + 4% = 8%
  • Front of bilateral chest = 9%

Adding these percentages together: 7% + 2% + 8% + 9% = 26%.

Therefore, the total percentage of burns is 26%.

Key Takeaway:

Using the standard method for burn estimation (likely a modified Rule of Nines, as values differ slightly from traditional adult Rule of Nines for head/neck), the total burn surface area for the described injuries (head/face, neck, both arms, and front of bilateral chest) sums to 26%.

question_text: Which organs are most commonly injured by air blast shock waves?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most commonly injured organ in an air blast shock wave is the tympanic membrane (TM). Since TM is not listed among the options, the next best choice is the lung.

Blast lung is a primary blast injury caused by the shock wave, resulting in immediate damage such as rupture of alveolar capillaries.

Blast Injury Overview:

  • Severity: Causes more extensive damage than bullet wounds due to complex blast wave dynamics.
  • Pressure: Explosion pressure waves can exceed 1000 pounds per square inch, involving both incident and reflected pressures.

Factors Contributing to Injury:

  • Impact of high-pressure waves.
  • Mechanical, chemical, and thermal damage.
  • Inhalation of toxic gases and smoke.

Types of blast injuries:

Intestine, kidney, and heart (Options A, C, and D): are not the most common injuries in air blast

explanation:
Explanation:

  • The blackening observed around a gunshot entry wound is caused by soot or smoke particles produced from the combustion of gunpowder, which stick to the skin near the wound.
  • This phenomenon typically occurs in close-range gunshot wounds where the gases and particles have enough force and proximity to deposit on the skin surface.

question_text: What is the study of the processes in a firearm known as?
explanation:
The study of the processes in a firearm is known as internal ballistics.

Ballistics is the science of mechanics that deals with the flight, behaviour and effects of projectiles.

Internal ballistics deals with the processes that takes place within a firearm.

Exterior ballistics deals with the behaviour of the projectile after leaving the barrel till it reaches the target.

Wound ballistics comprises the changes caused when a missile penetrates an animal or human body.

References: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th edition, Page No. 241.

question_text: What is the retrograde propulsion of tissue from the entry wound towards the firearm known as?
explanation:
The retrograde propulsion of tissue from the entry wound towards the firearm is known as back spatter.

In contact shots and sometimes in close shots, the muzzle blast and the negative pressure in the barrel following discharge may suck blood, hair, fragments of tissues and cloth fibres several cm. back inside the barrel called "back spatter" → Helps in identification of weapon.

Forward spatter: Splashing of blood & tissue fragments through the wound of exit.

Option A: Blowback phenomenon: This is seen at the entry wound in a contact shot against a bone, where the gases rebound against the bone and exit through the entry wound, creating a stellate shaped margin at the entry wound.

question_text: The fragments of lead of a bullet break off the lead core and are hurled out into the surrounding tissues. What is this phenomenon called?
explanation:
Lead snowstorm is the phenomenon caused by a firearm wound, when lead fragments are stripped from the bullet as it travels through the body causing multiple fragments to be present along the wound track.

X-rays of individuals shot with high velocity rifle ammunition show a characteristic radiologic picture, the so-called "lead snowstorm".

As the expanding bullet moves through the body, fragments of lead break off the lead core and are hurled out into the surrounding tissues.

An X-ray shows scores, if not hundreds, of small radiopaque bullet fragments scattered along the wound track(the lead snowstorm)

These fragments vary from dust-like to large irregular pieces of metal.

A rifle bullet does not have to hit bone for this phenomenon to occur.

This picture is not seen with handgun bullets, nor with rare exception, with full metal-jacketed rifle bullets.

Lead snowstorm phenomenon - radiology

Reference: Gunshot Wounds: Practical Aspects of Firearms, Ballistics and Forensic Techniques, Page No. 189.

question_text: During a radiological examination, a radiologist identifies a bullet present in the body surrounded by a dense fibrous tissue capsule. What type of bullet is it called?
explanation:
The kind of bullet identified by the radiologist as explained in the given scenario is known as a souvenir bullet.

Souvenir bullet is the one which has been lodged in the body for a long time with no fresh bleeding around it and surrounded by a dense fibrous tissue capsule. They can be visualized on X-rays. They are usually a result of bullet lodging in an inaccessible space which may result in more damage on attempted retrieval. E.g., Bullet in the spine.

Other options:

Tandem bullet(Piggyback bullet): The bullet may fail to be ejected and on firing second time, the second bullet may go off carrying the lodged bullet with it and both may enter the body through the same entrance wound or two different entrance wounds. This may be on account of some defect in the weapon or due to faulty ammunition or where the loaded firearm has not been used for a considerable period or prolonged exposure to high environmental temperature or humidity.

Incendiary bullets: The tip of the bullet contains white phosphorous. Used to cause fire in the target(E.g., to ignite fuel tank).

Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology: Principles & Practice, 5th Edition, Page No. 254.

question_text: Match the following
explanation:
Puppe's rule: Helps in determining the sequence of bullets hit the skull, when there are multiple bullet injuries to skull. The fracture line resulting from the later bullet will typically stop at the previously formed one.

Kennedy's phenomenon: Surgical intervention of a firearm wound leading to an artefact as the evaluation of wound as entry or exit wound and the range of firing etc., become difficult.

Rayalaseema phenomenon: Here a person is killed by stab injury and a bullet is implanted inside to mislead the investigation.

Ewing's postulates: Establishes a relationship between trauma and new growth.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 173, 177, 240.

question_text: Which is the most severely injured organ in blast injuries in underwater and air respectively?
explanation:
In underwater blasts, the intestines suffer the most damage.

A blast causes the most damage at an interface between tissues in contact with the atmosphere, which is why the lung usually suffers the most severe damage. However, the most commonly affected structure in air blasts is the tympanic membrane.

The gastrointestinal system suffers from the effect of a blast because, like the lung, it contains air and gases and is thus not a uniform medium for transit of the shock wave.

Victims of explosions in water suffer a reverse order of gastrointestinal to lung damage.

Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th edition, Page No. 269; The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 183.

question_text: Primary blast injury is:
explanation:
Air blast injuries are divided into the following 5 categories:

  1. Primary blast injuries
    • Caused by the direct pressure effects of the blast wave/shock wave on the victim
  2. Secondary blast injuries:
    • Caused by flying missiles that strike people
    • Marshal's Triad(Body stippling)
    • → Combination of Abrasions + Contusions + Punctate lacerations
  3. Tertiary blast injuries:
    • Caused by blast wind that can throw victims against solid objects
  4. Quaternary blast injuries:
    • All other injuries not included in the first three classes
    • These include flash burns, crush injuries and respiratory injuries
  5. Quinary blast injuries:
    • Illnesses, injuries or diseases caused by chemical, biological or radiological substance

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th Edition, Page No. 317.

The image shows a wound of entry surrounded by tattooing (peppering). There is no blackening (smudging). That means the target was beyond the reach of the smoke/soot but within the range of powder particles, i.e., intermediate range.

  1. Contact shot - Here the muzzle end is in contact with body. It may be firm/hard/tight contact or loose contact or angled contact.
