question_text: Which of the following is not an eligibility category for Medical Termination of Pregnancy between 20-24 weeks as per the MTP (Amendment) Act, 2021?
option_c: Woman requesting abortion due to financial difficulties
explanation:
Explanation:

Financial difficulties alone are not listed as an eligibility category for 20-24 week termination under the MTP (Amendment) Act, 2021.

Grounds for Terminating a Pregnancy as per MTP (Amendment) Act, 2021:

  1. Up to 20 weeks in case of
    • Failure of contraceptive in a woman or her partner
  2. Up to 24 weeks in case of
    • Survivors of rape (The Supreme Court ruled that regardless of exception 2 of section 63 of BNS (That time 375 IPC) which exempts criminalization of marital rape, for the purpose of MTP, 'rape' would include the husband's act of sexual assault or rape committed on his wife) (Option A)
    • Fetal abnormality
    • Incest
    • Minors (Option B)
    • Women with physical disabilities
    • Mentally ill women including those suffering from mental retardation (Option D)
    • Marital status changes during an ongoing pregnancy (widowhood and divorce)
    • Women with pregnancy in humanitarian settings or disaster or emergency situations as may be declared by the Government.
  3. MTP can be done even after 24 weeks in case of
    • Substantial fetal abnormalities diagnosed by a Medical Board which consist of, a) a Gynecologist b) a pediatrician c) a Radiologist or Sonologist and d) any other nominated by the state government/union territory (Should be a doctor).
  4. MTP can be done at any time, even by a single RMP, if it is immediately
    • necessary to save the life of the pregnant woman.

question_text: A superior police officer induces his female subordinate to have consensual sexual intercourse by offering promotion in her job. After getting the promotion, the subordinate lodges a complaint. The superior police officer is liable under:
explanation:
A person in authority (superior police officer), who induces or seduces any female (subordinate) to have sexual intercourse with him is explained under Section 68 BNS. Such sexual intercourse does not amount to the offense of rape.


Section 68 BNS: - Sexual intercourse by a person in authority

Whoever, being-

  1. in a position of authority or in a fiduciary relationship; or
  2. a public servant; or
  3. superintendent or manager of a jail, remand home or other place of custody established by or under any law for the time being in force, or a women's or children's institution; or
  4. on the management of a hospital or being on the staff of a hospital, abuses such position or fiduciary relationship to induce or seduce any woman either in his custody or under his charge or present in the premises to have sexual intercourse with him, such sexual intercourse not amounting to the offence of rape, shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than 5 years, but which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

References: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhitha, 2023, The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 321

question_text: A woman found out that her husband is having a consensual sexual relationship with another man and that the affair has been going on for a few months. She was deeply aggrieved and committed suicide. Upon investigation, the police found her suicide note where in she had stated all the facts with evidence. Under which of the following section can the husband be booked?
explanation:
In this scenario, the husband can be booked under Section 108 BNS which deals with the abetment of suicide.

Section 108 BNS: Abetment of suicide: If any person commits suicide, whoever abets the commission of such suicide, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

  • The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India on 27th September 2018 struck down IPC 497 (Which was dealt with adultery) dealing with adultery as unconstitutional. However, the court noted that if any aggrieved spouse commits suicide because of the life partner's adulterous relation then, if the evidence produced, it could be treated as an abetment to suicide.
  • There is no mention about adultery in Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhitha.
    Option (A): Section 63 BNS - Definition of Rape.
    Option (B): Section 64 BNS - Punishment for Rape.

Reference: Online Resource https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/india/supreme-court-strikes-down-adultery-as-an-offence-key-highlights/articleshow/65975511.

question_text: A child is born eight months following the death of the presumed father. Despite doubts about paternity from the paternal grandparents, DNA testing confirms the child is biologically related to their son. What term best describes this child?
explanation:
Explanation:

A posthumous child is one born after the death of the father. The scenario described fits this definition.

Explanation for other options:

Suppositious child (Option A):

  • This term describes a fictitious child where a woman may pretend to be pregnant and later present a living child as her own.
  • This can involve substituting one child for another or claiming a child after an abortion, typically for financial gain or to claim property.
  • In this case, there is no indication of deception or substitution, so this option does not apply.

Fabricated child (Option B): Fabricated or induced illness (FII) is an uncommon type of child abuse where a parent or caregiver intentionally exaggerates or causes symptoms of illness in a child.

Illegitimate child (Option D):

Also known as a bastard, this describes a child born out of lawful wedlock or not within a competent time after the dissolution of marriage.

  • In this scenario, the child is born to a woman who was married, making this option incorrect.
  • Certain conditions can render a child illegitimate, including if the alleged father is under the age of puberty, physically incapable of fathering children, not sexually accessible to the mother at the time of conception, or has blood group incompatibility.
  • Legitimate Child: A child born during a lawful marriage or within 280 days after the marriage has been dissolved by divorce or death of the husband, as long as the mother remains unmarried.

Fabricated or induced illness: From "Munchausen by proxy" to child and family-oriented action - PubMed

question_text: Which of the following tests is used to detect semen
explanation:
• Marsh test is used to detect Arsenic.
  • Phenolphthalein test is used to detect blood.
  • Paraffin test is used to detect gun powder residues from the hand.
  • Confirmatory tests for semen are:
    1. Microscopy - Presence of sperm
    2. Detection of sperm specific LDH isoenzyme by electrophoresis
  • Presumptive/Screening tests for semen are:
    1. UV light Seminal stains on clothes can be identified by UV rays which gives Blue white color.
    2. Seminal Acid Phosphatase (SAP) test → Most commonly done presumptive test for detection of semen.
    3. Barberio's test → Spermine picrate (yellow needle shaped crystals)
    4. Florence test → Choline iodide (Dark brown rhombic crystals)
    5. PSA (Prostate specific antigen)/P30 (P30 is better than SAP)

    7. Epithelial cells → FISH (Y chromosome) → Fluorescence in situ hybridization.
    8. TLC → Only test to detect both Choline and Spermine in seminal stain
    9. CPK → Even in old stains of 6 months can be detected
    10. Zinc test (Prostate).
    11. RSID (Rapid Stain Identification Series) test for semen Identification of semenogelin (Sg) → From seminal vesicle & Substrate for PSA

question_text: According to the MTP Act, consent for abortion procedure is needed from whom?
explanation:
According to the MTP Act, for medical termination of pregnancy, consent is needed from the woman only.

Salient features of:

  1. Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act, 1971
  2. The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021
  3. The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Rules, 2021
  4. Supreme Court ruling on 29/09/2022

Indications of MTP:

  1. The continuance of the pregnancy would involve a risk to the life of the pregnant woman or
  2. The continuance of the pregnancy would involve a risk of grave injury to her physical or mental health; or
  3. There is a substantial risk that if the child were born, it would suffer from any serious physical or mental abnormality.

Accordingly, there are four grounds for MTP:

  1. Therapeutic:
    • Continuance of the pregnancy would involve a risk to the life of the pregnant woman.
  2. Social:
    • Pregnancy caused by the contraceptive failure used by any woman or her partner.
    • The anguish caused by such pregnancy may be presumed to constitute a grave injury to the mental health of the pregnant woman.
  3. Humanitarian:
    • Pregnancy caused by rape.
    • The anguish caused by the pregnancy shall be presumed to constitute a grave injury to the mental health of the pregnant woman.
  4. Eugenic:
    • There is a substantial risk that if the child were born, it would suffer from any serious physical or mental abnormality.

Who can perform MTP?

  1. RMP with 6 months house job in ObG or
  2. RMP with 1 year experience in the department of ObG or
  3. RMP who holds MD/Diploma in ObG or
  4. RMP who have assisted in performance of minimum 25 MTPs, out of which 5 must have been performed independently.

Note: Up to 9 weeks, any RMP with 3 months of experience in ObG

Where it can be performed?

  1. Hospitals, established or maintained by the government or
  2. The places approved by the government.

Opinion of RMP

  1. Opinion of 1 RMP for MTP up to 20 wks.
  2. Opinion of 2 RMPs for MTP of 20-24 wks.

Grounds for Terminating a Pregnancy:

  1. Up to 20 weeks in case of
    • Failure of contraceptive in a woman or her partner
  2. Up to 24 weeks in case of
    • Survivors of rape (The Supreme Court ruled that regardless of exception 2 of section 63 of BNS (That time 375 IPC) which exempts criminalization of marital rape, for the purpose of MTP, 'rape' would include the husband's act of sexual assault or rape committed on his wife)
    • Fetal abnormality
    • Incest
    • Minors
    • Women with physical disabilities
    • Mentally ill women including those suffering from mental retardation
    • Marital status changes during an ongoing pregnancy (widowhood and divorce)
    • Women with pregnancy in humanitarian settings or disaster or emergency situations as may be declared by the Government
  3. MTP can be done even after 24 weeks in case of
    • Substantial fetal abnormalities diagnosed by a Medical Board which consist of, a) a Gynecologist b) a pediatrician c) a Radiologist or Sonologist and d) any other nominated by the state government/union territory
  1. MTP can be done at any time, even by a single RMP, if it is immediately necessary to save the life of the pregnant woman.

Consent for MTP:

  • Pregnancy can only be terminated on the written consent of the women.
  • Husband's consent is not required.

Privacy of the woman:

  • Pregnancy in a minor girl (<18 years) or mentally ill person cannot be terminated without the written consent of the parents or legal guardian.
  • The RMP should protect the privacy of the woman.

Admission register:

  • The admission register should be maintained for at least 5 years from the end of the calendar year.
  • A monthly statement should be sent to the Director of Health Services

Reference: Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act, 1971; The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021; The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Rules, 2021; Supreme Court ruling on 29/09/2022

  2. Social:
    • Pregnancy caused by the contraceptive failure used by any woman or her partner.
    • The anguish caused by such pregnancy may be presumed to constitute a grave injury to the mental health of the pregnant woman.
  3. Humanitarian:
    • Pregnancy caused by rape.
    • The anguish caused by the pregnancy shall be presumed to constitute a grave injury to the mental health of the pregnant woman.
  4. Eugenic:
    • There is a substantial risk that if the child were born, it would suffer from any serious physical or mental abnormality.

Who can perform MTP?

  1. RMP with 6 months house job in ObG or
  2. RMP with 1 year experience in the department of ObG or
  3. RMP who holds MD/Diploma in ObG or
  4. RMP who have assisted in performance of minimum 25 MTPs, out of which 5 must have been performed independently.

Note: Up to 9 weeks, any RMP with 3 months of experience in ObG

Where it can be performed?

  1. Hospitals, established or maintained by the government or
  2. The places approved by the government.

Opinion of RMP

  1. Opinion of 1 RMP for MTP up to 20 wks.
  2. Opinion of 2 RMPs for MTP of 20-24 wks.

Grounds for Terminating a Pregnancy:

  1. Up to 20 weeks in case of
    • Failure of contraceptive in a woman or her partner
  2. Up to 24 weeks in case of
    • Survivors of rape (The Supreme Court ruled that regardless of exception 2 of section 63 of BNS (That time 375 IPC) which exempts criminalization of marital rape, for the purpose of MTP, 'rape' would include the husband's act of sexual assault or rape committed on his wife)
    • Fetal abnormality
    • Incest
    • Minors
    • Women with physical disabilities
    • Mentally ill women including those suffering from mental retardation
    • Marital status changes during an ongoing pregnancy (widowhood and divorce)
    • Women with pregnancy in humanitarian settings or disaster or emergency situations as may be declared by the Government.
  3. MTP can be done even after 24 weeks in case of
    • Substantial fetal abnormalities diagnosed by a Medical Board which consist of, a) a Gynecologist b) a pediatrician c) a Radiologist or Sonologist and d) any other nominated by the state government/union territory
  4. MTP can be done at any time, even by a single RMP, if it is immediately necessary to save the life of the pregnant woman.

Consent for MTP:

  • Pregnancy can only be terminated on the written consent of the women.
  • Husband's consent is not required.

Privacy of the woman:

  • Pregnancy in a minor girl (<18 years) or mentally ill person cannot be terminated without the written consent of the parents or legal guardian.
  • The RMP should protect the privacy of the woman.

Admission register:

  • The admission register should be maintained for at least 5 years from the end of the calendar year.
  • A monthly statement should be sent to the Director of Health Services

Reference: Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act, 1971; The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021; The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Rules, 2021; Supreme Court ruling on 29/09/2022

question_text:
You are working as a medical officer at a PHC. A 17-year-old girl presents to you after an alleged sexual assault, the girl refuses physical examination. Which of the following steps would you take to proceed in this case?
1. Start treatment for STD and pregnancy.
2. Inform the police
3. Record refusal of consent
4. Take vaginal sample
5. Start medical examination
explanation:
In the given scenario, one need to start treatment for STD & pregnancy, inform the police, and record refusal of consent for examination.

Examination of a sexual assault victim and collection of vaginal samples shouldn't be forced upon, but an informed refusal is to be documented after explaining to them the consequences of choice.

Medical treatment and testing for pregnancy have to be done for all victims of sexual assault free of cost and police should be informed as per Sec. 357C of CrPC.

As the girl is under 18 years of age, as per POCSO (The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences) Act 2012, the medical practitioner should initiate treatment for exposure to sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) including prophylaxis for identified STDs (including HIV if suspected) and possible pregnancy and emergency contraceptives should be discussed with the victim and her parent/guardian.

Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology: Principles & Practice 5th edition, Krishan Vij, age No. 304, 309

question_text: Which of the following is not an indication for Medical Termination of Pregnancy under the MTP Act, 1971?
option_b: Pregnancy in a woman with German measles during first trimester
option_c: Pregnancy in a woman exposed to X-rays during pregnancy
option_d: Pregnancy due to maternal preference for child's gender
explanation:
Explanation:

Sex-selective abortion is illegal in India and is not a valid indication under 'The Medical Termination of Pregnancy (Amendment) Act, 2021' (MTP Act 2021)

Indications for MTP (As per MTP Act 2021)

  1. Therapeutic:
    • Continuance of the pregnancy would involve a risk to the life of the pregnant woman.
  2. Social:
    • Pregnancy caused by the contraceptive failure used by any woman or her partner.
    • The anguish caused by such pregnancy may be presumed to constitute a grave injury to the mental health of the pregnant woman.
  3. Humanitarian:
    • Pregnancy caused by rape (Option A).
    • The anguish caused by the pregnancy shall be presumed to constitute a grave injury to the mental health of the pregnant woman.
  4. Eugenic:
    • There is a substantial risk that if the child were born, it would suffer from any serious physical or mental abnormality.
    • Examples:
    • If a pregnant woman in the first 3 months suffers from:
      • German measles (10-12% incidence of congenital defects) (Option B)
      • Smallpox or chickenpox
      • Toxoplasmosis
      • Viral hepatitis
      • Any severe viral infection
    • If treated with teratogenic drugs:
      • Thalidomide, cortisone, aminopterin, antimitotic drugs
      • Hallucinogens, antidepressants
    • If exposed to radiation:
      • X-rays or radioisotopes (Option C)
      • Structural (anencephaly), chromosomal (Down's syndrome) or genetic abnormalities of the fetus.
    • Environmental:
      • An adverse social or economic environment (actual or reasonably expected) that could injure the pregnant woman's health.

question_text:
A young girl came to AIIMS Emergency OPD with her mother. Her birth date was 31/01/2007 and history of consensual peno-vaginal penetration by their neighbour was given by the patient. She refused for medical examination. What could you do as a MO attending such patient?
1. Should not inform police
2. Should inform police
3. Should counsel the mother and daughter
4. Should do examination even after refusal
5. Take refusal form
explanation:
When dealing with cases involving a minor (under 18 years of age) and allegations of sexual assault, specific legal and ethical protocols must be followed, as guided by the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 and other medical and legal standards:

Should Inform Police (2):

According to the POCSO Act, reporting such incidents to the police is mandatory. Failure to do so is punishable under the Act. As the patient is a minor, this falls under mandatory reporting even if the patient or her guardian does not wish to involve the authorities.

Should Counsel the Mother and Daughter (3):

Counseling is an essential part of the care provided to survivors of sexual assault. It helps both the child and the guardian understand their options, legal rights, and the importance of medical examination for health and forensic purposes. Counseling also helps address the psychological trauma associated with such incidents.

Take Refusal Form (5):

If the patient or guardian refuses medical examination, it is important to document this refusal legally. A refusal form signed by the patient (or in this case, the guardian) ensures proper medico-legal documentation while respecting the patient's autonomy.

Rule Out:

1 (Should not inform police): This is incorrect because informing the police is mandatory in cases involving minors under the POCSO Act. Not reporting such a case is a violation of legal obligations.

4 (Should do examination even after refusal): This is incorrect because a medical examination cannot be conducted without the patient's consent, even in cases involving minors. Respecting autonomy is critical, and only in cases where the patient is unconscious or unable to give consent can exceptions be made.

Key Takeaways:

Mandatory Reporting: Under the POCSO Act, it is legally obligatory to report any case of sexual assault involving a minor to the police, regardless of the victim's or guardian's wishes.

Consent for Examination: Even in sensitive cases involving minors, medical examinations cannot proceed without informed consent. Proper documentation of refusal is necessary to safeguard both the patient's and the physician's legal interests.

Counseling and Support: Providing psychological support and counseling is an essential part of managing sexual assault cases, ensuring the well-being of both the victim and their guardians.

question_text: An 11 years old girl was found to be quiet and shy in her classroom with intermittent crying for the past few days. Later, the principal discovered that her uncle was touching her genitals inappropriately. The duty of the principal is to:
explanation:
Relevant Law:

The Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012, mandates that any individual aware of an offense against a child must report it to the police or a Special Juvenile Police Unit (SJPU).

Failure to report such incidents is punishable under Section 21 of the POCSO Act.

Principal's Duty:

As a responsible adult and authority figure, the principal is legally obligated to report the incident immediately to the police.

The police initiate an investigation, ensure the child's safety, and involve other agencies like the Child Welfare Committee (CWC) if needed.

Why Police?

The police are empowered to register the First Information Report (FIR) and investigate the case under the POCSO Act and the Indian Penal Code (IPC).

They ensure the victim is referred to appropriate medical, psychological, and social support systems.

Rule Out Explanation:

Option (b): Inform Magistrate:

Incorrect. While the Magistrate may eventually oversee the legal proceedings, reporting to the Magistrate is not the primary duty of the principal under the POCSO Act.

Option (c): Inform Child Welfare Committee (CWC):

Incorrect. The CWC is primarily involved in the care and protection of children who need support or rehabilitation. However, reporting the offense directly to the police is the first and foremost duty.

Option (d): Inform Parents:

Incorrect. While informing parents may be appropriate in certain cases, the primary legal obligation is to report the incident to the police. The parents may be informed subsequently, depending on the child's circumstances and safety.

Key Takeaways:

Under the POCSO Act, reporting sexual offenses against children to the police is mandatory.

Failure to report such offenses can result in legal consequences for the person aware of the incident.

The police act as the primary point of contact to ensure a coordinated response, including medical, psychological, and legal support for the child.

Always prioritize the child's safety and well-being when handling such cases.

question_text:
The vaginal epithelial cells of a victim of rape on the accused can be identified by
A. Lugol's iodine test
B. Florence test
C. Precipitin test
D. Toluidine blue test
explanation:
The Toluidine blue test is a diagnostic tool used in sexual assault investigations to detect vaginal epithelial cells and injuries. Toluidine blue is a cationic dye that binds to the acidic components of damaged epithelial cells, highlighting areas of trauma or presence of vaginal cells. This test is highly effective for identifying epithelial cells under a microscope and is commonly used in forensic settings to confirm sexual assault evidence.

Key aspects of the Toluidine blue test:

  • It binds to nucleic acids, highlighting epithelial cells and injuries.
  • Frequently used on the accused's body or clothing for detecting epithelial cell remnants from the victim.
  • Aids in corroborating evidence in rape cases.

Rule Out:

  1. Lugol's iodine test:
    • This test is used to detect glycogen in vaginal epithelial cells. While it can identify glycogenated cells, it is not specific to forensic identification of epithelial cells on the accused.
  2. Florence test:
    • This test detects choline crystals in seminal fluid and is unrelated to identifying vaginal epithelial cells.
  3. Precipitin test:
    • This is used to differentiate between human and animal blood based on antigen-antibody reactions, making it irrelevant in detecting vaginal epithelial cells.
  4. A, B, & C / B & D / A, B, & D:
    • These options are incorrect because Florence test and Lugol's iodine test do not specifically identify vaginal epithelial cells in forensic contexts.

Key Takeaways:

  • The Toluidine blue test is the most reliable method to identify vaginal epithelial cells in cases of sexual assault.
  • Other tests like Lugol's iodine or Florence test are used for different forensic purposes, such as detecting glycogen or seminal fluid, but not specifically for epithelial cells on the accused.
  • Proper use of forensic tools enhances the accuracy and reliability of sexual assault investigations.

question_text: The fertilisation of two ova released at two different menstrual cycles refers to:
explanation:
The fertilisation of two ova released at two different menstrual cycles refers to super foetation.

  • SUPERFECUNDATION: Superfecundation is the fertilization of two or more ova from the same cycle by sperm from separate acts of sexual intercourse. Heteropaternal superfecundation occurs when two different males father fraternal twins. In common usage, the term superfecundation is often used instead of heteropaternal superfecundation.
  • SUPERFOETATION: Superfetation means the fertilization of an ovum from a subsequent ovulation in a woman who is already pregnant. Two fetuses are born either at the same time showing different stages of development, or two fully developed fetuses are born varying from 1-3 months.
  • FETUS PAPYRASEOUS (Fetus compressus): In twin pregnancy, one fetus may grow and develop more than other fetus. The second under-developed fetus may get compressed and flattened. Such fetus is termed as fetus papyraseous
  • FECUNDATION AB EXTRA: Fertilisation of ova by the semen deposited on vulva or inner aspect of the thigh.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 308

question_text: For a man to be found guilty of statutory rape, he must have had sexual intercourse with?

option_d: A girl below 18 years of age even with her consent
explanation:
Explanation:

Statutory Rape:

  • Sexual intercourse with a girl below 18 years of age is considered statutory rape, regardless of her consent. It is neither violent nor physically coercive, but still constitutes rape by law due to the girl's age.
  • Sexual intercourse with a woman who is under the influence of sedative drugs like GHB, rohypnol (flunitrazepam) etc., is called date rape.
  • Section 67 BNS: Sexual intercourse by husband upon his wife during separation: Whoever has sexual intercourse with his own wife, who is living separately, whether under a decree of separation or otherwise, without her consent, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which shall not be less than two years but which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine.

This offence is cognizable and bailable.

Note: This is not marital rape → Marital rape means, sexual intercourse with his own wife without her consent and as of today marital rape is not punishable in India.

  • As of now, sexual intercourse by a person with any woman other than his wife with her valid consent (If a girl aged less than gives consent for sexual intercourse, that consent is not valid) is not considered to be a criminal offence. As per The Supreme Court of India, in case of married couple, if any aggrieved spouse ended his/her life because of his/her partner's adulterous relation, it could be treated as an abetment to suicide if evidence was produced.

question_text: According to POCSO Act, aggravated penetrative sexual assault includes:
option_a: Sexual assault done by police officer
explanation:
Sexual assault done by a police officer is an aggravated sexual assault and not aggravated penetrative sexual assault (If penetration is present, then only it becomes aggravated penetrative sexual assault) according to POCSO (Protection of Children from Sexual Offences) Act 2012.

Depending on if there was penetration or not, it can be aggravated sexual assault (if there is no penetration) or aggravated penetrative sexual assault (if there was penetration). Both are different.

The POCSO Act 2012 defines a child as any person below eighteen years of age. It defines various forms of sexual offenses which include:

  1. Penetrative sexual assault
  2. Aggravated penetrative sexual assault
  3. Sexual assault
  4. Aggravated sexual assault
  5. Sexual harassment
  6. Using child for pornographic purposes

Depending on if there was penetration or not, it can be aggravated sexual assault (if there is no penetration) or aggravated penetrative sexual assault (if there was penetration). Both are different.

AGGRAVATED PENETRATIVE SEXUAL ASSAULT:

It means penetrative sexual assault (PSA) on a child

  1. By a police officer; or
  2. By a member of the armed forces or security forces; or
  3. By a public servant; or
  4. By the management or on the staff of a jail, remand home, protection home, observation home, or other place of custody or care and protection established by or under any law for the time being in force on the inmate of such place; or
  5. By management or staff of a hospital, whether government or private in that hospital; or
  6. By management or staff of an educational institution or religious institution in that institution; or
  7. By more than one person (gang penetrative sexual assault); or
  8. By using deadly weapons, fire, heated substance or corrosive substance; or
  9. Causing grievous hurt or causing bodily harm & injury or injury to the sexual organs of the child; or
  10. Which -
    1. physically incapacitates the child or causes the child to become mentally ill or causes impairment of any kind so as to render the child unable to perform regular tasks, temporarily or permanently;
    2. in the case of female child, makes the child pregnant as a consequence of sexual assault;
    3. iii. inflicts the child with HIV or any other life-threatening disease or infection which may either temporarily or permanently impair the child by rendering him physically incapacitated, or mentally ill to perform regular tasks;
    4. causes death of the child; or
  11. Whoever, taking advantage of a child's mental or physical disability, commits penetrative sexual assault on the child; or
  12. Whoever commits penetrative sexual assault on the child more than once or repeatedly; or
  13. Whoever commits penetrative sexual assault on a child below 12 years; or
  14. Whoever being a relative of the child through blood or adoption or marriage or guardianship or in foster care or having a domestic relationship with the parent of the child or who is living in the same or shared household with the child, commits penetrative sexual assault on such child; or
  15. Whoever being, in the ownership, or management, or staff, of any institution providing services to the child, commits PSA on the child; or
  16. Whoever being in a position of trust or authority of a child commits PSA on the child in an institution or home of the child or anywhere else; or
  17. Whoever commits PSA on a child knowing the child is pregnant; or
  18. Whoever commits PSA on a child and attempts to murder the child; or
  19. Whoever commits PSA on a child in the course of communal or sectarian violence or during any natural calamity or in similar situations; or
  20. Whoever commits PSA on a child and who has been previously convicted of having committed any offence under this Act or any sexual offence punishable under any other law for the time being in force; or
  21. Whoever commits PSA on a child and makes the child to strip or parade naked in public, is said to commit aggravated penetrative sexual assault.

Punishment: Minimum 20 years to life imprisonment (which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of natural life of that person) + Fine or with death

References: THE PROTECTION OF CHILDREN FROM SEXUAL OFFENCES ACT, 2012 (POCSO Act 2012)

question_text: An 11-year-old girl was found to be quiet and shy in her classroom with intermittent crying, for the past few days. It was discovered that her uncle was touching her genitalia inappropriately. The duty of the principal is to report this to?
explanation:
The principal must report this case to the police.

The POCSO Act, 2012 is a comprehensive law for the protection of children from the offences of sexual assault, sexual harassment and pornography. This is done while safeguarding the interests of the child at every stage of the judicial process by incorporating child-friendly mechanisms for reporting, recording of evidence, investigation and speedy trial of the offence through designated special courts.

Section 21(1) of the POCSO Act, 2012 requires mandatory reporting of cases of child sexual abuse to the law enforcement authorities and applies to everyone including parents, doctors and school personnel. Failure to report a suspicion of child abuse is an offence under the Act.

Reference: The protection of children from sexual offences act, 2012(pocso act 2012).

question_text: An 18-year-old girl was brought to the OPD. Genital examination revealed separated labia majora, flabby labia minora, tear in the fourchette, roomy vagina with intact hymen. These findings are indicative of:
explanation:
The given findings are suggestive of a false virgin. A false virgin is a deflorate, but hymen is intact.

The presence of unruptured hymen is a presumption but is not an absolute proof of virginity.

The diagnosis of virginity is difficult, and in many cases, a physical examination of the genital organs may not be helpful.

With an intact hymen, there are true virgins and false virgins.

The hymen is present always in a virgin in some form or other, but very rarely may be absent congenitally.

The hymen is usually ruptured at the time of the first coitus, and at first only presents a torn appearance.

Hymen may not be ruptured even after repeated acts of coitus, if it is loose, lax, folded and elastic, or thick, tough and fleshy, which permit displacement, distortion and stretching without rupture → As in case of False virgin

Cases have been recorded of women having sexual relations, of pregnant women and even prostitutes in whom the hymen was intact.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 305

question_text: While examining a man who is accused of rape, you find the presence of smegma on his corona glandis. Which of the following can be inferred from this finding?
option_a: The person has engaged in sexual act recently
option_b: The person has not engaged in sexual act in last 24 hours
option_c: The person has not engaged in sexual act in last 48 hours
option_d: The person has not engaged in sexual act in last 1 week
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of smegma indicates no sexual intercourse has occurred in the last 24 hours, since intercourse removes smegma, and it takes about 24 hours to accumulate.

Smegma:

  • If the accused is not circumcised, the foreskin may be retracted.
  • The presence or absence of smegma (a cheesy secretion from sebaceous glands, consisting mainly of desquamated epithelial cells) on the corona glandis should be noted.
  • The absence of smegma may indicate that intercourse might have been performed.
  • The presence of smegma rules out the possibility of complete penetration, because smegma gets rubbed off during intercourse.
  • Smegma will also be removed by bathing or washing.
  • Smegma usually requires about 24 hours to collect.

question_text: Dressing up in clothes of opposite sex with no desire to undergo sex change operation called?
explanation:
It is a paraphilia characterized by recurrent sexually arousing fantasies, sexual urges, or behaviour involving the wearing of clothes of the opposite sex and appearing as a member of the opposite sex. It is also called transvestic fetishism. It is usually seen in males who obtain sexual pleasure by wearing female clothes.

Fetishistic transvestism is a paraphilia whereas transvestism is a gender identity disorder. There is no hormonal/genital abnormality in fetishistic transvestism.

Dual-role transvestism: Term used to describe people who wear clothes of the opposite sex to experience being the opposite sex temporarily, but don't have a sexual motive or want gender reassignment surgery

Option C: Frotteurism refers to a person who obtains sexual gratification by contact with another person (rubbing his private parts against female buttocks, breasts, or thighs, in public places). It is punishable under Section 290 IPC, with fine up to 200 Rs.

question_text: A woman gave birth to twins. The father who believed that the children did not belong to him and requested DNA testing. After testing, it was found that one child did not belong to him. This case would be best described as?
explanation:
The given clinical scenario where one twin is found not belonging to the father of the other twin is suggestive of heteropaternal superfecundation.

Superfecundation is the fertilization of 2 different ova in the same menstrual cycle by separate acts of coitus. It can occur even after artificial reproductive therapy. Hence, after embryo transfer, intercourse must be avoided. Heteropaternal superfecundation is used to refer to instances of two different males fathering fraternal twins. This leads to the possibility of twins also being half-siblings. This may give rise to the doubt of adultery and infidelity.

Homopaternal superfecundation is fertilization of two separate ova from the same father, leading to fraternal twins.

Option A: Superfetation is the fertilization of 2 different ova released in different menstrual cycles (i.e., ovulation and fertilization during pregnancy). This can occur within 12 weeks of pregnancy after which the decidual space is obliterated.

Option C: Supposititious child is also known as a fictitious child. In such cases, a woman pretends to be pregnant and generally substitutes a male child for a female child born of her, or after an abortion. This is done for the purpose of claiming property.

Option D: Atavism is the reappearance of a characteristic in an individual after several generations of absence. For example, the child may not resemble his parents but resembles his grandparents. This is attributed to the recombination of genes.

Reference: Review Of Forensic Medicine And Toxicology Including Clinical And Pathological Aspects. Page No. 359, 360

question_text: A white cloth brought by police is exposed to Barberio's testing. This test detects which of the following in sample
explanation:
Barberio's Test: A saturated aqueous or alcoholic solution of picric acid when added to spermatic fluid produces yellow needle-shaped rhombic crystals of spermine picrate. The reaction depends on the presence of prostatic secretion.

OTHER TESTS FOR SPERM DETECTION

Florence Test: The stain is extracted by 10% hydrochloric acid, and a drop is placed on a glass slide and allowed to dry. A coverslip is placed over this, and a drop of Florence solution (potassium iodide, iodine, and water) is allowed to run under the coverslip. If semen is present, dark-brown crystals of choline iodide appear immediately. Choline originates from the seminal vesicles. The test is not proof of seminal fluid, but only of presence of some vegetable or animal substance. A negative reaction is proof that the stain is not seminal.

Acid Phosphatase Test: The prostatic secretion element of seminal fluid contains 500 to 1000 times greater acid phosphatase than any other body fluid. Undiluted semen has an acid phosphatase activity of 340 to 360 Bodansky units or 2500 to 3500 Angstrom units per ml. The concentration of acid phosphatase gradually falls with time in vaginal secretions, and positive reactions are found for periods of 36 hours, with gradual disappearance in 72 hours. Concentration in excess of hundred Bodansky units with or without motile sperms indicate that ejaculation occurred within twelve hours of examination. Dried seminal stains which have not undergone putrefaction retain acid phosphatase activity for weeks or months. This test is conclusive in the absence of demonstrable sperms or in aspermia.

Creatine Phosphokinase: Spermatozoa contain a high concentration of creatine phosphokinase. Normal seminal fluid contains 385 to 1400 units of CPK/ml. Levels over 400 are almost diagnostic of seminal stains. The enzyme is stable and can be demonstrated even in old stains of six months.

Immunological Method: MHS-5 produced from seminal vesicles and Mab 4 E6 can be detected on the sperm cells and in the ejaculated fluid. Prostate specific antigen (PSA, P30) is a glycoprotein produced by prostate and is found in seminal plasma (normal and aspermic semen), male urine and blood, but not in any tissues or fluid of the female. It is found in vaginal fluid up to 27 hours after sexual intercourse. Tests for P 30 have replaced the quantitative analysis for acid phosphatase. A positive PSA finding is a reliable indicator of semen, regardless of the presence of spermatozoa or elevated acid phosphatase level.

Fluorescent in situ hybridisation (FISH) has been suggested as a sensitive and specific test for detection of male epithelial cells in the post-coital vagina up to one week. Y-chromosome positive epithelial cells have Sexual Offences 435 been identified in vaginal swabs even in cases with no ejaculation.

Choline and Spermine Test: Liquid semen and dried seminal stains can be identified by a thin layer chromatographic technique. The test is based on the unique combination of choline and spermine which is present only in semen. Spermine is found in testes, pancreas, liver, spleen, brain, blood, bone marrow and body fluids, but its concentration is lower than in semen. One microliter of semen present can be detected by this method. The sensitivity of detection and identification has been enormously enhanced by amplification techniques, such as PCR (polymerase chain reaction). Y chromosome short tandem repeat (STR) markers have been successfully used to analyse mixed stains with a male component. After vasectomy, chemical and enzymatic tests for semen remain positive, though no sperms will be present.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, K S Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 337

question_text: A 32-year-old man enjoys dressing as a woman, adopts feminine mannerisms, and reports occasional sexual pleasure from cross-dressing without hormonal or genital abnormalities. What is the most likely diagnosis?

  • Characteristics:
    • Dress, manner, occupational interests, and associations are aimed at increasing the feeling of being a woman (in males).
    • Sexuality is relatively unimportant, except when it promotes feelings of femininity.
  • Occurrence:
    • Usually found in males.
    • They may obtain sexual pleasure by wearing female dress.
  • Psychological basis:
    • May depend on erotic attraction to the opposite sex.
    • Only a small percentage are homosexuals.
    • Rarely develops from fetishistic interest in clothing or specific body parts of the opposite sex.
  • Physical findings:
    • No hormonal disturbances or genital abnormalities.

Transsexualism (Option A): Characterised by a persistent desire to live as the opposite gender, often seeking hormonal or surgical transition, not just cross-dressing.

Frotteurism (Option C): It refers to a person who obtains sexual gratification by contact with another person (rubbing his private parts against buttocks, breasts, or thighs, in public crowded places), unrelated to gender identity or clothing.

Gender dysphoria (Option D): Refers to distress caused by a mismatch between one's gender identity and assigned sex, which may or may not involve cross-dressing.

question_text: During a sexual assault investigation involving an 18-year-old female and a 20-year-old male, the forensic team performed Barberio's test on collected stains. Which substance does this test detect?
explanation:
Explanation:

Barberio’s test is a chemical test used for the detection of spermine, a component of seminal fluid secreted by the prostate. When picric acid is added to the sample, yellow needle-shaped crystals (spermine picrate crystals) are formed, confirming the presence of semen.

Additional tests used in semen analysis in cases of sexual assault:

  • Fluorescence test: When a seminal stain is exposed to ultraviolet (UV) light, it produces a bluish-white fluorescence.
  • CPK (Creatine Phosphokinase) test: Used to identify old seminal stains, even up to 6 months old. Normal range: 660 IU/ml.
  • LDH isoenzyme detection of sperm: The most specific test for semen identification. The presence of a single intact sperm provides absolute confirmation.
  • Phadebas test: Used to detect saliva, particularly in cases involving oral sex, by identifying the enzyme L-amylase.

Explanation of other options:

Acid phosphatase (Option B): Another marker of semen, detected by the Brentamine test.

Choline (Option C): Identified by Florence test, which produces characteristic choline periodide crystals.

Fructose (Option D): Present in seminal plasma, tested by the resorcinol method to confirm seminal fluid origin.

References: Semen analysis

question_text: In case of sexual assault to a child, the hymen may not be ruptured because:
explanation:
In prepubertal girls, the hymen is anatomically positioned more deeply within the vaginal canal compared to postpubertal females. This deeper placement provides a degree of protection, making it less likely to be ruptured during sexual assault.

Additionally:

  • The hymen in children is often more flexible and elastic, but its deep location is a primary factor in preventing rupture during certain assaults.
  • Penetration may involve superficial structures without reaching or affecting the hymen.

Rule Out:

a) Elasticity of the hymen: While the hymen is elastic, in children, its deeper location is a more relevant factor in its preservation.

c) Hymen is undeveloped: The hymen is always present from birth and does not go through a "developmental" phase.

d) Hymen is tough in structure: The hymen's toughness varies among individuals, but its deep placement is more significant in this context.

Key Takeaways:

  1. In children, the deeply seated hymen often remains intact, even in cases of sexual assault.
  2. An intact hymen does not rule out sexual abuse; forensic examination and corroborating evidence are essential.
  3. Medical professionals must approach such cases with sensitivity and thoroughness.

question_text: In case of suspected sodomy, an anal swab was taken and on staining yellow needle shaped crystals of picrate were detected. Which test is done?
explanation:
The Barberio's test is used to detect the presence of sodium picrate crystals in the case of sodomy or sexual assault, which forms yellow needle-shaped crystals upon staining. These crystals are a product of the reaction between picric acid (used in the test) and semen, confirming the presence of semen in the anal swab sample.

  • The Barberio's test is specific for identifying sodium picrate crystals, and it is often used to confirm sodomy or sexual assault in forensic investigations.
  • The presence of these crystals supports the suspicion of semen and thus indicates sexual activity.

Rule Out:

b) Florence test: Involves the detection of crystals but is specifically used to detect sodium picrate crystals related to semen in other contexts.

c) Ammonium molybdate test: Used for detecting phosphate compounds but not specific to semen.

d) Acid phosphatase test: Detects acid phosphatase, an enzyme found in semen, but does not result in the formation of needle-shaped crystals like Barberio's test.

Key Takeaways:

  1. Barberio's test is the correct method to detect yellow needle-shaped crystals of picrate, indicating sodium picrate in semen.
  2. This test is specific to suspected sodomy or sexual assault cases.
  3. It is important to choose the right forensic test to confirm the presence of semen in the evidence.

question_text: Barberio's test detects
explanation:
Barberio's test is a forensic chemical test used to detect the presence of spermine. Spermine is a polyamine found in semen and other biological fluids. The test involves using a reagent, typically concentrated nitric acid or phosphotungstic acid, which reacts with spermine to produce characteristic needle-shaped crystals. This test is often employed in forensic investigations to confirm the presence of seminal fluid, particularly in cases involving sexual assault.

Rule Out

Choline (a):

Choline is a component of phospholipids and is not detected by Barberio's test. Tests specific to choline often involve enzymatic or spectrophotometric methods rather than crystal formation reactions.

Lecithin (c):

Lecithin is a phospholipid commonly found in biological tissues, particularly in cell membranes. It does not react with the reagents used in Barberio's test, and its detection requires specialized lipid analysis techniques, such as chromatography.

Blood (d):

Blood is tested using methods such as luminol, Kastle-Meyer test, or microscopic examination. Barberio's test does not react with components of blood and is specific to spermine found in semen.

Key Takeaways

Barberio's test is a classic forensic method to identify spermine, a key component of seminal fluid.

The formation of characteristic needle-shaped crystals is a positive indicator of spermine.

Proper identification of biological fluids like semen is critical in forensic investigations, especially in sexual assault cases.

Understanding the specificity of different forensic tests helps avoid confusion between bodily fluids or chemical substances.

question_text: Which of the following represents an illegal or abnormal method commonly used for criminal abortion?
explanation:
Explanation:

An abortion stick is an unsafe and abnormal method often employed in criminal abortions. It is typically a thin wooden or bamboo stick, 12-18 cm long, with one end or much of its length wrapped in cotton or cloth and soaked in substances such as marking nut juice, calotropis, jequirity, asafoetida, or toxic compounds like arsenic oxide, arsenic sulphate, mercuric chloride, or red lead. Traditional abortionists (often called dhaies) insert this stick into the cervix or uterus and leave it there until uterine contractions begin. This method is extremely dangerous and can lead to severe complications, including infection, uterine perforation, haemorrhage, and death.

Explanation for Other Options:

Dilatation and curettage (option A): A standard medical procedure used in legal abortions for uterine evacuation.

Mifepristone (option B): A medication used in medical abortion to safely terminate early pregnancies under medical supervision.

Vacuum aspiration (option D): A routine and safe method for early pregnancy termination performed in clinical settings.

Closed court proceedings (Option B): While closed court proceedings ensure limited public access, they are not as specific or protective as hearings conducted on camera.

Hearing in a different location (Option C): While certain situations might necessitate a different location for the hearing, it is not the standard protocol for recording evidence in sexual assault cases.

question_text: A 5-year-old child with a history of perianal pain is brought to the OPD. On subjecting the specimen from the perianal region to a test, it produces yellow rhombic crystals of spermine picrate. What is the test done?
explanation:
The test done in the scenario is the Barberio test.

Barberio's test:

  • Used to detect: Semen.
  • Stain used: Saturated aqueous or alcoholic solution of picric acid.
  • Finding: If semen is present, yellow needle-shaped rhombic crystals of spermine picrate

Florence test:

  • Used to detect: Semen.
  • Stain used: 10% hydrochloric acid and Florence solution (potassium iodide, iodine, and water)
  • Finding: If semen is present, dark brown rhombic or needle-shaped crystals of choline iodide appear immediately

Takayama test (Haemochromogen crystal test):

  • Used to detect: Bloodstains.
  • Stain used: Takayama reagent (sodium hydroxide. pyridine, glucose)
  • Finding: If bloodstain is present, pink feathery crystals of hemochromogen or reduced alkaline haematin appear in a few minutes

Teichmann's test (Haemin crystal Test):

  • Used to detect: Bloodstains.
  • Stain used: Glacial acetic acid and a small crystal of sodium chloride.
  • Finding: If bloodstain is present, faint yellowish red to brownish-black rhombic crystals of haemin or haematin chloride appear

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 337, 349

question_text: During the forensic analysis of semen from a rape victim, the detection of characteristic yellow needle-shaped crystals is noted. Which specific test is used to confirm the presence of sperm?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Barberio test, which is indicated by the presence of yellow needle-shaped crystals, is used to detect seminal fluid in such cases. This test specifically identifies spermine, a compound produced by the prostate, to confirm the presence of seminal fluid.


Barberio test

Explanation for other options:

Acid phosphatase test (Option B): This test detects seminal fluid due to the high concentration of acid phosphatase in semen. However, it does not produce yellow needle-like crystals.

Papanicolaou smear (Option C): Commonly known as the Pap smear, this screening test is used to identify cervical cancer and detect abnormalities in cervical cells

Florence Test (Option D): This test detects choline and results in the formation of distinct dark brown rhombic crystals.

question_text: Identify the test depicted in the image below that is conducted on the victim's clothing to detect blood stains.
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows the Teichmann test, also known as the haemin crystal test, which is a classical confirmatory test for detecting blood stains on clothing or other exhibits.

Key steps & findings:

  • A small portion of the suspected stain is placed on a glass slide.
  • Add 2-3 drops of glacial acetic acid and a tiny crystal of sodium chloride.
  • Cover with a coverslip and gently heat.
  • Presence of blood is confirmed when brownish-black rhombic crystals of haemin (haematine chloride)
  • Adding hydrogen peroxide produces bubbles of gas due to oxidation of the crystal.

This test remains reliable even on old or dried stains, making it invaluable in forensic investigations.

Explanation of Other options:

Barberio test (option A): Detects seminal fluid, not blood. Saturated picric acid added to semen produces yellow, needle-shaped rhombic crystals of spermine picrate.

Florence test (option B): Another semen test. Mixing the suspected stain extract with Florence reagent (iodine + potassium iodide) yields dark brown rhombic/needle-shaped crystals of choline iodide.

Takayama test (option C): Also a blood test, but it forms pink feathery crystals of haemochromogen (pyridine-haemochrome) using pyridine and glucose under heat.

Key takeaway:

  • The Barberio test specifically detects Spermine, a compound derived from the prostate, and is used to identify seminal fluid.

Explanation for other options:

Takayama test (Option C): Similar to the Teichmann test, the Takayama test is used for haemoglobin detection.

question_text: Which test is used to forensically determine if a bloodstain is of human origin?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Precipitin test is an immunological assay that uses species-specific antibodies (e.g., anti-human serum) to form a visible precipitate when mixed with blood from that species. It is the standard forensic method for determining the human origin of a blood sample.

Confirmatory tests for blood stain:

  • Chemical Confirmatory Tests:
    • Takayama Test (Option D ruled out) :Detects hemoglobin by forming red, feathery crystals of pyridine ferroprotoporphyrin.
    • Teichmann Test (Option A ruled out) :Converts hemoglobin to hemin, creating brownish-yellow rhomboid crystals, confirming blood presence.
  • Immunological Tests:
    • Precipitin Test (Option B):Identifies species origin through antibody-antigen reactions, using antisera specific to human blood.
    • HemaTrace Test: Uses monoclonal antibodies to detect human hemoglobin, showing a visible pink band for confir
  • Mass Spectrometry Techniques
    • Thread Spray Mass Spectrometry: Analyzes whole blood directly on textiles, differentiating species based on lipid composition and hemoglobin chains. It offers high sensitivity and specificity.

Explanation of other options:

Barberio test (Option C): The Barberio test is a chemical test used to confirm the presence of seminal fluid by detecting spermine, a compound found in prostatic secretion. In this test, a sample is treated with a solution of picric acid, which reacts with spermine to form distinctive yellow, needle-shaped crystals of spermine picrate

Key Takeaways:

  • Precipitin test: Determines species origin of blood.
  • Teichmann/Takayama: Confirm the presence of blood (any species).
  • Barberio/Florence: Confirm the presence of semen.

question_text: An old man who was lying on the roadside is brought to the casualty by the police. On detailed history, he reveals that he has had no food for the past few weeks. On examination, he is severely emaciated. What is the likely finding in the gall bladder?
explanation:
The given clinical scenario points to starvation. In this condition, the gall bladder is distended.

  • In starvation, bile does not get secreted into the duodenum due to the absence of food entering the stomach and intestine. Hence, bill gets accumulated in the gall bladder which gets distended.
  • In acute starvation, there is a feeling of hunger for the first 30 to 48 hours,
  • If both water and food are completely withdrawn death occurs in 10 to 12 days.
  • If food alone is withdrawn death occurs in 6 to 8 weeks or even more.
  • Death usually occurs when about 80 of body fat, and 20% of body protein are lost.
  • Newborns may survive for 7 to 10 days without food or water.
  • Life is threatened when more than 40 per cent of the original body weight has been lost, though the speed of loss is relevant (BK).
  • There is a reduction in the weight and size of all organs except the brain.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 258; Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th edition, Page No. 415

question_text: X-ray of a child shows a nobbing fracture. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • A "nobbing fracture" is a term for a rib fracture with a "string of beads" appearance on an X-ray, which can indicate child abuse (Battered baby syndrome).
  • Involvement of several consecutive ribs on one or both sides is often encountered in child abuse.
  • Damage may be fresh or old demonstrating different radiological appearances
    • These fractures occur when an assailant violently shakes the child (infantile whiplash syndrome/shaken baby syndrome) or squeezes from side to side, fracturing ribs near the spine on both sides, producing a 'nobbing' appearance on X-ray.
    • Mechanism:Ribs may be levered against the transverse processes causing breakage.
    • Fractures become more visible after 1-2 weeks due to callus formation.
    • Rib fractures near the axillary line can result from anteroposterior pressure rather than side squeezing.

Munchausen syndrome (Option B):

  • Adults feign illness or self-injury to gain medical attention.
  • When a parent or carer feigns an impression or produces a state of ill health in a child, it is labelled as factitious illness by proxy or Munchausen syndrome by proxy.

Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) (Option C):

  • Sudden, unexplained death of a seemingly healthy infant, usually during sleep.
  • No fractures or physical trauma are involved.
  • Usually, the parent finds the infant expired in the crib after putting them to
  • It is an unexpected death in a healthy infant, whose autopsy may not reveal a cause of death.

Hyperabduction shoulder injury (Option D):

  • Injury due to extreme shoulder abduction causing nerve or bone injury but unrelated to rib fractures or nobbing appearance.

Key Takeaways:

  • Nobbing fractures on X-ray strongly suggest non-accidental injury (child abuse).
  • Recognizing these signs is critical for timely intervention.

question_text: Suggestive of a case of victim of battered baby syndrome is
explanation:
Battered Baby Syndrome (BBS) refers to the physical abuse of an infant or young child, often resulting from repeated and multiple injuries inflicted over time. A key feature of this syndrome is the presence of multiple injuries at different stages of healing, suggesting that the abuse is chronic, with the child being injured repeatedly over time.

Key points:

  • Multiple injuries at different ages: This is characteristic of Battered Baby Syndrome as it indicates a pattern of repeated physical trauma, often with varying degrees of healing.
  • Injuries may include bruises, fractures, and internal injuries, some of which may be older while others are more recent.
  • The abuse can be physical, emotional, or both, and it may involve shaking, striking, or impact trauma.

Rule Out:

a) Stab wound: This is a sharp force injury that is generally not consistent with Battered Baby Syndrome, as it involves a single traumatic event and is usually caused by an external attacker.

c) Skull fracture: While skull fractures can occur in cases of abuse, they are not specific to Battered Baby Syndrome, as they can result from various causes, including accidents.

d) Fracture of long bone: A long bone fracture can occur in abuse cases, but the key feature of Battered Baby Syndrome is the repeated nature of the injuries, and long bone fractures can also occur due to accidents or other causes.

Key Takeaways:

  1. Battered Baby Syndrome is characterized by multiple injuries of varying ages, reflecting ongoing abuse.
  2. Medical professionals should consider child abuse as a cause when injuries are inconsistent with the child's developmental stage or history.
  3. Clinical suspicion is critical in identifying cases of child abuse, which often require immediate intervention for the safety of the child.

question_text: A 6-month-old male infant is brought to the emergency department by his parents with complaints of lethargy and poor feeding. On clinical examination, the child has bruises over the chest and abdomen and swelling around the knee joints. X-rays reveal multiple fractures of different stages of healing, including long bone fractures around the knees, posterior rib fractures, and subdural hematomas on neuroimaging. Based on the above findings and the image provided, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Definition:

  • Also called Child Abuse Syndrome, Caffey's Syndrome, or Maltreatment Syndrome.
  • Refers to repeated non-accidental physical injuries inflicted on a child by a parent or guardian.
  • May also include neglect of nutrition, care, and affection.

Classical Features:

  • Injuries inconsistent with the explanation given by caregivers.
  • Delay in seeking medical care for injuries.
  • Recurrent injuries over time, ranging from minor to severe.

Epidemiology:

  • Age: Mostly <3 years, but can occur at any age.
  • Sex: Slight male predominance (55-63%).
  • Family position: Often the eldest or youngest child; sometimes unwanted children.
  • Socioeconomic factors:
    • Parents often young (20-30 years), low education, lower social class.
    • Family may be isolated, with history of disharmony, emotional, or financial problems.
    • Fathers may have criminal records; mothers may have psychiatric or social issues.
    • Parental history of abuse in their own childhood is common.

History & Precipitating Factors:

  • Injuries are explained inconsistently or differently each time the child is taken to a doctor.
  • Violence may be triggered by normal child behavior (crying, soiling, etc.).
  • Delay between injury and medical attention is common.

Cause of Death:

  • Head injury is the most common fatal cause.
  • Rupture of internal organs may also lead to death.

Diagnosis:

  • Based on:
    • Nature and pattern of injuries.
    • Delay in seeking medical care.
    • Recurrence of injuries.
  • Radiological evaluation (X-ray) is essential to detect old fractures and metaphyseal injuries.
  • Differential diagnosis includes: scurvy, congenital syphilis, osteomyelitis, leukemia, rickets, osteogenesis imperfecta, and other metabolic or bone disorders.

question_text: All of the following changes occur in chronic starvation except?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In chronic starvation, the body undergoes multiple systemic changes.
  • Hyperthermia is not a feature. Instead, patients develop hypothermia due to decreased metabolic rate and impaired thermoregulation.

Changes in Chronic Starvation:

  • Loss of well-being, hunger, and hunger pains.
  • Mental and physical lethargy; easy fatigue.
  • Progressive weight loss (most rapid in first 6 months).
  • Polyuria.
  • Severe wasting: body weight reduced by ~40% of normal.
  • Pigmentation and anaemia.
  • Hypothermia (not hyperthermia) with peripheral vascular stasis in cold environments.
  • Hypotension.
  • Extreme lethargy, gross mental retardation, and loss of self-respect.
  • Oedema (first in feet and lower limbs).
  • Reduced resistance to infections (e.g., diarrhoea, dysentery, tuberculosis).

Explanation of Other Options:

Exhaustion (Option B):

  • A prominent feature is due to loss of energy reserves and progressive muscle wasting.
  • Patients show both mental and physical lethargy.

Heart Atrophy (Option C):

  • Seen in prolonged starvation.
  • The heart muscle shrinks due to protein-energy depletion.
  • Leads to weakened cardiac output.

Hypotension (Option D):

  • Common finding.
  • Due to reduced blood volume and atrophy of the heart.
  • Often associated with peripheral vascular stasis.

Reference: Chronic starvation

question_text: In which of the following conditions is a false positive hydrostatic test in fetus seen?
explanation:
False positive hydrostatic test in fetus seen in Putrefied fetus

Hydrostatic test

It is also known as the floatation test/Breslau's first life test

It is done to determine whether the newborn has respired(breathed) or not.

Principle:

  • The specific gravity of the lungs before respiration is about 1.050, i.e., heavier than water.
  • The specific gravity of the lungs after respiration is about 0.950(D/t presence of air), i.e., lighter than water.
  • Therefore, non-respired lungs sink in water and the respired lungs float.

Method:

  • Remove the lungs along with bronchi, trachea and larynx after ligating.
  • Place in a container containing water.
  • See whether they float or sink.
  • Separate each lung and test similarly.
  • Cut each lung into about 15-20 pieces and test for floatation.
  • Firmly press each piece between thumb and fingers(to expel the tidal air and putrefactive gases) and test again.

Inference:

  • If all the pieces float, it indicates that the respiration has taken place.
  • If all the pieces sink, it means the child has not breathed.
  • If some pieces sink and some pieces float, it indicates partial or feeble respiration.

Fallacies of hydrostatic test:

  1. The expanded lungs may sink(False - ve) in cases of
    • Acute edema
    • Pneumonia
    • Congenital syphilis
    • Atelectasis
  2. The unexpanded lungs may float(False + ve) in cases of
    • Putrefaction
    • Artificial respiration

Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 2nd edition, PC Dixit, Page No. 175-177.

question_text: Which of the following poisonings typically produces a bright red colour of post-mortem hypostasis (lividity)?
explanation:
Explanation:

A classic feature of fatal carbon monoxide (CO) exposure is a striking pink to bright cherry-red colouration of the skin, mucous membranes, internal organs, and post-mortem hypostasis.

CO binds to haemoglobin with far greater affinity than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin. This complex imparts a characteristic vivid red hue that persists even after death.

  • When a blood sample from such a case is diluted with water and viewed against a white background or strong light, the pinkish colouration is particularly noticeable.

Explanation for other options:

Opioid poisoning (option A): Typically produces cyanosis with bluish discolouration of lips, nails, and dependent parts due to respiratory depression and hypoxia. Post-mortem lividity is usually dark blue-violet rather than red.

Hydrogen sulphide poisoning (option C): Causes rapid death from respiratory failure. The lividity is generally greenish or dark brown because hydrogen sulphide reacts with haemoglobin to form sulfhaemoglobin, not a cherry-red colour.

Phosphorus poisoning (option D): Often results in jaundiced or yellowish skin changes and a garlicky odour, along with fatty degeneration of the liver. No characteristic bright-red lividity is associated with elemental phosphorus toxicity.

Key takeaway:

Postmortem staining in poisonings:

question_text: Yellow/fatty liver is characteristically seen in
explanation:
Phosphorus is a powerful hepatotoxic poison. Initially liver is swollen, yellow, soft, and fatty. Later there will be acute yellow atrophy.

Postmortem findings in phosphorus poisoning:

External

  1. Emaciation, purpuric haemorrhages in the skin, jaundice and the smell of garlic may be present.
  2. Mucous membrane of the mouth is corroded.
  3. Hypostasis is dark brown in color.

Internal

  1. Multiple haemorrhages are seen in the muscles, serosal and mucosal membranes of the GIT and respiratory tract, liver, kidneys, endocardium, pericardium, epicardium, peritoneum, lungs and brain.
  2. Stomach and intestines: Mucous membranes are yellowish or greyish white in colour, softened, thickened, inflamed and corroded in patches; luminous material may be found in the stomach. Contents may smell of garlic.
  3. Liver: Swollen, yellow, soft, fatty and easily ruptured.
  4. Kidneys: Enlarged, greasy, yellow.
  5. Heart: Flabby, pale and shows fatty degeneration.
  6. Lungs: Fat emboli may be found in the pulmonary arterioles and capillaries.

Histopathology: Toxic hepatitis with extensive necrosis, ballooning degeneration, and steatosis.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition, Page No. 566; Textbook of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, VV Pillay, 20th edition, Page No. 428

question_text: A patient was brought to emergency with history of intake of some unknown seeds. He had convulsions, opisthotonus and facial muscle spasm. The most likely poisoning is with:
explanation:
Signs and symptoms resemble poisoning due to nux vomica seeds.

Signs and symptoms are seen within 15-30 minutes of ingestion. A 'conscious' seizure is the characteristic presentation of strychnine poisoning.

Findings associated with poisoning are

  1. Bitter taste.
  2. Choking sensation in throat, and stiffness of the neck and face.
  3. Prodromal symptoms: Restlessness, increased acuity of perception, increased rigidity of muscles and muscular twitchings.
  4. Face: Cyanosed, look is anxious, eyes are staring, eyeballs are prominent, and the pupils are dilated. Mouth is filled with bloodstained froth.
  5. Convulsions: The threshold for CNS stimulation is lowered with the result that any sensory stimulus (light, pain, touch, or noise) may produce violent muscular spasm. Initially, clonic but eventually become tonic, and affect all the muscles at the same time.
  • Risus sardonicus results from raising of patient's eyebrows, bulging of eyes and contraction of the jaw and facial muscles in which the corners of the mouth are drawn back leading to an evil looking grin. This expression can be seen in tetanus too.
  • Convulsions are more marked in anti-gravity muscles resulting in hyperextension (opisthotonos)
  • Sometimes, the spasm of the abdominal muscles may bend the body forward (emprosthotonus) or sideways (pleurosthotonus).
  • Duration of convulsions is about half to 2 min and may recur for 12-24 hours (h). During convulsions the patient remains awake and aware of everything around him since strychnine does not cross the blood-brain barrier.
  • In between convulsions, muscles are completely relaxed and breathing is resumed. Patient is usually in pain, exhausted, anxious and anticipating the next series of convulsions.
  • After 5-15 min, on the slightest impulse, such as sudden noise, current of air or on gently touching the patient, another convulsion occurs with increased intensity.
  • Increased muscle tone, hyperreflexia, agitation, restlessness and convulsions lead to profound lactic acidosis, rhabomyolysis and hyperthermia.
  • Death occurs within 4-5 convulsions as the patient cannot breathe. Consciousness is not lost and the mind remains clear till death. At the time of death, the body 'freezes' even in the middle of convulsions resulting in 'cadaveric spasm.

Cause of death: Death is due to medullary paralysis or asphyxia due to spasm of respiratory muscles or due to exhaustion from convulsions.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition, Page No. 630

The vital reactions of a wound are of two types:

  • In the immediate vicinity of a wound edge, a central or superficial zone, 0.2 – 0.5mm deep shows decreasing enzyme activity, also known as the negative vital reaction
  • Surrounding the central area, a peripheral zone 0.1 – 0.3mm deep, exhibits an increase in enzyme activity, also known as positive vital reaction

question_text: Which of the following tissues is most resistant to knife penetration?
explanation:
The tissue most resistant to knife penetration is the skin, apart from bone or calcified cartilage.

When a knife-point impacts against the skin, the latter dimples, and resists. The tension developed in the stretched skin appears to act as an elastic reservoir and when the threshold of resistance is exceeded, penetration suddenly occurs.

Muscle offers little resistance to penetration. Uncalcified cartilage and subcutaneous tissue are easily penetrated by a sharp knife.

Skin is known to provide the most resistance to penetration with muscle and fat being more readily penetrated. Thus, once the skin is penetrated, assuming that a force continues to be applied, then the weapon will continue to penetrate to a depth dependent upon the length of the weapon.

Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology 4th Edition, Page No.156

question_text: Which of the following is not a major injury to the unrestrained driver of a vehicle in a deceleration impact?
explanation:
Lumbar spinal injury is not a major injury to the unrestrained driver of a vehicle in a deceleration impact. However, in these cases, cervical spinal injury is common. The heavy head goes forwards, and there is flexion of the cervical and thoracic spines. When the most common event – frontal impact – occurs, the unrestrained driver first slides forwards so that his legs strike the fascia/parcel-shelf area and may sustain fracture of the bones of legs and feet. The force may transmit from the knees through femur to pelvis and may sustain fracture of femur and pelvis.

Reference: Knight’s Forensic Pathology, 4th Edition, Page No.278

question_text: Which of the following statements about extradural haemorrhage is false?
option_a: Extradural haemorrhage may be ruled out in the absence of a skull fracture
option_b: A minimum of 35 ml of blood is required to accumulate for clinical signs to appear
option_c: The most common vessel affected is middle meningeal artery
option_d: It is the least common type of traumatic brain membrane haemorrhage
explanation:
Extradural haemorrhages (EDH) cannot be ruled out in the absence of a skull fracture.

Most extradural haemorrhages are associated with fractures of the skull, but about 15 per cent occur in intact skull.

They usually occur unilaterally in the parieto-temporal area, caused by the rupture of the middle meningeal artery(usually posterior branch).

It is the least common type of brain membrane bleeding.

The most common traumatic intracranial haemorrhage is sub-arachnoid haemorrhage.

Adams suggests that a minimum volume of 35 ml is needed before clinical signs are apparent, though other writers suggest 100 ml is usually the minimum associated with fatalities.

Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th edition. Page no 182, 183

question_text: Which is the most dangerous type of cervical spinal injury?
explanation:
Hyperextension is much more dangerous in causing spinal damage. It is because the weak anterior longitudinal ligament is incapable of preserving the integrity of the cervical spine during hyperextension.

question_text: Which is the most commonly injured organ in blunt trauma of abdomen?
explanation:

Liver is the most likely organ to be damaged in blunt abdominal trauma and is second only to the brain in overall visceral susceptibility.

Liver is the quite frequently involved organ in vehicular accidents and in falls. Its large size, fixed location solid consistency and relative inelastic nature make it an easy target for blunt injury to the upper abdomen and thorax, especially on right side.

(But as per Surgery books like Bailey & Love, most common organ involved in blunt abdominal trauma is Spleen)

In order of frequency. the structures most likely to be damaged in blunt abdominal trauma are liver, spleen, Kidney, Intestine, abdominal wall, Mesentery, pancreas and diaphragm.

question_text: A person is considered to be hypothermic when their temperature falls below:
explanation:
Hypothermia occurs when the body's core temperature drops below 35°C.

  • Mild hypothermia - Core temperature 32 to 35°C (90 to 95°F)
  • Moderate hypothermia - Core temperature 28 to 32°C (82 to 90°F)
  • Severe hypothermia - Core temperature below 28°C (82°F)

Hypothermia is caused by prolonged exposures to very cold temperatures. When exposed to cold temperatures, your body begins to lose heat faster than it's produced. Lengthy exposures will eventually use up your body's stored energy, which leads to lower body temperature.
