question_text: A 50-year-old man collapses after consuming a self-prepared herbal decoction. He is found to have bradycardia, hypotension, and life-threatening arrhythmias. On ECG, there is QT prolongation and frequent ventricular ectopics. Which of the following is least likely to be the cause of cardiotoxicity in such poisonings?
explanation:
Explanation:

Opium is a CNS depressant and respiratory suppressant, but not primarily cardiotoxic, unlike the other listed agents.

  • Aconite, Oleander, Nicotine are all well-known cardiac poisons causing bradycardia, arrhythmias, and even cardiac arrest.
  • Opium, derived from Papaver somniferum, mainly affects the central nervous system, leading to:
    • Miosis
    • Respiratory depression
    • Coma
  • It does not cause direct myocardial toxicity or conduction defects characteristic of the other poisons listed.

Key Takeaway:

Opium is not cardiotoxic, its toxic effects are CNS and respiratory in nature.

question_text: Poison which can be detected even in exhumated decomposed bodies
explanation:
Arsenic is a heavy metal that is highly stable and resistant to decomposition. It binds strongly to tissues, including hair, nails, and bones, and can persist in the body for many years, even after death and decomposition.

In cases of exhumation, arsenic can be detected in the following:

  1. Hair and nails: Arsenic deposits are often present and can be analyzed.
  2. Bones and soft tissues: Despite decomposition, arsenic remains detectable through chemical analysis.

This property makes arsenic one of the poisons that can be reliably identified in decomposed or buried bodies.

Rule Out:

a) Mercury: Though detectable in hair and nails, mercury may not persist as well in extensively decomposed bodies due to its volatile nature.

c) Copper: Copper is less stable and may not be detectable in highly decomposed bodies.

d) Bismuth: Bismuth is rarely used as a poison and does not persist in tissues as reliably as arsenic.

Key Takeaways:

  1. Arsenic is highly stable and can be detected even in exhumed, decomposed bodies, making it significant in forensic toxicology.
  2. Techniques like atomic absorption spectrophotometry (AAS) or inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS) are commonly used for detection.
  3. The persistence of heavy metals in the body helps solve poisoning cases even long after death.

question_text: Acute copper sulphate poisoning manifests with:
explanation:
Acute copper sulphate poisoning manifests with Acute hemolysis

Signs and symptoms of acute copper sulphate poisoning:

GIT: Metallic taste, ptyalism (increased salivation), burning pain in stomach, thirst, colicky abdominal pain, nausea, eructation and repeated vomiting. Vomitus is greenish- blue. Diarrhea with much straining, hemorrhagic gastroenteritis.

Renal: Oliguria, hematuria, hemoglobinuria, albuminuria and uremia.

Hepatic: Jaundice, tender hepatomegaly, hepatic encephalopathy.

Muscular system: Cramps or spasms of legs, paralysis of limbs, rhabdomyolysis.

CVS: Breathing difficulty, cold perspiration, methemoglobinemia, hypotension, tachycardia, circulatory collapse and shock.

CNS: Frontal headache, lethargy, drowsiness, insensibility, irreversible coma and death occurs.

  • Hemolysis and hemoglobinuria are present in severe cases. Individuals with G-6-phosphate deficiency may be at increased risk of hematologic effects of copper.
  • Multiorgan dysfunction syndrome may occur.
  • Early death is attributed to hypotension and shock, late death to hepatic and/or renal failure.

Copper poisoning affects the erythrocytes, the liver, and the kidneys in the order. Intravascular haemolysis appears 12-24 h following ingestion. Haemolytic anaemia is caused either by direct cell membrane damage or indirectly as a result of the inactivation of enzymes which protect against oxidative stress.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition, Page No. 553

question_text: A girl, otherwise healthy, sleeping on the floor suddenly develops nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, quadriplegia at night. Diagnosis is:
explanation:
Krait: Signs and symptoms are similar to cobra poisoning, but less rapid.

The signs and symptoms are

  • Abdominal pain
  • Ptosis
  • Dysarthria
  • Dysphagia
  • Chest pain
  • Quadriparesis
  • Respiratory paralysis
  • Death

Common krait hunt nocturnally and are quick to bite people sleeping on the floor, often without waking their victims, since the venom is painless. Victims wake up early morning, paralyzed - mistaken for STROKE

Option A: GBS will have a preceding history of diarrhoea 6 to 8 weeks before and will have ascending paralysis.

Option B: Poliomyelitis will have gradual onset flaccid paralysis. 

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition, Page No. 581

question_text: The usual fatal dose of white phosphorous:
explanation:
The usual fatal dose of white phosphorous is 60-120 mg.

  • Fulminating poisoning (death within 12 hours) may be seen when the patient takes a large dose.
  • Early death is due to cardiac dysrhythmias, secondary to electrolyte abnormalities, such as hypocalcaemia and hyperkalaemia.
  • Death after the first 24 h is due to hepatic failure.

Fatal dose: 60-120 mg (1 mg/kg) of white phosphorus.

Fatal period: Within 24 hours but may be delayed by 5-7 days.

Diagnosis: Oral and skin burns, luminescent 'smoking' vomitus and stools with a garlic odour, and GIT and biliary damage characterize white phosphorus poisoning.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition, Page No. 565

question_text: Smell of burnt rope due to poisoning with:
explanation:
Cannabis give rise to burnt rope smell.

Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, Anil Aggrawal, Page No. 560

question_text: Mild poisoning by organophosphate occurs when the ChE activity is
explanation:
• Mild poisoning usually occurs when cholinesterase activity is 20 to 50% of normal.
  • Moderate poisoning occurs when activity is 10 to 20% of normal.
  • Severe poisoning when activity is less than 10% normal.

Small, repeated exposures may gradually depress the cholinesterase activity to very low levels, often resulting in minimal symptoms.

References: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 396.

question_text: Smell of burnt rope is due to poisoning by:
explanation:
Explanation:

The smell of burnt rope is a distinctive feature of cannabis (marijuana) when it is smoked.

  • Cannabis contains Δ-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), and when burnt, it produces a strong, pungent odour often compared to burnt rope.
  • This smell is commonly recognized during forensic investigations or police raids involving illegal drug use.
  • It can linger on clothing and surroundings, serving as a forensic clue.

Aluminium phosphide (Option A): Produces a fishy or garlic like odour due to release of phosphine gas.

Arsenic (Option C): Has a mild garlic smell, especially in trioxide form.

Cyanide (Option D): Gives off a bitter almond smell; however, not all individuals can perceive it due to genetic anosmia.

question_text: Shoe polish-like smell is found in:
explanation:
Explanation:

Nitrobenzene poisoning is associated with a distinctive shoe polish-like odor, which serves as an important diagnostic clue in forensic toxicology. It is commonly found in shoe polish, solvents, and industrial chemicals.

Nitrobenzene can cause:

  • Cyanosis due to methemoglobinemia
  • Headache, dizziness, and CNS depression
  • Hemolysis in severe cases

Mercaptans (Option A): Produce a foul, rotten cabbage-like odor-not similar to shoe polish.

Camphor (Option B): Has a strong mothball or medicinal odor.

Paraldehyde (Option C): Produces an acrid or pear-like smell-not shoe polish-like.

Key Takeaway:

Shoe polish-like smell is characteristic of Nitrobenzene poisoning.

question_text: Not a sign/symptom of aconite poisoning
explanation:
Explanation:

Aconite poisoning typically causes hypotension, not hypertension, due to myocardial depression and arrhythmias.

Key Takeaway:

Aconite poisoning causes hypotension, bradycardia, paresthesias, GI upset, and visual disturbances - but not hypertension.

question_text: Match the following columns-
explanation:
Let us analyze the properties of the substances in Column-A and their corresponding uses or effects in Column-B:

Quinine (A-4): Abortifacient

Quinine, an antimalarial drug, has been historically used in high doses as an abortifacient. It can induce uterine contractions, leading to termination of pregnancy. However, such use is unsafe and obsolete in modern medical practice.

Chloral Hydrate (B-1): Stupefying Agent

Chloral hydrate is a sedative and hypnotic drug. It has been used historically as a stupefying agent to induce sleep or render individuals unconscious.

Zinc Chloride (C-2): Irritant

Zinc chloride is a chemical compound that acts as an irritant. It can cause inflammation and irritation when it comes into contact with tissues.

Potassium Carbonate (D-3): Corrosive

Potassium carbonate, a strong alkali, is corrosive and can cause severe tissue damage on contact, especially in high concentrations.

Thus, the correct matches are:

A-4: Quinine → Abortifacient

B-1: Chloral hydrate → Stupefying agent

C-2: Zinc chloride → Irritant

D-3: Potassium carbonate → Corrosive

Rule Out:

Option A: A-1, B-2, C-3, D-4

Incorrect: Quinine (A) is not a stupefying agent (1). Chloral hydrate (B) is not an irritant (2). The rest do not align correctly either.

Option B: A-4, B-1, C-2, D-3

Correct: This option matches the properties correctly.

Option C: A-2, B-4, C-3, D-1

Incorrect: Quinine (A) is not an irritant (2), and chloral hydrate (B) is not an abortifacient (4).

Option D: A-4, B-1, C-2, D-3

Correct: Matches all substances with their correct corresponding effects.

Key Takeaways:

Quinine: Historically used as an abortifacient due to its ability to induce uterine contractions.

Chloral Hydrate: A sedative with historical use as a stupefying agent.

Zinc Chloride: A chemical irritant causing tissue inflammation.

Potassium Carbonate: A strong corrosive agent due to its alkalinity.

Proper understanding of chemical effects is essential in forensic toxicology for identifying causes and mechanisms of injury or poisoning.

question_text: Cyanide antidote kit does not contain:
explanation:
The 3-step cyanide antidote kit is used for cyanide poisoning.

The kit contains:

  • 12 amyl nitrite pearls,
  • Two 10 ml vials of 3% sodium nitrite
  • Two 50 ml vials of sodium thiosulfate
  1. 0.3 ml ampoule (perles) of amyl nitrite is broken in a gauze and the victim is made to inhale for 30 seconds, every minute (1st step), and use a new pearls every 3 min. Stop amyl nitrite if systolic BP is < 80 mmHg.
  2. 10 ml of 3% solution (300 mg) of sodium nitrite is injected IV slowly over 5 min (2nd step), followed by 50 ml of 25% solution (12.5g0 of sodium thiosulfate over 10-20 min. by the same needle (3rd step).

The mechanism of action of amyl nitrite and sodium nitrite as antidotes for cyanide poisoning is to produce methemoglobinemia and vasodilation.

Intravenous sodium nitrite produces significant methemoglobinemia.

Methaemoglobin has a higher affinity for cyanide than cytochrome oxidase complex and removes cyanide from the cytochrome oxidase.

Cyanides combine with methaemoglobin and form non-toxic cyanmethemoglobin which in presence of rhodanese and sulphate donors, such as thiosulphate, converts cyanide to thiocyanate which is excreted in the urine.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th Edition, Page No. 642

question_text: In case of chronic lead poisoning, the levels of which of the following is elevated:
explanation:
In case of chronic lead poisoning, the levels of Delta-amino levulinic acid are elevated.

The following image depicts the mechanism of action of lead. Enzymes in brown are inhibited; those in green remain unaffected. Products in red are increased; those in blue are normal.

Lead inhibits the enzyme ALA dehydratase which leads to increased level of Delta-amino levulinic acid

Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, Anil Aggrawal, Page No. 622

question_text: Which of the following metals can be detected even in conflagrated human remains?
explanation:
Arsenic can be detected even in conflagration of human bones. Hence, it is possible to detect poisoning by arsenic even in charred bones and ashes.

Arsenic is volatile but much of the arsenic in bones is converted into arsenates, which are non-volatile.

In suspected cases of poisoning by arsenic, all the available ashes and burnt bones should be preserved for chemical analysis.

Reference: Textbook of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, 2nd Edition, P C Dixit, Page No. 184.

question_text: The starting dose of pralidoxime in OP poisoning is:
explanation:
Pralidoxime(2-PAM), a nucleophilic oxime, most effective when treatment is started early and if used within 48 hours and helps in regenerating AChE associated with skeletal muscle neuromuscular junctions(overcome the nicotinic effects of OPCs).

Dose: 1-2 g IV(20-40 mg/kg) over 5-20 min dissolved in 0.9% normal saline solution, may be repeated at 1-2 hours if muscle weakness is not relieved and again after 8-10 hours.

Alternatively, continuous infusion(200-400 mg/h) of 2-PAM is more effective because of shorter duration of action of a single dose.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition, Page No. 655.

question_text: Which of the following characterises the intermediate syndrome in OP poisoning?
option_d: Reported in all cases of OP poisoning
explanation:
Intermediate Syndrome:

In some cases of OP poisoning after one to four days muscle weakness and paralysis characterised by motor cranial nerve palsies, weakness of neck flexor and proximal limb muscles and acute respiratory paresis are seen due to prolonged cholinesterase inhibition and muscle necrosis.

It does not respond to oximes or atropine.

Delayed Syndrome(Now called Delayed encephalopathy and neuropathy syndrome): It sometimes occur 1-4 weeks after poisoning due to nerve demyelination and is characterised by flaccid weakness and atrophy of distal limb muscles or spasticity and ataxia. It rapidly progresses to a flaccid paresis which can ascend similar to Guillain-Barre syndrome. Reflexes are diminished. The disease may progress for 2 to 3 months and muscle wasting occurs.

References: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 396; Textbook of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, VV Pillay, 20th edition, Page No. 480, Gautam Biswas, Page no. 609.

question_text: A person has been brought to ER with salivation, watery eyes, diarrhea and urinary incontinence. What is the first line of management?
explanation:
The symptoms described - salivation, watery eyes, diarrhea, and urinary incontinence - are indicative of cholinergic toxicity, likely due to exposure to an organophosphate or carbamate pesticide or nerve agent. These substances inhibit acetylcholinesterase, leading to an accumulation of acetylcholine and overstimulation of cholinergic receptors.

The first-line treatment for cholinergic toxicity is the administration of atropine, an anticholinergic drug that works by blocking muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, thus alleviating the symptoms like excessive salivation, diarrhea, and urinary incontinence.

Rule Out:

  1. Calcium gluconate:
    • Calcium gluconate is used to treat calcium channel blocker toxicity or hyperkalemia but is not indicated in cholinergic poisoning.
  2. Pralidoxime:
    • Pralidoxime is an acetylcholinesterase reactivator and is used to treat organophosphate poisoning. However, it is typically administered after atropine. While it can reverse the effects of organophosphate toxicity, it is not the first-line treatment. Atropine is used first to manage symptoms.
  3. Obidoxime:
    • Obidoxime is similar to pralidoxime and is also used for organophosphate poisoning. Like pralidoxime, it is not the first-line treatment and is used in conjunction with atropine after initial management.

Key Takeaways:

  • Atropine is the first-line treatment for cholinergic toxicity and should be given immediately to address symptoms like salivation, watery eyes, diarrhea, and urinary incontinence.
  • Pralidoxime and obidoxime are useful in treating organophosphate poisoning but are not the first drugs used.
  • Calcium gluconate is not used in cholinergic poisoning and is irrelevant in this scenario.

question_text: Phossy jaw is caused by ?
explanation: Ans. is 'a' i.e., White Phosphorus Phossy jaw is caused by phosphorus poisoning. All phosphorus poisoning are caused by white (yellow) phosphorus (Red phosphorus is nontoxic). Phosphorus poisoning Phosphorus is a protoplasmic poison affecting cellular oxidation and causing anoxic necorbiosis, classically affecting liver. It increases fat deposition and inhibits glycogen deposition in liver. It is used in fire works (Diwali poisoning) and as rat poison. Lethal dose is 60-120 mg. Phosphorus occurs in two forms :? 1) White/yellow phosphorus : It is white, and becomes yellow on exposure to air. It is translucent, waxy, luminous and crystalline cylinders. It has garlic like odor. It is insoluble in water and luminous in dark. Its fumes show phosphorescence. 2) Red phosphorus : It is reddish brown, inert, odourless and tasteless. It is nontoxic (thus poisoning occurs only due to white phosphorus). It is put on the sides (striking surface) of match box (along with powdered galss). Acute poisoning It has following stages : i) 1st Stage (GI irritation) : There is nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and garlic odor. This stage lasts for 8 hours to 3 days. garlic odor. This stage lasts for 8 hours to 3 days. ii) 2nd Stage (Asymptomatic) : This stage lasts for 3 days. iii) 3rd Stage : There is liver and kidney damage due to absorbed phosphorus. Initially liver is enlarged due to acute fatty infiltration. Later liver shruks due to necrosis, i.e. acute yellow atrophy. Chronic poisoning Toothache is the first symptom which is associated with loosening of teeth, necrosis of gums and osteomyelitis of jaw. Therefore chronic phosphorus poisoning is also know as phossy jaw (or glass jaw). Postmortem appearance There is garlic odor. Viscera and stool glow in dark (due to luminosity). To preserve luminosity, viscera are preserved in saturated saline solution. Rectified spirit is not used as it causes loss of luminosity.

question_text: Acute liver failure is a clinical feature of which condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

Acute liver failure is a hallmark of Amanita poisoning, caused by the death cap mushroom. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, an enlarged and tender liver, jaundice, reduced urine output (oliguria), mental confusion, seizures, and coma.

Explanation for other options:

Organophosphate (OP) poisoning (Option A): typically presents with pinpoint pupils and excessive sweating (diaphoresis), but does not cause liver failure.

Belladonna poisoning (Option C): is characterized by tachycardia and hallucinations, without liver failure.

Morphine poisoning (Option D): leads to respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils, but does not result in liver failure.

Reference:

  1. Mushroom Poisoning - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics.
  2. Mushroom Poisoning - PubMed.
  3. The Deceptive Mushroom: Accidental Amanita muscaria Poisoning - PMC
  4. Diagnosis and Treatment of Amanita Phalloides-Type Mushroom Poisoning: Use of Thioctic Acid - PMC

question_text: All are features of organophosphorus poisoning, except:
explanation:
OP compounds usually cause miosis, not mydriasis.

Signs & symptoms of OP poisoning:

  1. Muscarinic manifestations: These symptoms can be easily remembered by the acronym SLUDGE: Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Defaecation, Gastrointestinal distress and Emesis.
    1. Bronchial tree: Bronchoconstriction, increased bronchial secretions, dyspnoea, cyanosis, pulmonary oedema.
    2. G.I.T.: Anorexia, salivation, nausea, vomiting, cramps, diarrhoea, faecal incontinence, tenesmus. Pancreatitis may develop.
    3. Sweat glands: Increased sweating.
    4. Salivary glands: Increased salivation.
    5. Lacrimal glands: Increased lacrimation.
    6. V.S.: Bradycardia or tachycardia, arrhythmias, conduction blocks, hypotension.
    7. Pupils: Miosis, occasionally unequal or dilated.
    8. Ciliary body: Blurred vision.
    9. Bladder: Urinary incontinence.
  2. Nicotinic manifestations:
    1. Striated muscle: Initial stimulus results in contraction. Later there is paralysis due to persistent depolarisation. Muscle weakness is due to accumulation of acetylcholine. Muscular fasciculations, cramps, weakness, areflexia.
    2. Sympathetic ganglia: Hypertension, tachycardia, pallor, mydriasis.
  3. CNS manifestations: Restlessness, emotional lability, headache, tremors, anxiety, drowsiness, confusion, slurred speech, ataxia, generalised weakness, coma, convulsions, depression of respiratory and cardiovascular centres.

    In some cases, only muscarinic or nicotinic or CNS effects are seen, but most cases show a combination of all three. Nicotinic effects are seen in 10 to 20% cases only.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 396.

question_text: The mechanism of action of Organophosphorus compounds on Acetylcholinesterase is by
explanation:
Organophosphorus (OP) compounds inhibit acetylcholinesterase (AChE) by forming a stable, irreversible covalent bond with the enzyme. This leads to the accumulation of acetylcholine (ACh) at synapses, resulting in continuous stimulation of cholinergic receptors.

Here's how it works:

  1. Organophosphates bind to the serine hydroxyl group in the active site of acetylcholinesterase.
  2. This binding is initially reversible but rapidly becomes irreversible due to "aging"-a chemical process that strengthens the bond between the enzyme and the organophosphate.
  3. The inhibited enzyme cannot hydrolyze acetylcholine, leading to overstimulation of both muscarinic and nicotinic receptors, which causes symptoms such as salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation (SLUD), muscle twitching, and paralysis.

The irreversible nature of this inhibition necessitates treatment with pralidoxime (2-PAM), which can reactivate acetylcholinesterase if administered before aging occurs.

Rule Out:

  1. Competitive inhibition:
    • This occurs when a compound competes directly with the substrate (acetylcholine) for the active site but does not permanently disable the enzyme. OP compounds do not merely compete but irreversibly inhibit the enzyme.
  2. Non-competitive inhibition:
    • Non-competitive inhibitors bind to a site other than the active site, altering the enzyme’s function. OP compounds directly interact with the active site of acetylcholinesterase, making this option incorrect.
  3. Reversible competitive inhibition:
    • OP compounds initially form a reversible bond, but they become irreversible due to aging. Hence, this option is incomplete and incorrect.

Key Takeaways:

  • Organophosphorus compounds inhibit acetylcholinesterase via irreversible competitive inhibition by forming a covalent bond with the enzyme.
  • This inhibition leads to an accumulation of acetylcholine, causing overstimulation of cholinergic receptors.
  • Early administration of antidotes like pralidoxime is critical to reversing the inhibition before the bond becomes permanent (aging).

question_text: The manifestations of muscarinic effects of organophosphorus poisoning are all except
explanation:
Organophosphorus poisoning causes cholinergic toxicity by inhibiting the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, leading to the accumulation of acetylcholine at synapses. The muscarinic effects of cholinergic toxicity are due to the overstimulation of muscarinic receptors. These include symptoms such as:

  1. Diuresis:
    • Organophosphates can cause increased urinary output as a result of excessive stimulation of muscarinic receptors in the kidney and bladder, leading to diuresis.
  2. Bradycardia:
    • Muscarinic stimulation typically results in slowed heart rate (bradycardia), as acetylcholine affects the vagus nerve and decreases heart rate.
  3. Bronchoconstriction:
    • Excessive stimulation of muscarinic receptors in the lungs can lead to bronchoconstriction, causing difficulty in breathing.

Rule Out:

  • Mydriasis (pupil dilation):

Mydriasis (dilated pupils) is not a muscarinic effect. In fact, excessive stimulation of muscarinic receptors typically causes miosis (constriction of pupils). Mydriasis occurs due to the sympathomimetic effect or due to drugs that block muscarinic receptors (anticholinergics), not from muscarinic overstimulation.

Key Takeaways:

  • Muscarinic effects of organophosphorus poisoning include diuresis, bradycardia, and bronchoconstriction.
  • Mydriasis (pupil dilation) is not a muscarinic effect; it is more associated with anticholinergic or sympathomimetic effects.

question_text: Ophitoxaemia is:
explanation:
Ophitoxaemia characterizes the clinical spectrum of snakebite envenomation.

Epidemiology:

Snakebite is more prevalent in rural than urban areas, commonly seen in summers, in males, farmers and mostly at night. Most of the bites are on lower extremities since the victims are bitten by treading on or near the snake.

History:

The time elapsed since the bite is important to determine if the process is confined locally or if systemic signs have developed. Obtain a description of the snake to determine its species.

Onset of symptoms and sudden progression are more common with elapidae bite rather than Viperidae. Most cobra, krait and sea snakebites would show symptoms within the first 6 hours, the shortest time is for the sea snakes. Early and intense pain implies significant envenomation.

Local signs and symptoms:

Fang marks, pain, bleeding, bruising, lymphangitis, lymph node enlargement, inflammation, blistering, local infection, abscess formation and necrosis.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition, Page No. 580

question_text: A 28-year-old male was brought to the emergency department with complaints of vomiting, altered sensorium, and shallow breathing. On examination, pupils were found to be constricted (miosis). Which of the following poisons is least likely to cause this pupillary finding?
explanation:
Explanation:

Miosis (pinpoint pupil) is a classic sign seen in several types of poisoning, especially those that stimulate the parasympathetic system or depress the central nervous system.

  • Opium (opioids) causes intense miosis due to its direct depressant effect on the midbrain (Option B).
  • Organophosphorus compounds (OPC) increase acetylcholine at muscarinic receptors, leading to miosis (Option D).
  • Phenol, though primarily a corrosive, may also cause CNS depression and miosis (Option C).
  • Paracetamol, however, does not affect pupil size. It primarily causes hepatic necrosis, and CNS signs like altered mental status, but not miosis.

question_text: Antidote for lead poisoning is:
explanation:
BAL chelating agent is used in Mercury,Arsenic &Lead poisoning.

Option A: EDTA/BAL used for Pb poisoning.

Option D: Panicillamine: antidote for copper poisoning

Option B: Deferoxamine antidote for iron toxicity

question_text: A dye factory worker presented to ER with an alleged history of burning pain in the mouth, throat & abdomen, conjunctivitis, nausea & vomiting and dark loose stools. The suspected poisoning is
explanation:
Arsenic poisoning is commonly encountered in industrial and occupational settings such as dye factories, where exposure to arsenic compounds may occur. The clinical presentation described aligns closely with the effects of acute arsenic poisoning.

Key Clinical Features of Arsenic Poisoning:

Burning Pain in the Mouth, Throat, and Abdomen:

Arsenic is a potent irritant to mucosal surfaces, causing severe pain along the gastrointestinal tract.

Conjunctivitis:

Arsenic exposure can irritate the eyes, leading to redness and inflammation of the conjunctiva.

Nausea and Vomiting:

A classic symptom of arsenic poisoning due to its corrosive and systemic effects.

Dark Loose Stools:

Arsenic damages the intestinal lining, leading to bloody or dark-colored diarrhea.

Other Findings (in severe cases):

Hypotension, tachycardia, renal damage, and central nervous system symptoms (encephalopathy).

In a dye factory setting, arsenic exposure can occur through ingestion, inhalation, or dermal absorption, and the symptoms observed are typical of acute toxicity.

Rule Out:

Option A: Lead

False: Lead poisoning, especially chronic, presents with anemia, abdominal colic, constipation, and neurological symptoms like wrist drop. Acute symptoms like burning pain or conjunctivitis are not characteristic of lead poisoning.

Option B: KMnO4 (Potassium Permanganate)

False: Potassium permanganate poisoning would cause caustic burns and staining of the mucosa (brown or black) rather than conjunctivitis or dark stools. It is less commonly associated with systemic toxicity symptoms like nausea or burning abdominal pain.

Option D: Phosphorus

False: Phosphorus poisoning (e.g., from yellow phosphorus in rat poison) causes a garlic-like odor in breath, luminous vomit, and liver damage. Conjunctivitis and dark loose stools are less specific for phosphorus poisoning.

Option C: Arsenic

Correct: Fits the described symptoms perfectly, including the occupational exposure in a dye factory.

Key Takeaways:

Arsenic Poisoning Features: Burning pain, gastrointestinal symptoms (vomiting, diarrhea), conjunctivitis, and systemic effects.

Occupational Risks: Dye factory workers and others exposed to industrial chemicals should be monitored for arsenic toxicity.

Differentiating Arsenic from Other Toxins: Focus on the combination of burning pain, gastrointestinal irritation, and dark stools, which are hallmark features.

Management: Includes gastrointestinal decontamination and the use of chelating agents like dimercaprol or DMSA (succimer).

Proper identification of the toxic agent is crucial for timely intervention and recovery.

question_text: A person was found dead with bluish green frothy discharge at the angle of mouth and nostrils. Probable cause can be:
explanation:
Postmortem findings in copper poisoning

  1. Skin may be yellow due to jaundice.
  2. Greenish-blue froth from the mouth and nostrils
  3. Mucous membrane of the mouth and tongue may have bluish or greenish-blue tinge.
  4. Internally, some discoloration is present in the mucous membrane of the esophagus and stomach.
  5. Stomach: Gastric mucosa is congested with desquamation and haemorrhages at places.
  6. Small intestine: Mucosa (upper part) may show necrosis.
  7. Liver: Soft and fatty. It shows centrilobular necrosis and biliary stasis.
  8. Kidneys: It may show acute proximal tubular necrosis.

Haemoglobin casts may be seen in the tubules.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition, Page No. 553, 554

question_text: Minamata Bay disease refers to chronic toxicity with:
explanation:
Explanation:

Minamata Bay disease was due to chronic organic mercury intoxication (Methyl mercury).

Minamata disease:

  • It is due to chronic organic mercury intoxication caused by eating contaminated fish and shellfish.
  • In Minamata Bay (Japan), a factory discharged inorganic mercury into the water.
  • The mercury was methylated by bacteria and subsequently ingested by fish.
  • Local villagers ate the fish and began to exhibit signs of chronic mercury poisoning.
  • Symptoms include disturbances in hand coordination, gait and speech, chewing and swallowing difficulties, visual blurring, tremors, rigidity, seizures and clouding of consciousness.

Key Takeaway:

Minamata disease is caused by chronic methylmercury poisoning from consumption of contaminated seafood.

question_text: Which of the following is the preferred treatment for Datura poisoning?
explanation:
Explanation:

Physostigmine is the antidote of choice for Datura poisoning because it acts as a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor.

Toxic Components:

Datura contains hyoscine (scopolamine), hyoscyamine, and traces of atropine.

Mechanism of Action:

Initially stimulates the brain's higher centers and motor areas, followed by depression of vital centers in the medulla, which can lead to paralysis.

Clinical Features:

  • Dry mouth and throat
  • Difficulty swallowing and talking
  • Hoarseness
  • Flushed face
  • Dilated pupils
  • Photophobia and double vision
  • Agitation and restlessness
  • Delirium
  • Urinary retention
  • Dry, hot skin
  • Skin exfoliation may occur

Severe cases may progress to coma or death due to respiratory paralysis.

Treatment:

  • Gastrointestinal Decontamination:Administer activated charcoal to absorb the toxin; use a cathartic if needed.
  • Antidote:Slow intravenous injection of Physostigmine (1-2 mg), repeated as necessary based on symptoms.
  • Symptomatic Treatment:Pilocarpine (5 mg subcutaneously) may be used for severe anticholinergic symptoms.
  • Supportive Care:Monitor vital signs closely and manage respiratory or cardiovascular complications as required.

Explanation of other options:

Neostigmine (Option D) does not cross blood brain barrier

question_text: A 3-year-old child sleeping in a hut woke up in the middle of the night screaming. Her mother thought the child had a nightmare and tried to pacify her. After some time, the child started sweating profusely and the hands became cold. She vomited a couple of times. The mother immediately rushed her to the emergency services. Her pulse was 150/minute and her BP 90/60 mm Hg. This child is likely to have:
explanation:
The history and signs & symptoms are suggestive of scorpion sting.

Action of Scorpion venom:

Scorpion venom is neurotoxic, hemotoxic and cardiotoxic, but predominantly neurotoxic. The venom is a potent autonomic stimulator, resulting in the release of massive amounts of catecholamines from the adrenals. It has also some direct effect on the myocardium.

Signs and Symptoms of scorpion sting:

In case of haemolytic venom, reaction is mainly local and simulates viperine bite, but the scorpion sting bite shows only one hole in the centre of the reddened area at the site of bite.

Neurotoxic bite simulates cobra bite.

Dysfunction of cranial nerve and hyperexcitability of skeletal muscles develop within hours.

Local:

Little swelling, but prominent radiating pain, reddening, paraesthesia, and hyperesthesia which is accentuated by tapping on the affected area (tap test).

Systemic effects

Nausea, vomiting, restlessness, fever, headache, giddiness, sweating, muscular fasciculations, jerking and shaking (may be mistaken for a seizure), slow pulse, cyanosis, convulsions, coma and respiratory depression, and death may occur from pulmonary edema or cardiac failure in children.

Complications:

Tachycardia, hypertension, arrhythmias, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, and acidosis.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition, Page No. 586, 587

question_text: All are true of organophosphorus compounds poisoning, except:
explanation:
Explanation:

Atropinization: Atropine blocks the muscarinic manifestations and has no effect on nicotinic receptors (on muscle weakness or paralysis) and does not affect the rate of regeneration of inhibited AChE.

Dose: 2-4 mg IV (0.05-0.2 mg/kg in children) repeated after every 5-15 minutes till atropinization, the dose should be adjusted to maintain this effect for at least 24 hours (maintenance dose: 0.02-0.05 mg/kg).

Anti-cholinesterase agents (Option A): Organophosphorus compounds (OPC) are irreversible acetylcholinesterase (IACh) inhibitors, causing ACh buildup.

Bradycardia (Option B): Seen due to excess acetylcholine acting on muscarinic receptors.

Paralysis (Option D): A late nicotinic effect due to persistent depolarization at neuromuscular junctions.

explanation:
INSECTICIDES:

  1. Organophosphorus(OP) compounds[OPC]
    • Alkyl phosphates → HETP, TEPP, OMPA, Malathion etc.

question_text: Hyperbaric oxygen is given in the treatment of:
explanation:
Treatment of CO poisoning consists of removal from the source of exposure, immediate administration of high-flow or 100% O2 and aggressive supportive measures.

  1. Remove the victim from the source of exposure.
  2. Maintain patent airway, fresh air and orthobaric oxygen (100% oxygen at atmospheric pressure) by tight-fitting high-flow reservoir face mask or endotracheal tube. Oxygen therapy is started if COHb > 10% and should be given for 4-6 hours. The immediate effect of oxygen is enhancement of the dissociation of COHb.
  3. The use of Hyperbaric Oxygen (HBO) is controversial.
    • Hyperbaric oxygen [HBO] - Oxygen at higher pressures, up to 3 ATA. Administer HBO for 90-120 min.
    • Benefits of HBO
      • Decreases the half-life of CO
      • Increases amount of dissolved O2 by 10 times
      • Prevents lipid peroxidation in cerebral neurons, thereby minimizing incidence of neurologic damage
      • Prevents leukocyte adherence to brain microvascular endothelium
      • Accelerates regeneration of inactivated cytochrome oxidase.
      • This is the treatment of choice in patients who present with syncope, coma, or seizure, focal neurological deficit, if COHb > 25% (or >15% in pregnancy)
  4. HBO at PO2 of 2-3 atmospheric pressure mixed with 5% CO2 may be given through mask or intratracheal tube.

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy involves breathing pure oxygen in a pressurized environment. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is a well-established treatment for decompression sickness, a potential risk of scuba diving. Other conditions treated with hyperbaric oxygen therapy include serious infections.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th Edition, Page No. 647, Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, Anil Aggrawal, Page No. 721

question_text: A 30-year-old male was brought to the emergency department after suspected cyanide poisoning in an industrial accident. The medical team initiates treatment with the standard cyanide antidote kit. Which of the following agents is NOT included in the standard cyanide antidote kit?
explanation:
Explanation:

The standard 3-step cyanide antidote kit contains:

  • 12 amyl nitrite pearls (Inhalation)
  • Two 10 ml vials of 3% sodium nitrite (I.V.)
  • Two 50 ml vials of sodium thiosulfate (I.V.)

Steps:

  1. 0.3 ml ampoule (pearl) of amyl nitrite is broken in a gauze and the victim is made to inhale for 30 seconds, every minute (1st step), and use a new pearl every 3 min. Stop amyl nitrite if systolic BP is < 80 mmHg.
  2. 10 ml of 3% solution (300 mg) of sodium nitrite is injected IV slowly over 5 min (2nd step), followed by 50 ml of 25% solution (12.5g of sodium thiosulfate over 10-20 min. by the same needle (3rd step).

These work synergistically to detoxify cyanide by forming cyanmethemoglobin and converting it into thiocyanate, which is excreted via urine.

  • Amyl nitrite and sodium nitrite induce methemoglobinemia. Methemoglobin binds cyanide more avidly than cytochrome oxidase.
  • Sodium thiosulfate acts as a sulfur donor in the presence of the mitochondrial enzyme rhodanese, facilitating the conversion of cyanide to thiocyanate.

Sodium bicarbonate is not part of the standard cyanide antidote kit. It may be used for acidosis correction but has no direct role in cyanide detoxification.

Related Important Points and Concepts:

Sodium thiosulfate (Option A): Sulfur donor; helps convert cyanide to thiocyanate.

Sodium nitrite (Option B): Produces methemoglobin which binds cyanide.

Amyl nitrite (Option D): First-line inhalational agent to induce rapid methemoglobinemia.

Key Takeaway:

Sodium bicarbonate is not a component of the cyanide antidote kit; it is only used for supportive correction of acidosis.

question_text: A 40-year-old man is rescued unconscious from the wreckage of a crashed aeroplane. He had been trapped in a confined cabin surrounded by thick smoke for over 10 minutes. On arrival at the emergency department, he is comatose with deep cherry-red discolouration of the skin. What is the primary cause of death in such cases of smoke inhalation?
explanation:
Explanation:

Victims of smoke inhalation are affected by carbon monoxide poisoning. In carbon monoxide poisoning, the cause of death is anaemic hypoxia

  • Carbon monoxide (CO) binds to haemoglobin with approximately 250 times more affinity than oxygen, forming carboxyhemoglobin.
  • This drastically reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood, despite normal oxygen partial pressure in the lungs.
  • Hence, the tissue receives less oxygen-this is classic anaemic hypoxia.
  • CO also inhibits cytochrome c oxidase in the electron transport chain, exerting a histotoxic effect, but the dominant and fatal mechanism is reduced oxygen delivery to tissues due to displaced haemoglobin function.

Explanation of Other Options:

Histotoxic hypoxia (Option A): CO inhibits cytochrome c oxidase, but this effect is secondary to impaired oxygen delivery.

Ischemic hypoxia (Option B): Involves inadequate perfusion (e.g., in shock), which is not the main mechanism here.

All the above (Option D): While multiple forms may be present, only anaemic hypoxia is the dominant and fatal mechanism.

Key Point:

While CO poisoning has histotoxic effects, the lethal hypoxia is predominantly due to anaemic hypoxia, which is why (C) is the most accurate single-best answer.

question_text: In which poisoning is cherry red hypostasis seen on post-mortem examination?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Carbon monoxide poisoning produces the classic cherry-red (cherry-pink)discoloration of skin, mucous membranes, conjunctiva, nail beds, lividity, internal organs, and blood.
  • This is due to the formation of carboxyhemoglobin, which imparts the bright red hue.
  • With decomposition, this coloration changes to dark green → brown.
  • Post-mortem features of CO poisoning:
    • Cherry-pink lividity due to carboxyhemoglobin.
    • Discoloration of internal organs (bright red).
    • Pulmonary congestion & edema with frothy lungs.
    • Brain changes: congestion, swelling, and pink discoloration of white matter.

Explanation of Other Options:

Hydrogen Sulphide (Option B):

  • Produces a rotten egg smell.
  • Blood and viscera turn greenish-purple (not cherry-red).
  • General signs of asphyxia are present.

Yellow Phosphorus (Option C):

  • Acts as a potent hepatotoxin.
  • PM findings: garlicky odour, jaundice (icterus) due to liver failure, multi-organ failure.
  • Does not cause cherry-red hypostasis.

Hydrogen Cyanide (Option D):

  • Extremely lethal poison.
  • PM findings: brick-red blood and cheeks, frothing at the mouth, dilated pupils, edematous, congested organs.
  • Color is brick-red (due to impaired tissue oxygenation), not cherry-red hypostasis.

Reference: CO

question_text: What is the cause of death in smoke inhalation?
explanation:
• Victims of smoke inhalation are affected by carbon monoxide poisoning. In carbon monoxide poisoning, the cause of death is anaemic hypoxia
  • Carbon monoxide has a higher affinity to haemoglobin compared to oxygen and hence the amount of haemoglobin available for oxygen transport is markedly reduced.
  • It displaces oxygen from its combination with haemoglobin and forms a relatively stable compound known as carboxyhemoglobin. It thus reduces the oxygen content of the blood, and hence, that of the tissues. It acts as a chemical asphyxiant and produces death due to anaemic anoxia.

References:Textbook of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology: Principles & Practice 5th edition Page no: 113; The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 101

question_text: Cyanide odour is of:
explanation:
The bitter almond odour of hydrocyanic acid may be noticed on opening the body. About 20 to 40% persons cannot smell the gas, and the ability to detect it is a sex-linked recessive trait.

In cases of suspected cyanide poisoning, the cranial cavity should be opened first, as the odour is usually well-marked in the brain tissues.

External postmortem findings in case of cyanide poisoning

  1. Smell of bitter almonds near the body.
  2. Face, lips and body surfaces show irregular pink patches, or rarely, cyanotic tinge.
  3. Bright red postmortem lividity
  4. Fine froth at the mouth.
  5. Eyes: Bright, glistening, prominent with dilated pupils.
  6. Rigor mortis appears early.
  7. Jaws are firmly closed.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th Edition, Page No. 645; The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 478

question_text: A person was found dead by his wife in his garage with his car running. Carbon monoxide gas poisoning was confirmed to be the cause of his death. What will be the colour of postmortem staining in this case?
explanation:
Explanation:

Carbon monoxide poisoning leads to formation of carboxyhemoglobin (COHb), which imparts a cherry red color to the skin and postmortem lividity.

This occurs because CO binds to hemoglobin with 250× more affinity than oxygen, forming a stable compound that gives the blood a bright red hue. This color is a forensically important clue in suspected CO poisoning cases.

Key Takeaway:

Cherry red discoloration of postmortem staining is a hallmark finding in carbon monoxide poisoning due to formation of carboxyhemoglobin.

question_text: Mechanism of cyanide poisoning is by inhibiting:
explanation:
Explanation:

Mechanism of cyanide poisoning is by inhibiting Cytochrome c oxidase

Action:

  • Cyanide inhibits the action of cytochrome c oxidase, carbonic anhydrase and probably of other enzyme systems.
  • It blocks the final step of oxidative phosphorylation and prevents the formation of ATP and its use as energy source.
  • Cyanide acts by reducing the oxygen carrying capacity of the blood, and by combining with the ferric iron atom of intracellular cytochrome c oxidase, preventing the uptake of oxygen for cellular respiration.
  • There is an interference with the intracellular oxidative processes in the tissues and it kills by creating histotoxic or cytotoxic anoxia, although the blood may contain a normal oxygen content.

DNA synthesis (Option A): Not involved in cyanide toxicity; this is affected by agents like methotrexate.

Protein synthesis (Option D): Seen with toxins like diphtheria toxin or ricin-not cyanide.

Key Takeaway:

Cyanide causes histotoxic hypoxia by inhibiting cytochrome c oxidase and halting cellular respiration.

question_text:
Which of the following substances are antidotes for cyanide poisoning?
1.Amyl nitrate
2.Sodium nitrate
3.Sodium thiosulphate
4.Benzyl thiocyanate
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Amyl nitrate: Induces methemoglobinemia, which binds cyanide to form cyanomethemoglobin.
  • Sodium nitrate: Also induces methemoglobinemia, complementing amyl nitrate's action.
  • Sodium thiosulphate: Acts as a sulfur donor, converting cyanide to thiocyanate via rhodanese.
  • Benzyl thiocyanate: Not a recognized antidote.

question_text: A 30-year-old man is found unconscious in a closed garage with the car engine running. He is brought to the emergency department with severe headache, cherry-red discoloration of the skin, and altered sensorium. Pulse oximetry is falsely normal. Arterial blood gas shows normal PaO₂. What type of hypoxia is most likely in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

Carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning leads to anaemic hypoxia by binding competitively and reversibly to hemoglobin, forming carboxyhemoglobin (COHb), which cannot carry oxygen.

  • CO has 200-250 times higher affinity for hemoglobin than oxygen.
  • This reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood, even if PaO2 remains normal.
  • Hence, tissue hypoxia occurs without an actual fall in oxygen tension-this defines anaemic hypoxia.

Although CO can inhibit cytochrome c oxidase (a feature of histotoxic hypoxia), the predominant and primary mechanism in CO poisoning is anaemic hypoxia.

Histotoxic hypoxia (Option B): Seen in cyanide poisoning, where oxygen delivery is normal, but cells can't use it due to blocked electron transport chain.

Anoxic hypoxia (Option C): Results from inadequate oxygen in the environment or blocked airways-not the mechanism here.

Stagnant hypoxia (Option D): Due to reduced blood flow (e.g., shock, heart failure), which is not applicable in this context.

Key Takeaway:

Carbon monoxide poisoning primarily causes anaemic hypoxia by reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of hemoglobin.

question_text: A patient is brought to the emergency department with greenish skin discoloration and a characteristic rotten egg odor. Which poison is the most probable cause?
explanation:
Explanation:

Hydrogen sulfide (H2S) is an extremely poisonous gas recognized by its distinctive rotten egg odor. It interferes with cellular respiration by blocking cytochrome oxidase, resembling the action of cyanide but presenting with unique clinical features.

Characteristic features of hydrogen sulfide poisoning:

  • Skin: Greenish discoloration resulting from sulfhemoglobin formation.
  • Odor: Foul, rotten egg smell characteristic of the gas.
  • Respiratory system: Intense pulmonary irritation leading to dyspnea and respiratory failure.
  • Central nervous system: Manifestations include headache, dizziness, seizures, and coma.
  • Cardiovascular system: Bradycardia, hypotension, and sudden collapse may occur.
  • Onset: Toxicity develops rapidly due to cellular hypoxia.
  • Mechanism: Inhibition of cytochrome c oxidase disrupts the electron transport chain, causing cellular hypoxiaand subsequent metabolic acidosis.

Explanation of other options:

Carbon monoxide (Option A): Produces cherry-red discoloration of the skin and mucosa, odorless gas.

Nitrite (Option B): Causes methemoglobinemia leading to chocolate-brown blood.

Cyanide (Option C): Produces pink or bright red skin and a bitter almond odor.

Key takeaways:

  • Rotten egg odor and greenish hue = Hydrogen sulfide.
  • Mechanism: inhibition of cytochrome c oxidase → tissue hypoxia.
  • Seen in sewage workers, mines, and industrial exposures.

References: H2S

question_text: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes
explanation:
CO combines reversibly with haemoglobin to form carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) producing anaemic hypoxia (Blood O2-carrying capacity is reduced).

  • It has a high affinity for Hb (about 250 times more than O2).
  • It inhibits electron transport by blocking cytochrome A3 oxidase and cytochrome P450 and hence intracellular respiration.

Anaemic hypoxia occurs when the oxygen carrying ability of the blood decreases, and thus, this defect is specifically associated with the blood. This implies that fewer hemoglobin molecules (or oxygen-binding sites) are available for binding oxygen.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th Edition, Page No. 645

question_text: A deceased individual is found to have a body temperature of 39°C during examination. What is the most likely explanation for this elevated postmortem temperature?
explanation:
Explanation

Septicemia, which is a systemic infection with widespread inflammation, is a common cause of fever in both living and deceased individuals.

  • It can cause hyperthermia due to the body's inflammatory response.
  • Elevated body temperature within the first two hours after death points toward a diagnosis of Postmortem caloricity.

Postmortem Caloricity:

  • Refers to the condition where the body temperature remains elevated for the first two hours after death.

Note: Burns do not typically cause postmortem caloricity.

Explanation for other options:

Cyanide poisoning (Option A): Cyanide poisoning typically causes rapid death and may lead to hypothermia rather than fever. Cyanide inhibits cellular respiration, leading to metabolic acidosis, but does not usually result in a fever like septicemia.

Corrosive poisoning (Option C): Corrosive poisoning (e.g., acid or alkali ingestion) can cause significant damage to tissues, but it does not typically result in a high body temperature like 39°C. It might lead to shock and other complications, but fever is not the hallmark sign.

Intra-abdominal haemorrhage (Option D): Intra-abdominal haemorrhage typically results in hypovolemic shock due to blood loss, leading to low body temperature (hypothermia) rather than fever.

question_text: A patient presents with a skin lesion as shown in the image below. Which of the following is least likely to cause it?
explanation:
The given image shows a scald injury. Burns from corrosive substances show ulcerated patches and are usually free from blisters; hair is not singed and the red line of demarcation is absent.

A ‘scald’ refers to tissue damage from hot liquids, like

  • Hot water
  • Hot oils
  • Molten rubber
  • Liquid chemicals
  • Steam.

Molten metals are usually at such a high temperature that the results are similar to dry burns.

A scald, unless from some superheated oil, does not cause charring, carbonization or singeing of surface hairs, as does dry heat. It resembles a first-degree dry burn. Scalds are sharply demarcated lesions with reddening, desquamation, and blistering.

Reference: Knight's Forensic Pathology, 4th edition, Page No. 312; The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 245

question_text: A chronic alcoholic assaulted his neighbour. He had quit drinking 4 days back but now has delirium tremens. He is:
option_b: Family is responsible for his act
explanation:
Medico-legal Aspects of delirium tremens:

  • It is a medical emergency and should be treated on an inpatient basis.
  • When a person is in delirium tremens commits any illegal act, he is not held responsible by the reason that he is considered to be mentally unsound during this state (Sec. 22 BNS).
  • 22 BNS: Act of a person of unsound mind. -Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition. Page No. 606

question_text: An alcoholic patient is brought for medical examination for alleged assault of his neighbour. On examination, abnormal behaviour with irrelevant talk is noted. He has history of abstaining from alcohol for past 4 days and is diagnosed to be a case of delirium tremens. What is true according to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhitha?
option_a: He is criminally responsible for his act
option_b: He is partially responsible for his act
option_c: Have diminished responsible for his act
option_d: Not responsible for his act under section 22 BNS
explanation:
Sec. 22 BNS: Act of a person of unsound mind.-Nothing is an offence which is done by a person who, at the time of doing it, by reason of unsoundness of mind, is incapable of knowing the nature of the act, or that he is doing what is either wrong or contrary to law.

Delirium tremens is a psychiatric condition arising as a result of abstinence from alcohol. In case of delirium tremens, he doesn't know that what is he doing. So, he is not criminally responsible for his act under section 22 BNS.

Reference: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhitha, 2023

question_text: The common preservative used for viscera to be sent for chemical analysis is
explanation:
Formalin is the most commonly used preservative for viscera (organs or body parts) that are sent for chemical analysis, particularly in cases of suspected poisoning or forensic investigations. It is a 10% solution of formaldehyde in water and acts as an excellent preservative, preventing decomposition of biological tissues and allowing accurate toxicological analysis.

Key points:

  • Formalin helps preserve the integrity of the tissues, maintaining their chemical composition for analysis.
  • It is widely used in forensic and pathological labs to store organs for post-mortem examination.
  • Formalin also helps prevent bacterial or fungal growth that could alter the chemical analysis of samples.

Rule Out:

a) Glycerine: While glycerine can be used for preserving certain specimens, it is not typically used for toxicological analysis of viscera.

c) Rectified spirit: Alcohols like rectified spirit can be used for preserving tissue in some situations but do not have the same preservative qualities for chemical analysis as formalin.

d) Supersaturated common salt solution: This solution can preserve tissues but is not typically used for toxicological analysis in forensic cases.

Key Takeaways:

  1. Formalin is the standard preservative used in forensic medicine and toxicology for preserving viscera for chemical analysis.
  2. It helps to prevent decomposition and maintain the integrity of tissues until analysis can be performed.
  3. Proper preservation of viscera is crucial for obtaining accurate results in post-mortem toxicology.

question_text: Vitamin deficiency seen in alcoholic with dementia is:
explanation:
Chronic alcoholics may have severe thiamine (Vitamin B-1) deficiency, which may give rise to a condition called Korsakoff’s psychosis which manifests with impairment of short- term memory (dementia) along with compensatory confabulation.

KORSAKOFF'S PSYCHOSIS

Korsakoff's psychosis often follows Wernicke's encephalopathy, so they are referred to as Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

Cause: Severe, untreated thiamine deficiency, secondary to chronic alcohol abuse.

Signs and Symptoms:

It presents as an organic amnestic syndrome, characterized by:

  • Inability to learn new information,
  • Impairment of short- term memory
  • Compensatory confabulation.

The pathological lesion is usually widespread, but changes are seen in bilateral dorsomedial nuclei of thalamus and mammillary bodies. The changes are also seen in periventricular and periaqueductal grey matter, cerebellum and parts of brainstem.

Sometimes, alcohol dementia may be associated with Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which is caused by long-term or excessive drinking resulting in neurological damage and impairment of memory.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition. Page No. 607

question_text: What is a Molotov cocktail?
explanation:
Molotov cocktail is an incendiary bomb that is thrown by hand.

The Molotov cocktail is an incendiary bomb which is thrown by the hand. In a crude type of this bomb, a bottle is filled with gasoline or petrol or diesel or any other flammable material and a rag to serve as a wick. The wick is lighted and thrown at the target. Various acids and chemicals are sometimes added to increase the destructive effects.

question_text: The only test to detect both choline and spermine in seminal stain is
explanation:
Florence test:

  • The stain is extracted by 1 % hydrochloric acid and a drop is placed on a glass slide.
  • A drop of Florence solution (Postassium iodine, iodine and water) is allowed to run under the cover slip.
  • If semen is present, dark-brown crystals of choline iodide appear immediately.
  • They are rhombic crystals resembling haemin.
  • A negative test means the fluid is not semen.

Barberio's test:

  • A saturated aqueous or alcoholic solution of picric acid when added to spermatic fluid, produces yellow needle shaped rhombic crystals of spermine picrate.
  • In Barberio's test, the presence of spermine in semen is detected.

The Acid phosphatase test:

  • Acid phosphatase activity of human semen per ml is 340 - 360 Bodansky units or 2500 - 3500 Angstorm units.
  • It is the most commonly used presumptive test for the detection of seminal fluid.
  • The prostatic secretion element of seminal fluid contains a very much higher percentage of acid phosphatase.

Thin layer chromatography detects both choline and spermine in seminal stain.

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th edition, Page No. 337

question_text: Which of the following test shows yellow needle shaped crystals of spermine picrate?
explanation:
Barberio's test:

  • Used to detect: Semen.
  • Stain used: Saturated aqueous or alcoholic solution of picric acid.
  • Finding: If semen is present, yellow needle-shaped rhombic crystals of spermine picrate

Florence test:

  • Used to detect: Semen.
  • Stain used: 10% hydrochloric acid and Florence solution (potassium iodide, iodine, and water)
  • Finding: If semen is present, dark brown rhombic or needle-shaped crystals of choline iodide appear immediately

Takayama test (Haemochromogen crystal test):

  • Used to detect: Bloodstains
  • Stain used: Takayama reagent (sodium hydroxide. pyridine, glucose)
  • Finding: If bloodstain is present, pink feathery crystals of hemochromogen or reduced alkaline haematin appear in a few minutes

Teichmann's test (Haemin crystal Test):

  • Used to detect: Bloodstains.
  • Stain used: Glacial acetic acid and a small crystal of sodium chloride.
  • Finding: If bloodstain is present, faint yellowish red to brownish-black rhombic crystals of haemin or haematin chloride appear

Reference: The Essentials of Forensic Medicine & Toxicology, KS Narayan Reddy, 35th Edition, Page No. 337, 349

question_text:
A person of interest in a homicide case is on the run from the police. He wishes to remove the tattoo on his left arm which is very prominent. Which of the following methods may be used for the same?
1. Surgical excision
2. Scarification with sandpaper
3. Caustic soda
4. Rubbing with isopropyl alcohol
5. Electrolysis
explanation:
Methods for deliberate tattoo removal include

  1. Surgical methods:
  • Complete excision and skin grafting
  • Production of burn by means of red hot iron
  • Scarification with sandpaper
  • Carbon dioxide snow
  1. Electrolysis
  2. Caustic substances remove pigment by producing inflammatory reaction and a superficial scar, e.g., mixture of papain in glycerine, zinc chloride and tannic acid
  3. LASER beam: By exposure to laser beams, the particles of the dye get vapourised and expelled from the tissues in gaseous form
  4. Confluent smallpox and sometimes chronic eczema in children can obliterate tattoo marks

question_text: Average fatal level of ethanol in blood in a non-addict is:
explanation:
Fatal dose of alcohol in a non-addict is:

150-250 ml of absolute alcohol consumed in 1 hour.

Risk of death is increased if Blood Alcohol Concentration (BAC) is >300mg/dl., and death is typical if the BAC is between 400-500 mg/dl.

Explanation of BAC levels:

.020 - Light to moderate drinkers begin to feel some effects

.040 - Most people begin to feel relaxed

.060 - Judgment is somewhat impaired

.080 - Definite impairment of muscle coordination and driving skills.

This is the legal intoxication level in most states.

But in India, as per Motor Vehicle Act, the permissible level of BAC is 30mg/dl

.100 - Clear deterioration of reaction time and control. This is legally drunk in all states.

.120 - Vomiting usually occurs

.150 - Balance and movement are impaired. Here the equivalent of a 1/2 pint of whiskey is circulating in the blood stream.

.200 - Most people begin to experience blackouts

.300 - Many people lose consciousness

.400 - Most people lose consciousness and some die

.450 - Breathing stops. This is a fatal dose for most people.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and Toxicology by Gautam Biswas, 5th edition, Page No. 599; https://awareawakealive.org/educate/blood-alcohol-content

question_text: According to Indian  'Motor Vehicle Act 1988', punishable quantity of alcohol in blood while driving a vehicle:
explanation:
According to Motor Vehicle Act 1988, the maximum permissible BAC while driving is 30mg/dl.

In India, driving under the influence of alcohol or drunk driving is punishable if the BAC exceeds 30mg/dl.

  • In India, according to Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act 2019, for the first offence, punishment is imprisonment up to 6 months with/without fine up to Rs. 10,000. For the subsequent offence, the punishment is up to 2 years of imprisonment with or without fine up to Rs. 15,000.
  • Under this Act, there can be arrest without warrant, a breath test and a laboratory test can also be carried out.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition. Page No. 604

question_text: Delirium tremens is seen in:
explanation:
DELIRIUM TREMENS

This is an acute organic brain syndrome, usually seen within 2-4 days of complete absence from heavy alcohol drinking in chronic alcoholics, and most severe alcohol withdrawal syndrome.

Causes

  • Sudden excess or sudden withdrawal of alcohol.
  • Long continual ingestion of alcohol.
  • Shock due to severe trauma, e.g., fracture in a chronic alcoholic.
  • Acute infections, like pneumonia or influenza in a chronic alcoholic.

Signs and Symptoms

There is an acute attack of mental illness in which there is:

  1. Clouding of consciousness with disorientation in time and space.
  2. Coarse muscular tremors of face, tongue and hands.
  3. Insomnia with reversal of sleep-wake cycle, and loss of memory.
  4. Psychomotor agitation, ataxia, uncontrollable fear, and tendency to commit suicide/homicide/violent assault or cause damage to property.
  5. Marked autonomic disturbances with tachycardia, fever, sweating, hypertension and pupillary dilatation.
  6. Peculiar type of delirium of horrors due to hallucinations of sight and hearing. Tactile hallucinations of insects and ants crawling under the skin or on the beds may occur.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition. Page No. 606

explanation:

Confabulation is pathological loss of memory. Confabulation is the creation of false memories in the absence of intentions of deception. It is seen in Korsakoff's psychosis.

KORSAKOFF'S PSYCHOSIS

Korsakoff's psychosis often follows Wernicke's encephalopathy, so they are referred to as Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

Cause: Severe, untreated thiamine deficiency, secondary to chronic alcohol abuse.

Signs and Symptoms:

It presents as an organic amnestic syndrome, characterized by:

  • Inability to learn new information,
  • Impairment of short- term memory
  • Compensatory confabulation.

The pathological lesion is usually widespread, but changes are seen in bilateral dorsomedial nuclei of thalamus and mammillary bodies. The changes are also seen in periventricular and periaqueductal grey matter, cerebellum and parts of brainstem.

Sometimes, alcohol dementia may be associated with Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which is caused by long-term or excessive drinking resulting in neurological damage and impairment of memory.

Reference: Review of Forensic medicine and toxicology, Gautam Biswas, 5th edition. Page No. 607

question_text:
A 48-year-old man with a history of chronic alcohol consumption is brought to the emergency department by his relatives. He is agitated, disoriented, and visibly tremulous. He claims to see "snakes on the wall" and feels "insects crawling under his skin." His relatives report that he had stopped drinking two days ago after continuous use for several years. On examination, he is febrile, hypertensive, diaphoretic, and has coarse tremors in both hands.
What is the most likely underlying cause of his current condition?
option_a: Sudden cessation of alcohol in a dependent individual
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient presents with classical features of delirium tremens, the most severe form of alcohol withdrawal syndrome, typically occurring 48-72 hours after abrupt cessation in dependent individuals.
Key features include:

  • Hallucinations-chiefly visual (zoopsia), and occasional auditory
  • Tactile hallucinations (formication) can also occur when a heavy drinker suddenly stops
  • Agitation, confusion, irrelevant talk, disorientation
  • Autonomic instability (fever, tachycardia, hypertension)
  • Tremors and psychomotor agitation
  • Often precipitated by stopping alcohol suddenly in long-term heavy drinkers

Explanation of other options:

Alcohol intoxication (Option B): Typically causes CNS depression, slurred speech, incoordination not hallucinations or tremors.

Hepatic encephalopathy (Option B): May cause altered sensorium but is usually accompanied by flapping tremors (asterixis) and jaundice not vivid hallucinations.

Opioid withdrawal (Option B): Causes lacrimation, yawning, mydriasis, and diarrhea-not delirium or visual hallucinations.

Key Takeaway:

Delirium tremens is triggered by abrupt cessation of alcohol in dependent individuals and is a medical emergency.

question_text: A 36-year-old male presents to the emergency department with vomiting, abdominal pain, and visual disturbances after ingesting homemade alcohol. Which of the following statements regarding methanol poisoning is NOT true?
option_a: Effects are due to formic acid
explanation:
Explanation:

Methanol is metabolized in the liver by alcohol dehydrogenase to formaldehyde, which is then converted by aldehyde dehydrogenase into formic acid. This formic acid is the toxic metabolite responsible for methanol's harmful effects, such as metabolic acidosis and damage to the optic nerve, potentially leading to blindness.

  • Fomepizole prevents the metabolism of methanol into its toxic byproducts like formaldehyde and formic acid.
  • It does this by competitively inhibiting the alcohol dehydrogenase enzyme, which is the enzyme responsible for the initial steps of methanol breakdown.
  • By blocking this enzyme, fomepizole allows the body to excrete unchanged methanol, preventing the buildup of toxic substances that cause severe metabolic acidosis and blindness
  • Fomepizole is a specific competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase, not aldehyde dehydrogenase.
  • High anion gap metabolic acidosis is a hallmark laboratory finding.
  • Blindness results from the toxic effects of formic acid on the optic nerve and retina.

Dose: Loading dose of 15 mg/kg over 30 minutes, followed by 10 mg/kg every 12 hours for 4 doses, then 15 mg/kg every 12 hours.

question_text: A 50-year-old factory worker was brought to the emergency room with complaints of headache, vomiting and blurring of vision after he consumed local spirit. Which of the following is used for the treatment of his condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Fomepizole is the drug of choice for methanol poisoning.
  • It acts as a competitive inhibitor of alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH), thereby preventing methanol metabolism into its toxic metabolites-formaldehyde and formic acid.
  • Blocking this pathway reduces systemic toxicity and protects the optic nerve from permanent damage.

Clinical Features of Methanol Poisoning:

  • Gastrointestinal: Nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea.
  • Neurological: Headache, dizziness, confusion, agitation, seizures.
  • Visual: Blurred vision, diplopia, or complete blindness due to optic nerve damage.
  • Metabolic: Severe metabolic acidosis (due to formic acid accumulation) → tachypnea, tachycardia, fatigue.
  • Respiratory: Distress, hypoxia, possible pulmonary edema in severe cases.

Explanation of Other Options:

Flumazenil (Option B):

  • Used as an antagonist of benzodiazepines (e.g., diazepam, lorazepam).
  • Indicated in benzodiazepine overdose with CNS depression.
  • Not effective for methanol poisoning.

N-acetylcysteine (Option C):

  • Antidote for paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose.
  • Works by replenishing glutathione stores and reducing NAPQI toxicity in the liver.
  • Has no role in methanol toxicity.

Naloxone (Option D):

  • Pure opioid antagonist used in opioid overdose (e.g., heroin, morphine).
  • Reverses respiratory depression and coma caused by opioids.
  • Ineffective in methanol poisoning.

Reference: Fomepizole
